title: Trees and Plants Near Power Lines in the Northern Mariana Islands
bodyText: Commonwealth utility law limits trees and plants near overhead power lines, and it can put that duty on a tenant. Nothing that can grow to more than half the height of a power line may be planted within twelve feet of it (measured along the ground from the point directly under the line), and no part of a tree or plant may come within fifteen feet of an overhead line. Private landowners, "or where appropriate, lessees or renters", must keep the trees and plants on their land in line with these limits; the utility (CUC) handles public and ancestral lands. If CUC finds a violation, it gives written notice of the problem and the proposed fix and allows 30 days to cure; it may require the owner, lessee or renter to remove the growth, charge for removing it if they can't do so safely or if it is near a main (primary) line, and add a fine of up to $300. Other violations of the chapter carry civil penalties of $5,000 to $10,000. The statute doesn't say when a lessee rather than the owner is the right person, so treat yourself as responsible unless the lease clearly gives this job to the tenant. What to do: check for trees and plants near overhead lines before the tenancy starts and at each inspection; if the tenant handles yard care, say in the lease whether that includes keeping growth clear of power lines and that the tenant must not plant trees under them; never let anyone without training cut near a live line, and call CUC instead.

title: Voucher Tenancies: Lease Approval and Move-Out Claims in the Northern Mariana Islands
bodyText: If the tenant pays part of the rent with a Housing Choice Voucher from the Northern Marianas Housing Corporation (NMHC), the Corporation's rules add steps around the lease. Before the tenancy starts, the family submits a Request for Lease Approval signed by you and the voucher holder with a copy of the proposed lease; the lease may be signed up to sixty days before the housing assistance contract but not without NMHC's approval, and NMHC approves only if the unit passes inspection, the rent is reasonable, the security deposit is approvable and the lease complies with HUD and NMHC requirements and Commonwealth law. The HUD tenancy addendum must be added to your lease word for word and controls over any conflicting term (see "edu-subsidy-habitability-proration-mp"). At the end of the tenancy, if you want to submit a damage claim against the tenant under the program, you must tell NMHC that the tenant moved out and ask for a close-out inspection within ten days of learning of the move-out (unless the housing assistance contract ended because of your own breach); NMHC's older plan (which the Law Revision Commission treats as superseded where it conflicts with the current one) says a damage claim won't be approved unless the move-out inspection is requested and done before any work starts, although the same section says there are no move-out inspections for contracts effective on or after October 2, 1995; the cautious course is not to start repairs before NMHC inspects. These steps don't change your duty to refund the balance of the deposit within ten days after the property is returned (see "edu-security-deposit-return-mp"). What to do: for a voucher tenant, send NMHC the lease before signing, keep the addendum attached, and on move-out notify NMHC and wait for its inspection before repairing, while still meeting the ten-day deposit refund.

title: Acceptable Payment Methods in the Northern Mariana Islands
bodyText: We found no Commonwealth statute, regulation or court rule that tells a residential landlord which payment methods it must accept. Northern Mariana Islands law has no rule requiring you to take cash or a card at the tenant's choice, no ban on requiring rent by electronic payment or an online platform, no ban on a surcharge for paying by card, and no rule against requiring certified funds after a returned payment. The Commonwealth's legal tender is U.S. currency, but that does not make you accept any particular method. So the lease sets the methods: list them in the "Acceptable Payment Methods" clause and change them only on written notice. Cautious course: we treat the Consumer Protection Act as reaching residential leasing, and it bars unfair or deceptive practices, so if you charge a fee for one method (for example a card convenience fee), state the fee in the lease, keep it to your actual processing cost, and keep at least one method that carries no fee. Federal housing-program rules may set payment terms for subsidized units; follow the program's rules there.

title: Algorithmic Rent Setting in the Northern Mariana Islands
bodyText: We found no Commonwealth statute, regulation or court rule that mentions setting rents with an algorithm or pricing software. But Northern Mariana Islands law has a general restraint-of-trade statute: it is illegal for one or more persons to create or use a combination whose effect is to restrict trade or commerce or to fix prices to the public, an agreement that does so is void to that extent, a violation is a misdemeanor (fine of $50 to $5,000), and a person injured in business or property may sue for three times the damages plus attorney's fees. The statute mostly speaks of merchandise and commodities, and no court decision we searched says whether it reaches rents, so treat it as able to reach coordinated rent-setting. Federal antitrust law (the Sherman Act) also bans contracts, combinations and conspiracies in restraint of trade, including in the territories, as a felony; whether and how it reaches the CNMI hasn't been settled here, so assume it does. Cautious course: set your rents and lease terms yourself. Don't agree with other landlords on rents, concessions or terms, don't share your nonpublic rent, occupancy or lease data with competing landlords, and don't use a pricing service that pools competitors' nonpublic data to recommend rents. Using public market data, or software that works only from your own data, is the safer path.

title: Application Fees in the Northern Mariana Islands
bodyText: We found no Commonwealth statute, regulation or court rule that caps, bans or regulates the application or screening fee a private residential landlord charges, requires a refund when the unit goes to someone else, requires written screening criteria in advance, or makes you screen applicants in a set order. So the fee and your screening process are your choice, with these limits from other law. Treat the Consumer Protection Act as reaching residential leasing: state the fee and what it covers in writing before you take it, charge no more than a reasonable amount tied to your actual screening cost, and refund it if you don't screen the applicant. Don't use your screening criteria to exclude or treat anyone differently because of race, color, religion, creed, sex, familial status, marital status, disability, national origin, ethnic background, age, citizenship, or place of birth or residence. If you take money to hold a unit or secure the lease (beyond the screening cost), treat it as a security deposit and refund the balance within ten days after the tenancy ends or the deal falls through. If you turn down an applicant, or ask for a larger deposit or a co-signer, because of anything in a credit or background report, federal law requires you to tell the applicant: give notice of the decision, any credit score you used, the name, address and phone number of the reporting agency, a statement that the agency didn't make the decision and can't explain it, and notice of the applicant's right to a free copy of the report within 60 days and to dispute it. For NMHC or Section 8 units, follow the program's own rules.

title: Application of Payments in the Northern Mariana Islands
bodyText: We found no Commonwealth statute, regulation or court rule that sets the order in which you must apply a tenant's payment among rent, late fees and other charges. The lease decides: the "Application of Payments" clause applies each payment to the oldest unpaid rent first, then to other charges, unless the tenant directs otherwise in writing. Applying payments to rent first is also the cautious course, because the three-day notice for nonpayment under the Holdover Tenancy Act is about unpaid rent, and a ledger that moves rent money to fees can make it look as if rent is unpaid when it is not. Keep a written ledger showing how you applied each payment, and give the tenant a copy on request. Public-land leases from the Department of Public Lands follow that agency's own rules; they do not apply to a private landlord.

title: Collection Fees in the Northern Mariana Islands
bodyText: Northern Mariana Islands law limits what can be added to a tenant's past-due debt when a collection agency collects it. The Commonwealth's Fair Debt Collection Practices Act covers anyone who regularly collects debts owed to someone else, and also a landlord who collects its own debts under a name that suggests a third party is collecting. A debt collector may not collect interest or any fee, charge or expense on top of the amount owed unless the agreement that created the debt (the lease) expressly authorizes it and it is legally chargeable, may collect its own fee only if it is reasonably related to the work done and legally collectable from the tenant, and may not claim that fees can be added when they cannot. You, collecting in your own name, are not a "debt collector" under the Act, but if you plan to use a collection agency, put an express collection-cost term in the lease (see "collection-fee-mp"), keep the charge tied to the real cost, and don't let the agency add anything the lease does not authorize. In a possession case under the Holdover Tenancy Act, the winning side, landlord or tenant, may recover reasonable court costs and attorney's fees.

title: Money Due at Signing in the Northern Mariana Islands
bodyText: We found no Commonwealth statute, regulation or court rule that limits what you may collect when the lease is signed: no cap on the security deposit, no limit on collecting first and last month's rent, and no list of permitted move-in charges. Unless the lease says otherwise, rent is due at the start of each rental period without demand. List every amount due at signing, and when it is due, in the "Due at Signing" clause. Two limits from other law: money held as security is a security deposit, so refund its balance within ten days after the property is returned; and if a servicemember tenant lawfully ends the lease under federal law, refund rent paid in advance for any period after the termination date within 30 days. Keep move-in charges reasonable and stated in the lease, since the Consumer Protection Act (which we treat as reaching residential leasing) bars unconscionable terms.

title: Fee Transparency in the Northern Mariana Islands
bodyText: We found no Commonwealth statute, regulation or court rule that requires you to advertise or state rent as a single all-in figure, to list fees on the first page of the lease, to itemize mandatory fees, or to follow special rules for a lease that renews automatically. (The CNMI's all-in pricing rule applies only to rental cars.) Two general rules still apply. It is a crime to advertise or make a statement about property you are offering that you know, or should know, is untrue or misleading; and the Consumer Protection Act, which we treat as reaching residential leasing, bars unfair or deceptive practices and misstating a tenant's rights or obligations. Cautious course: state every required fee, with its amount or how it is figured, in the lease; don't charge a fee the lease doesn't state; make sure any rent you advertise matches what the tenant will actually pay each month, or say which mandatory charges are extra; and if the lease renews automatically, say so plainly next to the notice the tenant must give to stop it.

title: Fees for Services Not Provided in the Northern Mariana Islands
bodyText: We found no Commonwealth statute, regulation or court rule that specifically bars you from charging a fee for a service you don't provide (for example an amenity, trash pickup or a utility the tenant doesn't receive). But the Consumer Protection Act, which we treat as reaching residential leasing, makes it unlawful to represent that something was supplied as promised when it was not and to engage in any unfair or deceptive practice, and a tenant who wins can recover actual damages, an equal amount again for a wilful violation, and attorney's fees. Cautious course: charge a service or amenity fee only for a service the tenant actually receives; describe each one in the lease (the "Services and Utilities Provided" clause lists what you provide); and stop or credit the fee for any period the service is not available.

title: Fees as Rent in the Northern Mariana Islands
bodyText: We found no Commonwealth statute, regulation or court rule that defines "rent" for a residential lease or says whether fees the lease calls "additional rent" count as rent. That matters because the quick route for nonpayment under the Holdover Tenancy Act is a three-day written notice demanding "the rent" or possession; other breaches use the lease's own cure rule or, if the lease is silent, a 15-day written notice to cure or leave. No court decision we searched says whether a fee can be folded into the three-day notice. Cautious course: put only the unpaid rent in a three-day notice; collect late fees, damage charges and other fees separately, by a written demand, a 15-day notice to cure, or a money claim in court. Don't rely on a lease sentence turning fees into rent to shorten the notice. For NMHC public housing or Section 8 units, follow the program's rules on what may be charged and how.

title: Government Fees on Rentals in the Northern Mariana Islands
bodyText: The main government fee on a residential rental in the CNMI is the Division of Building Safety's annual inspection fee for the Certificate of Compliance that apartments and residential rentals (including single-family houses) must have; it is paid to the CNMI Treasury before the inspection is scheduled. If you are in the business of renting, you may also need a Commonwealth business licence, which carries its own fee. We found no Commonwealth statute or regulation that bars or limits passing a government fee on to a tenant, so you may do it only if the lease says so: use the optional "government-fee-reimbursement-mp" clause, which covers the annual inspection fee and excludes fines, permit fees and reinspection fees caused by your own violations. A fee you have not agreed with the tenant in the lease should not be added later. Local fees set by a senatorial-district local law may also apply; check with the municipality.

title: Government Fines and Tenants in the Northern Mariana Islands
bodyText: We found no Commonwealth statute, regulation or court rule that bars you from passing a government fine to your tenant, or that limits a pass-through to fines the tenant caused. So the lease decides: you may require the tenant to reimburse a fine or abatement cost caused by the tenant, a household member or a guest, but only if the lease says so. Cautious course: don't pass on a fine that results from your own failure (for example a building-code or certificate violation you were responsible for), since a one-sided term like that could be attacked as unconscionable under the Consumer Protection Act, which we treat as reaching residential leasing. Some laws fine an owner or lessee directly: under the Cannabis Act, an owner or lessor who knowingly lets premises be used to make, sell or give away marijuana unlawfully, or as a place to use it unlawfully, commits a violation, and a building whose owner knowingly lets it be used to make, sell or possess marijuana unlawfully can be subject to a lien for the occupants' fines; and Saipan's scrap-metal local law fines an owner or lessee who doesn't remove scrap metal. Act promptly on any unlawful use you know about, and check local laws for your island. The clause "tenant-caused-fines-as" is available for the lease.

title: Late Fees in the Northern Mariana Islands
bodyText: We found no Commonwealth statute, regulation or court rule that caps a late fee on residential rent, requires a grace period, requires notice before you collect a late fee, or says that accepting late rent waives your rights. So the amount and grace period are set by the lease (the "Late Fee" clause). The limit to watch is the usury law: no court will enforce interest above 1% a month on a contract involving a principal sum over $300 (2% a month where the principal sum is $300 or less), and receiving more than 2% a month for forbearing to collect money is a crime. Whether a late fee counts as interest under those rules is unsettled, so take the cautious course: charge a single, reasonable late fee once for each late payment, sized to your real costs of handling it; don't add a daily or compounding late charge; and keep any interest on unpaid amounts at or below 1% a month. Put the fee in the lease, because a collection agency may not add a fee the lease doesn't expressly authorize. State the grace period in calendar days and say what happens if the last day is a weekend or holiday; court time-counting rules apply to statutes, not to your lease. For NMHC or Section 8 units, follow the program's rules on late charges.

title: Late Fee Limits in the Northern Mariana Islands
bodyText: We found no Commonwealth statute, regulation or court rule that caps a residential late fee, whether as a percentage of rent or a dollar amount, and none that sets a different cap for subsidized or older tenants. The only outside limit is the usury law, and it is unsettled whether it reaches a late fee; see "edu-late-fee-mp" for the cautious course (one reasonable fee per late payment, no daily or compounding charge, any interest at or below 1% a month).

title: Lease-Type Parity in the Northern Mariana Islands
bodyText: We found no Commonwealth statute, regulation or court rule that requires the same terms for month-to-month and fixed-term tenants, bars charging more for a month-to-month tenancy, or caps the difference. The Holdover Tenancy Act only sets defaults: if the lease doesn't state its length, it runs by the rent period (monthly rent makes a month-to-month tenancy), and unless the lease says otherwise either side may end a month-to-month tenancy by written notice at least 15 days before the end of a monthly period. So you may offer different rents or terms for different lease lengths. Apply each option the same way to every applicant, and don't steer anyone to a lease type because of a protected characteristic such as familial status, disability, national origin or age.

title: Time Limits for Lawsuits in the Northern Mariana Islands
bodyText: Northern Mariana Islands law gives a landlord six years from the date a claim arises to sue for unpaid rent, damage to the property or other money owed under the lease, because such claims fall under the general six-year limit. Claims for personal injury have two years. If the tenant has made partial payments on an account, the claim is treated as arising at the time of the last item proved in the account, so the six years run from then. Time the tenant spends living outside the Commonwealth after the claim arises doesn't count. The lease can't shorten or lengthen these periods: any agreement for a different limitation period is invalid, so don't put one in the lease. Claims against you have their own limits too: a Consumer Protection Act claim has four years, and a fair housing complaint has one year to the agency and two years to sue in court. Keep your rent ledger, lease and move-out records for at least six years after the tenancy ends.

title: Rent Concessions in the Northern Mariana Islands
bodyText: We found no Commonwealth statute, regulation or court rule on rent concessions (free months, move-in credits, reduced rent for a period). So a concession is whatever the lease says: describe it, with its amount and the months it covers, in the "Rent Concession" clause, so there is no later dispute about the rent actually owed. Watch the price-freeze law: while a Governor's price freeze is in effect it is a felony to raise housing rent, and EO 2026-020 (Sept. 23, 2026) kept the April 2026 freeze in effect for Rota; a freeze ends when the Governor rescinds it or the emergency declaration ends, so check the Governor's current orders (governor.cnmi.gov) to see whether it still is. If a concession is set to end while a freeze is in effect for your island, the tenant's payment would go up; the cautious course is to keep the concession going until the freeze ends. State the full Monthly Rent in the lease and describe the concession as a reduction from it.

title: Rent Control and Price Freezes in the Northern Mariana Islands
bodyText: The CNMI has no rent control or rent stabilization: no Commonwealth statute or regulation caps rent or rent increases in ordinary times, requires rental registration, or protects tenants who pay with a housing voucher, and we found no law letting a municipality regulate rents. The one rent limit is the emergency price-freeze law. When the Governor declares typhoon condition two, tropical storm condition one, or a state of significant emergency or major disaster, the Governor may declare a price freeze, and while it lasts housing rentals, including apartments and condos, are frozen; raising rent is a felony (fine up to $10,000, up to a year in prison, or both) and carries a civil penalty of up to $2,500 per violation. EO 2026-020 (Sept. 23, 2026) kept the April 2026 freeze in effect for Rota; a freeze ends when the Governor rescinds it or the emergency declaration ends, so check the Governor's current orders (governor.cnmi.gov) to see whether it still is. Before raising rent, or letting a scheduled increase take effect, check whether a freeze covers your island (the Governor's executive orders are posted at governor.cnmi.gov). The lease's rent-increase clauses ("rent-increase-midterm-mp", "rent-escalation-mp") already pause increases during a freeze. NMHC Section 8 units follow the program's rent rules, and senatorial-district local laws may add requirements.

title: Demand for Rent in the Northern Mariana Islands
bodyText: Unless the lease says otherwise, rent is due at the start of each rental period without any demand or notice from you, and it can be prorated by the day. But before you can have a tenant removed for not paying rent, you must give a written three-day demand: a notice requiring payment of the rent or possession of the premises within 3 days, not counting Saturdays, Sundays and legal holidays, in substantially the form the Holdover Tenancy Act prescribes, with the amount owed, the property address, the deadline date, and your name, address and telephone number. Serve it by handing a copy to the tenant, or, if the tenant is not at the property, by leaving a copy there. The lease can't shorten that period or change the form or the way it is served. The notice gives the tenant the choice to pay or leave; accept full payment made within the three days. If the tenant does neither, you may file for possession in the Superior Court.

title: Rent Increases During the Term in the Northern Mariana Islands
bodyText: If you want the rent to change during a fixed term, the lease must say so: use the optional "rent-escalation-mp" clause for scheduled or index-based increases, or "rent-increase-midterm-mp" for an increase on written notice. Both stop any increase from taking effect while a Governor's price freeze is in effect for your island; raising housing rent during a freeze is a felony, and EO 2026-020 (Sept. 23, 2026) kept the April 2026 freeze in effect for Rota; a freeze ends when the Governor rescinds it or the emergency declaration ends, so check the Governor's current orders (governor.cnmi.gov) to see whether it still is. We found no Commonwealth statute that bars retaliatory rent increases in general or that gives a landlord a safe harbour for increases written into the lease. But it is unlawful to threaten or interfere with anyone for exercising fair housing rights, and the common-law rules CNMI courts follow may protect tenants who complain about conditions. So don't time or size an increase to punish a complaint, a repair request or a fair housing claim, and keep a written record of the business reason for each increase.

title: Rent Increase Notice in the Northern Mariana Islands
bodyText: We found no Commonwealth statute or regulation that sets how much notice you must give before raising rent. For a fixed-term lease, rent can change during the term only as the lease allows (see the optional clauses "rent-escalation-mp" and "rent-increase-midterm-mp"). For a periodic tenancy, the law's notice rule is the one for ending the tenancy, which applies unless the lease sets its own: written notice at least 15 days before the end of a monthly period, 7 days before the end of a weekly period, 30 days before the end of a quarter, or 60 days before the end of a yearly period. Cautious course: give written notice of an increase at least that far ahead, effective on the first day of a new rental period, and keep a copy. Never raise rent, or let an increase take effect, while a Governor's price freeze is in effect for your island: it is a felony, and EO 2026-020 (Sept. 23, 2026) kept the April 2026 freeze in effect for Rota; a freeze ends when the Governor rescinds it or the emergency declaration ends, so check the Governor's current orders (governor.cnmi.gov) to see whether it still is. For NMHC voucher units, follow the program's rules: the housing agency reviews the rent for reasonableness before an increase to the owner.

title: Rent Installments in the Northern Mariana Islands
bodyText: Northern Mariana Islands law lets the lease decide when rent is paid. Unless the lease says otherwise, rent for each period is due at the start of the period without demand, and it can be prorated by the day. So you may agree to split the monthly rent into installments (for example half on the 1st and half on the 15th): use the "Rent Installments" clause and state each amount and due date. Installments paid on that schedule are not partial payments, and a late fee should apply only to an installment that is actually late. Because a lease that says nothing about its length runs by the rent period, state the lease term separately so a twice-a-month schedule isn't read as a half-month tenancy. If an installment goes unpaid, the three-day nonpayment notice demands the unpaid rent then due.

title: Paying Rent in the Northern Mariana Islands
bodyText: Unless the lease says otherwise, rent is due at the beginning of each rental period without any demand or notice from you, and rent can be prorated by the day (useful for a first or last partial month). The lease may set a different due date or schedule; the "Rent Payment" clause states the monthly rent, requires payment in advance without deduction or setoff except as the law allows, and moves a due date that falls on a weekend or legal holiday to the next business day. We found no Commonwealth statute that lets a tenant withhold rent, pay it into escrow, or repair and deduct. Courts in the CNMI follow the common law where no statute speaks, and it may let a tenant reduce rent for serious defects you fail to fix, so keep the property in good repair and respond to repair requests in writing before treating a short payment as a default.

title: Rent Receipts in the Northern Mariana Islands
bodyText: We found no Commonwealth statute or regulation written for landlords that requires a rent receipt, and no rule that makes a missing receipt a defense to an eviction or presumes earlier months paid from a later receipt. But the Sales Receipt Act of 2002 requires every person who receives gross revenue from a sale in the Commonwealth to give the payer a receipt, and rent received in the course of a business counts as gross revenue for tax purposes. Whether renting a home is a "sale" under that Act is unsettled. The penalties are real (fines of $350, $750, then $1,500 with a six-month business licence revocation), so if you rent as a business, take the cautious course: give a numbered written or printed receipt for every rent payment, however paid, showing your business name, the date, what was paid for (for example "Rent, unit 2B, May 2026"), the amount and the payment method, and keep a copy for at least six years. Receipts also protect you in any dispute about what was paid.

title: Rent Reporting in the Northern Mariana Islands
bodyText: We found no Commonwealth statute, regulation or court rule on rent reporting: nothing requires you to offer positive rent reporting, nothing bars you from reporting on-time or late rent, and nothing requires advance notice to the tenant before you report. If a collection agency collects a debt for you, the Commonwealth's Fair Debt Collection Practices Act lets it report the debt to a credit reporting agency, but treats a false report that a tenant is wilfully refusing to pay a just debt as illegal coercion. Cautious course: report only amounts that are actually owed and not genuinely in dispute, tell the tenant in writing before you or your agency report a debt, correct any error promptly, and state in the lease if you report rent payments. If you report rent yourself, federal law also applies to you: don't report anything you know or have reasonable cause to believe is wrong, and don't keep reporting an item after the tenant tells you, at the address you give for such notices, that it is wrong and it is in fact wrong. Giving tenants a clear address for disputes is the safer practice.

title: Taxes on Rent in the Northern Mariana Islands
bodyText: There is no sales tax on residential rent in the CNMI, so an ordinary long-term lease carries no tax that you add to the tenant's rent. Short stays are different: a 15% occupancy tax applies to anyone who occupies a room or unit, including an apartment, condominium or private residence, for less than 90 consecutive days. The owner or manager must collect it from the occupant and file a monthly return and pay it by the 20th of the following month. If you rent month to month and a tenant stays less than 90 days, or you rent short-term (for example through Airbnb), check with the Division of Revenue and Taxation whether you must collect it. Separately, you pay tax on your rent: the business gross revenue tax if you rent in the course of a business (no tax if your total yearly gross revenue is $5,000 or less; above that, the rate applies to the whole amount), or the earnings tax on half of your net rental income if you don't. You may build those costs into the rent, but don't add a new tax charge during the term unless the lease allows it, and never during a Governor's price freeze.

title: Listing Required Fees in the Northern Mariana Islands
bodyText: We found no Commonwealth statute, regulation or court rule that requires a residential lease to list every fee, or that sets a notice period before you add a new one. But a fee the lease doesn't mention is hard to collect: a collection agency may not add any fee or charge that the lease does not expressly authorize, and a surprise fee could be attacked as unfair or deceptive under the Consumer Protection Act, which we treat as reaching residential leasing. So list every fee you may charge in the lease (what it is for, the amount or how it is figured, and when it is due), and don't add a new fee during the term without the tenant's written agreement. Never add or raise a fee while a Governor's price freeze is in effect for your island. The clause "fees-and-charges-vi" lists the Lease's fees in one place.

title: Returned Payments in the Northern Mariana Islands
bodyText: If a tenant's rent check bounces for lack of funds, the CNMI Bad Checks Act gives you a statutory remedy. Send the tenant a written demand, delivered personally or by certified mail to the address on the check, for the check amount plus any lawful bank charges. If the tenant doesn't pay within 30 days, you can sue (small claims court is allowed) for the check amount plus 12% a year interest or, if your demand carried the conspicuous treble-damages notice the statute prescribes, three times the check amount (at least $50 and at most $750 per check), plus pre-judgment attorney's fees of $125 to $250 per check if the demand also carried the statute's attorney-fee notice. Copy both notices word for word from 7 CMC § 2442 into your demand letter. Separately, the lease may set a reasonable returned-payment fee (no statute caps it) and may require certified funds after a returned payment; state the fee as a dollar amount in the lease. Accepting a post-dated check doesn't take away the civil remedy, but the criminal presumption of intent to defraud doesn't apply to post-dated checks.

title: Government Shutdowns and Rent in the Northern Mariana Islands
bodyText: We found no Commonwealth statute, regulation or court rule that delays rent, bars late fees, or limits eviction or credit reporting for federal or Commonwealth government workers who miss pay because of a government shutdown, furlough or austerity cut in hours. The lease's ordinary rent and late-fee terms apply. If a tenant tells you a shutdown has interrupted their pay, consider agreeing in writing to a short payment plan or waiving the late fee; a written agreement avoids later disputes about whether the default was excused. Servicemembers on active duty have separate federal protections.

title: Statutory Caps on Charges in the Northern Mariana Islands
bodyText: We found no Commonwealth statute, regulation or court rule that caps what a private residential landlord charges: no rent cap in ordinary times, no security-deposit cap, and no cap on application, late, pet, key, cleaning or other fees. The limits that do apply are these. Interest: no court will enforce interest above 1% a month on a contract involving a principal sum over $300 (2% a month where the principal sum is $300 or less), and receiving more than 2% a month for forbearing to collect money is a crime. Bounced checks: the statutory treble-damages award is at least $50 and at most $750 per check. Emergencies: during a Governor's price freeze you may not raise rent at all. Without a statutory cap, keep every charge reasonable and stated in the lease, because the Consumer Protection Act (which we treat as reaching residential leasing) bars unconscionable terms, and refund the balance of any security deposit within ten days after the property is returned. NMHC and Section 8 units follow program rent limits.

title: Subsidy Abatement for Failed Inspections in the Northern Mariana Islands
bodyText: If you rent to an NMHC voucher (Section 8) tenant, NMHC inspects the unit against federal Housing Quality Standards. Federal and NMHC rules require you to maintain the unit to those standards and, after written notice of a deficiency, to fix a life-threatening one within 24 hours and any other within 30 calendar days (unless NMHC approves more time). If you don't, NMHC stops paying its share of the rent starting the first of the next month, and after six months of abatement the assistance contract ends automatically. During an abatement you may not collect the missing subsidy from the tenant: under the NMHC rules and the federal voucher regulations the tenant owes only the tenant's share, NMHC's failure to pay is not a lease violation by the tenant, and you may not end the tenancy because NMHC stopped paying. The HUD tenancy addendum, which must be in your lease word for word, overrides any lease term to the contrary. Fix deficiencies within the deadlines, keep repair records, and talk to NMHC early if parts or contractors are delayed. If the tenant, a household member or a guest caused the deficiency (beyond ordinary use), tell NMHC: it may waive your duty to fix it, and if it does, it may not withhold or abate your payment; the family must then fix it within the same 24-hour or 30-day deadlines, and the program can end the family's assistance. For tenants without a subsidy, no Commonwealth statute sets a rent reduction for an unfit unit, but the courts' common-law rules may, so fix serious defects promptly.

title: Late Fees for Subsidized Tenants in the Northern Mariana Islands
bodyText: We found no Commonwealth statute or regulation that sets a special late-fee rule for subsidized tenants. For NMHC voucher (Section 8) units, though, the NMHC rules and the federal voucher regulations limit what you may collect from the family: only the tenant's share, never the part the subsidy covers, and the housing agency's failure to pay is not the tenant's lease violation. So charge a late fee, if one is in the written lease and the program allows it, only when the tenant's own share is late, measure it on that share, and never charge the tenant because NMHC's payment was late or abated. Any change to add a fee must be in writing, with a copy to NMHC, and the HUD tenancy addendum in your lease overrides any conflicting lease term, so check it before charging a fee. For other subsidized housing, follow the program's rules. The general late-fee guidance in "edu-late-fee-mp" also applies.

title: Tax and Insurance Pass-Throughs in the Northern Mariana Islands
bodyText: We found no Commonwealth statute that regulates passing tax or insurance increases on to a residential tenant, and the Commonwealth has no general real property tax (a senatorial district may levy one by local law). So a pass-through exists only if the lease creates it. Use the optional "tax-insurance-escalation-mp" clause, which leads with property insurance (including typhoon coverage), states the tenant's percentage share, requires written notice with the bill and your calculation, credits back any later reduction, and pauses any new charge while a Governor's price freeze is in effect for your island. A pass-through raises what the tenant pays for housing, so it must not take effect during a freeze; EO 2026-020 (Sept. 23, 2026) kept the April 2026 freeze in effect for Rota; a freeze ends when the Governor rescinds it or the emergency declaration ends, so check the Governor's current orders (governor.cnmi.gov) to see whether it still is.

title: Interest on Unpaid Amounts in the Northern Mariana Islands
bodyText: We found no Commonwealth statute that gives a landlord interest on unpaid rent or damages before judgment (whether a court would award it under the common law is unsettled; case law not searched), so put it in the lease if you want it. If it does, keep the rate within the usury law: no court will enforce interest above 1% a month on a contract involving a principal sum over $300 (2% a month where the principal sum is $300 or less), excess interest you collect is credited to the principal, and receiving more than 2% a month is a crime. Once a court enters a money judgment, the judgment bears interest at 3% a year by statute. A collection agency may add interest only if the lease expressly authorizes it. Use the optional "unpaid-damages-interest-mp" clause: simple interest at no more than 1% a month, starting a stated number of days after the amount is due, with no interest on late fees or on interest.

title: Move-In and Move-Out Inspections in the Northern Mariana Islands
bodyText: We found no Commonwealth statute, regulation or court rule that requires a move-in or move-out inspection, a written condition checklist, a joint walk-through, or a signed damage list, and none that makes a tenant lose a claim by failing to sign or dispute a list. But you must refund the balance of the security deposit within ten days after the property is returned (a fine of up to $1,000 per violation applies), and without a record of the unit's condition at move-in you will have trouble showing which damage the tenant caused. Cautious course: inspect the unit with the tenant at move-in, record its condition in writing with dated photos, have both of you sign and give the tenant a copy; offer a walk-through at move-out; and keep the records with the lease. The clauses "existing-condition" and "move-in-condition-report-as" are available for the lease. NMHC voucher units also go through NMHC's own inspections.

title: Deposit Deduction Schedules in the Northern Mariana Islands
bodyText: We found no Commonwealth statute, regulation or court rule that lists what you may deduct from a security deposit, lets or forbids a lease to set fixed cleaning or carpet-cleaning charges in advance, or requires a special notice for such a schedule. The law only requires you to refund the balance of the deposit within ten days after the property is returned. So deductions are set by the lease: limit them to unpaid amounts and to damage beyond normal wear and tear, as the "Use of Security Deposit" clause does. If you want a pre-set charge (for example for professional carpet cleaning), state it in the lease, keep it close to the real cost, and charge it only when the work is actually needed and done; a flat charge unrelated to cost could be attacked as unconscionable under the Consumer Protection Act. Give the tenant a written list of each deduction with the refund.

title: Unclaimed Deposit Refunds in the Northern Mariana Islands
bodyText: We found no Commonwealth unclaimed-property law that applies to landlords: no rule makes an unclaimed deposit refund "abandoned" after a set time, requires you to report it or turn it over to the government, or lets you keep it. The deposit law requires you to refund the balance within ten days after the property is returned (a fine of up to $1,000 per violation applies). So send the refund within ten days to the forwarding address the tenant gives you or, if none, to the tenant's last known address, and keep proof of mailing. If the refund comes back or the check is never cashed, keep the money for the tenant, record your efforts to reach them, and pay it when they ask. Don't put a clause in the lease that forfeits an unclaimed refund to you.

title: Deposit Installments in the Northern Mariana Islands
bodyText: We found no Commonwealth statute, regulation or court rule that gives a tenant the right to pay a security deposit in installments. You may require the full deposit at signing, or agree to installments: if you do, list each installment and its due date in the "Due at Signing" clause, and say whether a missed installment is a default like unpaid rent (it is not rent, so use the lease's ordinary breach notice, not the three-day rent notice). Whatever is paid is a security deposit, and its balance is refunded within ten days after the property is returned.

title: Deposit and Last Month's Rent in the Northern Mariana Islands
bodyText: We found no Commonwealth statute, regulation or court rule on using a security deposit as the last month's rent. Unless the lease or a written agreement allows it, the tenant still owes the last month's rent, and you keep the deposit until the property is returned and then refund its balance within ten days. If you collect last month's rent in advance, label it as prepaid rent in the lease (not as part of the deposit) and apply it to the last month. Federal law requires a refund, within 30 days, of rent paid in advance for any period after a servicemember tenant lawfully ends the lease.

title: Deposit Refund After Move-Out in the Northern Mariana Islands
bodyText: Your ten days to refund the balance of the security deposit start when the property is returned to you. We found no Commonwealth statute that defines when a rental is "returned", requires the tenant to give you a forwarding address, or requires you to send a private tenant a notice or itemized list of deductions. Cautious course: count the ten days from the day the tenant moves out and gives up possession, even if keys come back later (handing back the keys, or a written confirmation that they have left, is good evidence of that day, but don't wait for either if you know they have gone); ask for a forwarding address in writing at move-out; and send the refund, with a written list of each amount kept and why, within ten days. The lease clause "security-deposit-return-mp" sets this out. For NMHC project-based voucher units the program requires the written list of deductions and a prompt refund of the balance.

title: Domestic Violence and Deposit Timing in the Northern Mariana Islands
bodyText: We found no Commonwealth statute, regulation or court rule that lets a victim of domestic violence end a residential lease early, so there is also no special rule on when the deposit is refunded after such a termination. The ordinary rule applies: refund the balance within ten days after the property is returned. If one co-tenant leaves because of abuse and others stay, the property hasn't been returned yet; if you agree in writing to release the departing tenant, settle in that agreement how that tenant's share of the deposit will be handled. A court may order an abuser to repay a victim's rental-housing deposits as restitution. For federally assisted housing (including NMHC voucher and tax-credit units), federal law bars treating the abuse as a lease violation by the victim and lets you split the lease to remove only the abuser.

title: Resolving Deposit Disputes in the Northern Mariana Islands
bodyText: We found no Commonwealth statute, regulation or court rule that sets a special fast-track procedure for security-deposit disputes or lets you settle the deposit early, for example when a tenant abandons the unit. The ordinary rule applies: refund the balance within ten days after the property is returned (a fine of up to $1,000 per violation applies), with a written list of anything you keep. If you and the tenant disagree, either of you may use the Superior Court's small claims procedure for claims of $5,000 or less (not counting interest, fees and costs), which is designed to be quicker and less formal, and parties often appear without a lawyer. If a tenant appears to have abandoned the unit, confirm it in writing before treating the property as returned.

title: Fees in Lieu of a Deposit in the Northern Mariana Islands
bodyText: We found no Commonwealth statute, regulation or court rule on fees, bonds or insurance offered in place of a security deposit. You may offer one, but take care: money a tenant pays to secure the lease is treated as a security deposit, refundable within ten days after the property is returned, whatever the lease calls it. If you offer a true nonrefundable fee in place of a deposit, tell the tenant in writing, before signing, that it is not refundable, that it is not insurance for the tenant, and that the tenant still owes you for damage and unpaid rent; offer the ordinary deposit as an alternative; and don't charge both. A product sold by an insurer may be regulated as insurance, so check that any provider you use is licensed in the CNMI.

title: Furnished Rentals in the Northern Mariana Islands
bodyText: We found no Commonwealth statute, regulation or court rule with special rules for furnished rentals: no separate furniture deposit rule, no required inventory and no different refund deadline. If you rent furnished, use the "Furnishings" clause to list each item and its condition (or attach a signed inventory with photos), so you can show what was there and in what shape at move-in. Any extra deposit you take for the furniture is part of the security deposit, and its balance is refunded within ten days after the property is returned, less only damage beyond normal wear and tear. If you let furnished rooms to lodgers, separate lodging-house rules may apply.

title: Holding Deposits in the Northern Mariana Islands
bodyText: We found no Commonwealth statute, regulation or court rule on holding deposits (money an applicant pays to take a unit off the market before signing the lease). Because the deposit law requires the balance of a security deposit to be refunded within ten days, and it is unsettled whether that reaches a holding deposit, take the cautious course: put the terms in writing before you accept the money (amount, how long you will hold the unit, and what happens to the money); credit it to the security deposit or first month's rent if the lease is signed; and refund it in full within ten days if you decide not to rent to the applicant or the deal falls through for a reason that isn't the applicant's fault. If you intend to keep any part when the applicant backs out, say so in writing beforehand and keep it to a reasonable amount tied to your real loss.

title: Penalties for Deposit Lapses in the Northern Mariana Islands
bodyText: We found no Commonwealth statute, regulation or court rule that requires you to tell a tenant about a right to a move-in or move-out inspection, so there is no penalty for leaving that notice out, and no rule makes you forfeit the right to keep part of the deposit or pay double or treble the deposit for any lapse. The penalty that does exist is in the deposit law itself: a court fine of up to $1,000 per violation for failing to refund the balance within ten days after the property is returned. A tenant may also sue for the amount wrongly kept. See "edu-condition-inspection-mp" for the cautious practice on inspections.

title: Nonrefundable Deposits and Fees in the Northern Mariana Islands
bodyText: We found no Commonwealth statute, regulation or court rule on nonrefundable deposits or fees, or on how to disclose them. The deposit law requires you to refund the balance of any security deposit within ten days after the property is returned, so don't call any part of a deposit "nonrefundable": money held to cover damage or unpaid rent is a deposit, and what is left after proper deductions goes back to the tenant. If you charge a genuine one-time fee for something else (for example a pet fee or a cleaning fee for a service you will perform), list it in the lease by name and amount and say plainly that it is a fee, not a deposit, and is not refunded; the "Nonrefundable Fees" clause does this and treats any other security money as part of the deposit.

title: Separate Notice of Nonrefundable Fees in the Northern Mariana Islands
bodyText: We found no Commonwealth statute, regulation or court rule that requires a nonrefundable fee to be disclosed in a separate notice or document, or to be separately signed or initialed. Listing each fee by name and amount in the lease, and saying it is not refundable, is enough under Northern Mariana Islands law; see "edu-nonrefundable-deposit-notice-mp". Remember that money held as security is always a refundable deposit, whatever the paperwork calls it.

title: Security Deposit Limits in the Northern Mariana Islands
bodyText: We found no Commonwealth statute, regulation or court rule that caps the security deposit a private residential landlord may charge, so the amount is up to you and the tenant, and you may raise it at renewal by agreement. Keep it reasonable: a deposit far above the risk could be attacked as unconscionable under the Consumer Protection Act, which we treat as reaching residential leasing, and many landlords use one or two months' rent. Units in NMHC's Section 8 programs are different: NMHC's older administrative plan caps the deposit at one month's rent, but the Law Revision Commission's comment treats that plan as superseded where it conflicts with NMHC's later voucher rules, and the later project-based voucher rules let NMHC bar deposits above what you charge unassisted tenants or what the market charges, or let the owner collect the amount the owner thinks appropriate, so check with NMHC before setting the deposit for an assisted tenant. Whatever you collect, refund the balance within ten days after the property is returned.

title: Holding Security Deposits in the Northern Mariana Islands
bodyText: We found no Commonwealth statute, regulation or court rule that tells a residential landlord (or a property manager or broker) how to hold security deposits: no trust or escrow account requirement, no ban on mixing deposits with your own money, no duty to tell the tenant where the deposit is held, and no rule on who keeps any interest. What the law does require is a refund of the balance within ten days after the property is returned. Good practice is still to keep deposits in a separate bank account, so the money is there when the refund is due and your records show each tenant's deposit; if you use a property manager, require that in your management agreement. The optional clause "security-deposit-no-interest-pr" says the deposit earns no interest and may be held with other funds.

title: Interest on Security Deposits in the Northern Mariana Islands
bodyText: We found no Commonwealth statute, regulation or court rule that requires you to pay interest on a tenant's security deposit, so you don't owe interest unless the lease promises it. If you choose to pay interest, state the rate and when it is paid in the lease; if you don't, the optional clause "security-deposit-no-interest-pr" says so. Either way, refund the balance of the deposit within ten days after the property is returned.

title: Waiving Deposit Rights in the Northern Mariana Islands
bodyText: We found no Commonwealth statute, regulation or court rule that expressly says a tenant can't waive deposit rights in the lease. But the duty to refund the balance of a security deposit within ten days after the property is returned is enforced by a court fine, and a lease clause claiming the tenant gave up that refund (or agreed to a longer deadline) would likely be treated as misstating the tenant's rights under the Consumer Protection Act, which we treat as reaching residential leasing. So don't put a deposit waiver, forfeiture or extended-refund term in the lease; keep to the ten-day refund and deduct only what the lease properly allows.

title: Deposits When Rental Property Is Sold in the Northern Mariana Islands
bodyText: We found no Commonwealth statute, regulation or court rule that says what happens to security deposits when a rental property is sold: nothing requires the seller to hand them to the buyer, makes the buyer liable for deposits it never received, or requires a notice to tenants. Because the tenant will look to whoever is landlord at move-out for the ten-day refund, take the cautious course: in the sale contract, have the seller transfer every deposit (or credit it against the price) and give the buyer a list of deposits by tenant; then tell each tenant in writing who holds the deposit and where to send rent. If you are the buyer, assume you will owe the refunds and get the money or the credit at closing. Also note that a lease for more than one year that isn't recorded may not bind a buyer in good faith who records first, so record long leases (they must be acknowledged before a notary). For voucher units, NMHC processes a change of owner only on the new owner's written request with the closing documents.

title: Security Deposit Penalties in the Northern Mariana Islands
bodyText: Northern Mariana Islands law states one consequence for a late deposit refund. If you require a security deposit, you must refund the balance within ten days after the property is returned, and a court may fine you up to $1,000 for each violation. That fine is the only penalty the Commonwealth's deposit law sets. We found no Commonwealth statute, regulation or court rule that makes you forfeit the right to keep any part of the deposit, pay the tenant double or treble the deposit, give up a damage claim, or lose anything for failing to send a list of deductions, keep the deposit in a separate account or tell the tenant where it is held. The tenant can still sue you for any balance you owe. Cautious course: we treat the Consumer Protection Act as reaching residential leasing. Keeping a deposit without a basis could be treated as an unfair practice, and a tenant who wins such a claim recovers actual damages, an equal extra amount for a wilful violation, and costs and attorney's fees. Federal law: if a servicemember (or a servicemember's dependent) lawfully ends a lease under the Servicemembers Civil Relief Act, knowingly holding the deposit to cover rent for the period after the lease ends is a federal crime. What to do: refund the balance within ten days after the property comes back, as the "security-deposit-return-mp" clause says; send a written list of any deductions with the refund even though no law requires it; and keep your move-out photos and receipts. Government landlords and Northern Marianas Housing Corporation voucher units follow their own rules.

title: Security Deposit Return in the Northern Mariana Islands
bodyText: Northern Mariana Islands law sets one deposit-return rule: if you require a security deposit, refund the balance within ten days after the property is returned. Count ten calendar days from the day the tenant moves out and gives up possession, even if keys come back later (returned keys or a clear move-out are good evidence of that day); the statute counts from that one event, not from a tenant demand, the end of the lease term or a forwarding address. The lease may not give you longer; you may refund sooner. The "security-deposit-return-mp" clause states this rule and the lease should use it. We found no Commonwealth statute, regulation or court rule that requires a written itemized list of deductions, a forwarding address, a written demand by the tenant, a particular refund method, or a separate claim notice, and none that lets a lease fix a different refund time. Paying by check, cash or electronic transfer is your choice; the deadline is the same. No unit-count threshold applies. Unclaimed refunds: the Commonwealth's unclaimed-funds rules we found cover banks and money held by the courts, not landlords, and no rule lets you keep an uncashed or unclaimed refund. Cautious course: if a refund check goes uncashed, keep the money for the tenant, keep a record of your attempts to pay it, and pay it on request. Federal law: if a servicemember lawfully ends a lease under the Servicemembers Civil Relief Act, rent paid in advance for the period after the lease ends must be refunded within 30 days. Northern Marianas Housing Corporation project-based voucher units also require a written list of every deposit charge before refunding the balance; follow the program rules for those units. What to do: inspect promptly when the tenant leaves, send the balance within ten days with a short written list of any deductions (good practice and useful evidence), and keep copies.

title: Security Deposit Standards in the Northern Mariana Islands
bodyText: We found no Commonwealth statute, regulation or court rule that requires a landlord, however many units it has, to post or hand out the standards it uses to set or calculate security deposits, and none that limits the amount of a deposit. Northern Mariana Islands law regulates only when the balance comes back (within ten days after the property is returned). What does limit you is the fair housing law: you may not set different deposit terms for a tenant because of race, color, religion, sex, familial status, marital status, disability or national origin (the Commonwealth Fair Housing Act and the federal Fair Housing Act). Cautious course: we also treat the Consumer Protection Act's anti-discrimination rule as reaching landlords, so don't vary deposits by age, creed, ethnic background, citizenship, or place of birth or residence either. What to do: if you use more than one deposit amount (for example by unit size, credit result or pet), write the standard down, apply it the same way to every applicant, and keep it on file so you can show it if a fair housing complaint is made. Northern Marianas Housing Corporation voucher units need NMHC approval of the deposit amount.

title: Security Deposit Use in the Northern Mariana Islands
bodyText: We found no Commonwealth statute, regulation or court rule that lists what a landlord may take out of a security deposit. Northern Mariana Islands law says only that you must refund the balance within ten days after the property is returned, so what you may deduct is set by the lease. The library's "Use of Security Deposit" clause ("security-deposit-use") limits deductions to unpaid rent and other amounts the tenant owes under the lease and to damage the tenant caused beyond ordinary wear and tear, and it carries MP as written; use it rather than an "any default" clause. Pre-set cleaning or repair charges: no Commonwealth law bars a lease from naming set charges (for example a carpet-cleaning fee or a per-key charge), but we treat the Consumer Protection Act as reaching residential leasing, and it bars unconscionable contract terms and unfair practices. Cautious course: tie any pre-set charge to the actual cost of work that is actually needed, don't deduct it when the work isn't needed, and never deduct for ordinary wear and tear. For disability modifications you permit, you may, where reasonable, condition permission on the tenant's agreeing to restore the interior, reasonable wear and tear excepted. What to do: keep the deposit for unpaid rent and real damage, record the condition at move-in and move-out, keep receipts for repairs, and send a written list of deductions with the balance.

title: Utility Deposit Return in the Northern Mariana Islands
bodyText: Utility deposits in the Northern Mariana Islands are mostly the Commonwealth Utilities Corporation's (CUC) business, not yours. CUC must collect a one-month security deposit from every residential account, hold it in an interest-earning trust fund, use it to cover any past-due bill before it disconnects, and refund it with earned interest within thirty days after the service is disconnected. If the CUC account is in the tenant's name, CUC refunds the tenant directly and you have no refund duty. If the account is in your name, CUC refunds you when you close it. If you collect your own deposit for utilities (for example where utilities stay in your name and the tenant reimburses you), treat that money as a security deposit: we treat every landlord as covered by the Commonwealth's deposit law, so refund the balance within ten days after the property is returned, less unpaid utility charges the lease makes the tenant's responsibility. We found no other Commonwealth rule on landlord-held utility deposits. What to do: say in the lease whose name each utility account is in (the "Utilities Paid by Tenant" clause, "utilities-responsibility"), and if you hold any utility deposit, list it in the lease with the security deposit and refund it on the same ten-day schedule.

title: Tenant Alterations in the Northern Mariana Islands
bodyText: Northern Mariana Islands law lets the lease bar or limit tenant alterations, with one exception: the fair housing laws. Under the Commonwealth Fair Housing Act and the federal Fair Housing Act you may not refuse a tenant with a disability permission to make reasonable modifications, at the tenant's expense, that may be necessary for full enjoyment of the premises. Where it is reasonable, you may make permission conditional on the tenant agreeing to restore the interior to its prior condition at the end of the tenancy, reasonable wear and tear excepted. We found no Commonwealth statute, regulation or court rule that shifts the cost of disability modifications to the owner of a larger or assisted building; under both acts the cost is the tenant's. Federally assisted housing has an extra owner-side rule: when a recipient of federal financial assistance alters dwelling units in a multifamily project, the altered units must, to the maximum extent feasible and short of undue financial and administrative burden, be made accessible; follow your program's rules there. Building permits: construction, enlargement or alteration work under the Commonwealth Building Safety Code may need a permit from the Building Safety Division (small repairs under $3,000 that don't touch structure or exits need none), so require the tenant to get your written consent and any permit before work starts. What to do: use the "No Alterations" clause ("no-alterations"), which keeps the reasonable-modification right; answer modification requests in writing; and if you require restoration, say so when you approve the request.

title: Bed Bugs and Pest Treatment in the Northern Mariana Islands
bodyText: We found no Commonwealth statute, regulation or court rule on bed bugs, and none that sets a tenant's duty to report pests, prepare a unit for treatment, or pay for treatment, or a landlord's duty to inspect or treat within a set time. So these are lease terms: the library's "Pest Reporting and Treatment" clause ("pest-cooperation-pr") carries MP and is the one to use. Two related rules exist. First, if a licensed applicator fumigates a building for termites and the building is a single-owner complex with several units, the applicator must tell every tenant at least 14 days before; book fumigation early enough for that notice and pass on what the applicator gives you. Second, on Saipan, the Nuisance Abatement and Blighted Property Maintenance Act makes owners of commercial property keep exterior areas free of sources of insect or rodent infestation; check local rules on Tinian and Rota. Cautious course: we assume you owe a duty to keep the dwelling fit to live in, and a serious infestation can breach it, so treat infestations promptly at your cost unless the tenant caused them, and don't rely on a clause that shifts all pest responsibility to the tenant. What to do: use the cooperation clause, respond to reports quickly with a licensed pest-control operator, document the treatment, and charge the tenant only where the lease allows and the tenant caused the problem.

title: Carpet Cleaning in the Northern Mariana Islands
bodyText: We found no Commonwealth statute, regulation or court rule on carpet cleaning at move-out. Northern Mariana Islands law doesn't require, forbid or condition a lease term making the tenant pay for professional carpet cleaning, so it is a contract term. The library's "Professional Carpet Cleaning at Move-Out" clause ("carpet-cleaning-ar") carries MP and is the one to use. Cautious course: we treat the Consumer Protection Act as reaching residential leasing, so keep the charge to the actual reasonable cost of a cleaning that is actually done, don't charge for ordinary wear and tear, and refund the rest of the deposit within ten days after the property is returned. It helps to have the carpets professionally cleaned before the tenant moves in and to say so in the move-in condition record. What to do: use the clause, keep the cleaning receipt, and list the charge on your written deduction list.

title: Cold-Weather Vacating Notice in the Northern Mariana Islands
bodyText: This topic does not arise in the Northern Mariana Islands. Rules elsewhere that make a tenant warn the landlord before leaving a unit empty in cold weather exist to stop pipes freezing; the islands are tropical, with no freezing season, and we found no Commonwealth statute, regulation or court rule on cold-weather vacating, freezing pipes or a heating season. If you want notice before a tenant leaves the unit empty for a long time (for example for typhoon preparation, water leaks or security), use the library's "Notice of Extended Absence" clause ("extended-absence-notice-ks"), which carries MP; see "edu-extended-absence-notice-mp".

title: Construction Liens for Tenant Work in the Northern Mariana Islands
bodyText: Northern Mariana Islands mechanics' lien law (4 CMC §§ 5801-5809) lets a licensed construction contractor or a supplier of construction material claim a lien for unpaid work or materials on the improvement and on the interest in the land of the "owner" who contracted for it. The statute's "owner" includes a lessee for a term of years who signs the contract, so when your tenant hires the contractor the lien is aimed at the tenant's leasehold. The law does not say whether your own interest is exposed when you consented to the tenant's work, and there is no lease-text or notice procedure that keeps your interest free of liens; a lien attaches only after the Superior Court finds probable cause at a hearing, and the claim must be filed within 60 days after completion. Individual workers have no lien except through a licensed contractor employer. Two points matter to landlords: a court enforcing a lien against a commercial owner may eject tenants or redirect rents to the lien claimants until the lien is paid, so pay your own contractors; and ejection is a last resort where the lien is on an owner's principal residence. Cautious course: use the library's "No Liens for Tenant Work" clause ("no-liens-ar"), which carries MP; require written consent before any tenant work, require the tenant to use licensed contractors and give you lien releases or proof of payment, and be ready to appear at the probable-cause hearing if you are served. Liens cannot attach to Commonwealth government property.

title: Noise and Disturbance in the Northern Mariana Islands
bodyText: Northern Mariana Islands law has no landlord-tenant rule on noise or disturbance, so the lease sets the standard: the library's "No Disturbance or Nuisance" clause ("no-disturbance") carries MP. Two pieces of Commonwealth law sit behind it. Disturbing the peace is a crime: wilfully doing something that unreasonably annoys or disturbs another person so that they are deprived of peace and quiet can bring up to six months in jail, so serious or repeated noise can be reported to the Department of Public Safety. And a material breach of the lease that is not about rent (such as repeated disturbance) can end the tenancy: if the lease is silent on how breaches are handled, you must first serve fifteen days' written notice to cure or leave, by hand delivery or by leaving a copy at the unit if the tenant is absent; the lease may set its own cure period and notice method. Only the Superior Court can then order the tenant out. On your side, we assume you must not yourself interfere with the tenant's use and quiet enjoyment of the home (Restatement not read; case law not searched). What to do: write down each complaint with dates and witnesses, give the tenant a written warning, and use the written breach notice before going to court.

title: Move-In Condition in the Northern Mariana Islands
bodyText: We found no Commonwealth statute, regulation or court rule that requires a landlord to give a move-in condition statement, inventory or checklist, to hold a walk-through, or to let the tenant list defects within a set time. A condition record is still your best evidence when you deduct from the deposit, which must be refunded (less proper deductions) within ten days after the property is returned. The library's "Existing Condition of Property" clause ("existing-condition") carries MP; it records the tenant's acceptance of the condition without waiving your repair duties. Cautious course: we assume you owe a duty to keep the dwelling fit to live in, and a tenant's acknowledgment of the move-in condition does not excuse defects that make the unit unfit; and if you know of a defect, tell the tenant rather than describing the unit as sound, since we treat the Consumer Protection Act as reaching residential leasing. What to do: do a dated walk-through with the tenant at move-in and move-out, take photos, have both of you sign the record, and give the tenant a copy. Northern Marianas Housing Corporation voucher units also go through the program's move-in and move-out inspections.

title: Extended Absence in the Northern Mariana Islands
bodyText: We found no Commonwealth statute, regulation or court rule that requires a tenant to tell the landlord about an extended absence, that requires the lease to contain such a term, or that gives a landlord a special right to enter during a tenant's absence. So it is a lease term: the library's "Notice of Extended Absence" clause ("extended-absence-notice-ks") carries MP and is the one to use; it is useful in the islands for typhoon preparation, leaks and security. An absence alone does not end the tenancy or let you treat the unit as abandoned; see "abandoned-property-mp" for property left behind, and recover possession only through the Superior Court (the statutory route; we assume self-help is unlawful). If you must serve a written default notice while the tenant is away, the statute allows leaving a copy at the premises when the tenant is absent. Two related rules: on Saipan an unsecured vacant building or dwelling is a public nuisance under the Nuisance Abatement and Blighted Property Maintenance Act, so keep an empty unit locked and secure; and Northern Marianas Housing Corporation voucher families may not be absent more than 180 consecutive days and must get NMHC approval for long absences. What to do: use the clause, keep the tenant's emergency contact on file, and secure the unit if you learn it is empty.

title: Home Child Care in the Northern Mariana Islands
bodyText: We found no Commonwealth statute, regulation or court rule that makes a landlord allow a tenant to run a family child care home, or that limits what a lease may require (insurance, liability terms or consent) if the tenant wants to. So a lease may ban, allow or condition home child care, for example through the "Residential Use Only" clause ("residential-use-only"), which carries MP. The Commonwealth does regulate the activity itself: "family day care" (care in a private home for five or more unrelated children) must be licensed by the Department of Community and Cultural Affairs, and a private home used as a licensed child care facility falls under the Smoke-Free Air Act's indoor smoking ban. Cautious course: a ban that falls more heavily on families with children can raise fair housing questions, so apply any rule the same way to every tenant, and if you allow child care, require proof of the license and of liability insurance naming you. What to do: say in the lease whether a licensed home child care is allowed and on what conditions.

title: Home Businesses in the Northern Mariana Islands
bodyText: We found no Commonwealth statute, regulation or court rule that makes a home-based business a permitted use of a rented dwelling or stops a lease from restricting one. A lease may ban or limit business use; the library's "Residential Use Only" clause ("residential-use-only") carries MP. If you allow a home business, the tenant carries the public-law duties: anyone engaging in a business in the Commonwealth needs a business licence from the Department of Finance for each line of business and location, and on Saipan the zoning regulations list a separate "Home Business" zoning permit (fee $25); check local zoning on Tinian and Rota. Home food businesses have their own rules under the Cottage Food and Microenterprise Home Kitchen Operations Act (2026): a cottage food operation (baked goods, jams, dry snacks) needs a sanitary permit and a food handler's certificate, and a microenterprise home kitchen selling cooked meals needs an annual permit and a home-kitchen inspection, with sales capped at $50,000 a year and 30 meals a day or 60 a week. That Act says nothing about landlords, so it does not override a lease ban, but it gives qualifying home food businesses residential (not commercial) utility rates. What to do: decide whether you allow home businesses; if you do, say which kinds, require the tenant to hold the business licence and any zoning, sanitary or kitchen permit, keep customer traffic and signage within limits you set, require insurance, and keep the right to inspect on notice; if you don't, say so in the lease.

title: Co-Tenant Liability in the Northern Mariana Islands
bodyText: We found no Commonwealth statute, regulation or court rule on co-tenants' liability under a residential lease. Whether co-tenants are each liable for the whole rent is therefore a lease term: the library's "Joint & Several Liability" clause ("joint-liability") carries MP and makes each tenant responsible for the full rent and all lease obligations. How co-tenants share the rent among themselves is a matter between them (the Commonwealth's contribution statute covers fault-based claims for injury or harm, not lease debts; case law not searched). We found no Commonwealth rule saying that accepting one co-tenant's share of the rent waives your claim against that co-tenant for the rest; the point would turn on contract law and case law, which this library has not searched. Cautious course: when you accept a partial payment, give a written receipt saying it is accepted toward the full rent with all rights reserved against every tenant. Utility accounts: two or more people who join in one CUC water service application are jointly and severally liable for its bills. What to do: have every adult occupant sign the lease as a tenant, and serve any default notice on each tenant.

title: Yard Care and Irrigation in the Northern Mariana Islands
bodyText: We found no Commonwealth statute, regulation or court rule on who must care for the yard, landscaping or irrigation of a rental, and no rule requiring tenant maintenance tasks to be set out in a separate signed agreement. One statute does reach yard care: trees and plants near overhead power lines, which a tenant may have to keep clear (see "edu-power-line-vegetation-mp"). Otherwise the lease allocates yard care: the library's "Landscaping & Irrigation" clause ("landscaping-irrigation") carries MP. On Saipan, the Nuisance Abatement and Blighted Property Maintenance Act declares nuisance vegetation over 15 inches across most of a parcel, and untended weeds or undergrowth, a public nuisance (Third Senatorial District only; check Tinian and Rota local rules). The notice from the Saipan administrator usually goes to the owner, so whoever the lease makes responsible, check that the yard is being kept up. What to do: say in the lease exactly which yard tasks the tenant does and which you do, supply any equipment you expect the tenant to use, and inspect the outside of the property periodically.

title: Utility Liens for Tenant Bills in the Northern Mariana Islands
bodyText: We found no Commonwealth statute, regulation or court rule that makes a tenant's unpaid water, sewer, power or garbage bill a lien on the rental property or collectible from a landlord who is not the customer, and no procedure (affidavit, lease clause or notice to the utility) for avoiding one. The Commonwealth Utilities Corporation (CUC) bills the "customer": the person who applied for service and is responsible for the bills at that location. CUC's remedies for an unpaid bill are against that customer's account: it first applies the customer's security deposit, then may disconnect after the statutory protections.
