Two points to watch: CUC's electric rules treat the owner or operator of commercial premises, not the tenants, as the customer; an apartment building used solely for residential purposes is a residential customer, but a single-meter building that also houses a commercial business, or worker housing paid for by a business, is billed as commercial, and in those buildings you are the customer and owe the bill; and on Saipan, if the Commonwealth abates a public nuisance on your property (for example uncollected trash) under the Nuisance Abatement and Blighted Property Maintenance Act, its costs become a lien on your property, which is a separate rule from utility billing. What to do: where the tenant pays utilities, have the account opened in the tenant's name, keep it out of yours, and use the "Utilities Paid by Tenant" clause ("utilities-responsibility") and the "Evidence of Utility Payment" clause ("utility-payment-evidence").

title: Occupancy Limits in the Northern Mariana Islands
bodyText: Occupancy limits: we found no Commonwealth statute, regulation or court rule that sets a general maximum number of occupants for a private rental (by bedroom, floor area or air space), and none that lets neighbours enforce one. The fair housing laws preserve any reasonable occupancy limit set by Commonwealth, local or federal law, but where none applies your own limit must be reasonable and must not be a way to exclude families with children, since familial status is a protected class under the Commonwealth Fair Housing Act and the federal Fair Housing Act. Northern Marianas Housing Corporation programs apply their own unit-size standards to the units they fund. Who may stay after a tenant dies: we found no Commonwealth rule giving an occupant or relative the right to take over a dwelling lease when the tenant dies, or ending the lease automatically; the point turns on the lease, the tenant's estate and case law, which this library has not searched. Federal law lets the spouse or dependent of a servicemember who dies in military service end the lease within one year after the death. What to do: name every occupant in the "Permitted Occupants" clause ("permitted-occupants"), which carries MP; set any occupancy limit by a neutral standard (for example two persons per bedroom plus one) and apply it to everyone; and if a tenant dies, deal with the estate's representative and any remaining co-tenant in writing rather than changing the locks; recover possession only through the Superior Court (the statutory route; we assume self-help is unlawful).

title: Prohibited Tenant Acts in the Northern Mariana Islands
bodyText: We found no Commonwealth statute, regulation or court rule listing acts a residential tenant must not do (such as damaging the unit, disturbing neighbours or refusing reasonable entry). These are lease terms: the library's "Prohibited Acts by Tenant" clause ("prohibited-acts-renter-wy") carries MP and is the one to use. Some of the same conduct is also a crime anywhere in the Commonwealth: vandalising private property (fines from $250 to $10,000 plus community service, rising with repeat offences), criminal mischief such as tampering with property in a way that endangers people or interrupts water or power, and disturbing the peace. A breach of these lease terms is a non-rent breach: if the lease is silent on the procedure, serve fifteen days' written notice to cure or leave before filing for possession in the Superior Court; the lease may set its own period and notice method. What to do: use the clause, document damage with photos and dates, and report crimes to the Department of Public Safety separately from your lease remedies.

title: Residential Use in the Northern Mariana Islands
bodyText: We found no Commonwealth statute, regulation or court rule that limits a residential tenant to residential use or sets a special remedy (such as rescission or damages) when a tenant uses the property for another purpose. The use limit is a lease term: the library's "Residential Use Only" clause ("residential-use-only") carries MP. A tenant who breaks it commits a non-rent breach; if the lease is silent on the procedure, serve fifteen days' written notice to cure or leave before filing for possession in the Superior Court. Other uses bring public-law duties that can reach you. Short stays: renting rooms or a home to transient occupants (stays under 90 days, including a private residence or bed and breakfast) carries the Commonwealth's 15 percent hotel occupancy tax, collected by the person who operates, owns or manages the place; this is a reason to bar short-term subletting unless you handle the tax. Business use: a business needs a business licence and, on Saipan, a home-business zoning permit (see "edu-home-business-mp"); a residence that includes a commercial business is billed by CUC as a commercial customer. Every residential rental, including Airbnb-type rentals, needs the Building Safety annual certificate of compliance. What to do: keep the clause, and write any permitted exception (home office, licensed child care) into the lease expressly.

title: Smoking and Cannabis Rules in the Northern Mariana Islands
bodyText: Northern Mariana Islands law lets you decide whether tenants may smoke in their own units. The Smoke-Free Air Act bans smoking (which by definition includes electronic cigarettes) in the enclosed lobbies, hallways and other common areas of apartment buildings, condominiums and other multiple-unit residential buildings, and as the person in control of those areas you must post "No Smoking" signs, remove ashtrays, tell violators of the ban and report violations, with fines of up to $200, $300 and then $500 per violation (each day counts separately) if you don't. Inside a private residence or apartment, smoking is not regulated by the Act (unless the home is used as a licensed child care, adult day care or health care facility), and the Department of Public Health's rules leave it to the owner's discretion; you may also declare your whole property non-smoking and post the required signs. Marijuana: the Commonwealth's cannabis law expressly does not change landlord-tenant law, so a lease may ban marijuana smoking, vaping and growing. A tenant may grow only on property lawfully in their possession by an appropriate lease or with the possessor's consent, and the home-grow registration for a rental unit requires the landlord's written agreement and the signed rental agreement. Knowingly letting your property be used to sell marijuana or as a place to use it illegally is itself a violation; smoking marijuana near anyone under 21 is unlawful. We found no Commonwealth rule that protects a tenant's smoking or vaping, that makes smoke drift a statutory nuisance, or that prescribes lease wording for a smoking policy. What to do: state your policy in the "Smoking Policy" clause ("smoking-policy"), which carries MP, covering tobacco, e-cigarettes and marijuana and where on the property each is allowed; post no-smoking signs in common areas; and decide in writing whether you consent to home growing.

title: Subletting and Assignment in the Northern Mariana Islands
bodyText: We found no Commonwealth statute, regulation or court rule that limits a landlord's right to bar subletting or assignment, requires consent not to be unreasonably withheld, or treats a landlord's silence as consent. So the lease controls: the library's "No Subletting or Assignment" clause ("no-sublet-assign") carries MP and requires your written consent. Northern Mariana Islands law does assume that subtenants and assignees exist: the summary possession procedure reaches the tenant's assigns and under-tenants, so a court order for possession removes them too. Three related rules: (1) assigning a lease for a term of more than one year, or granting a sublease for more than one year, must be done by a written instrument signed by the party making the transfer, and an agreement that cannot be performed within a year must be in writing; (2) a sublet or assignment gives the new occupant an interest in land, so the Constitution's land-alienation limits apply, and any sublease or assignment, with renewal rights, must stay within 55 years for a person who is not of Northern Marianas descent; (3) a short-term sublet (stays under 90 days) brings the 15 percent hotel occupancy tax, and an Airbnb-type rental needs the Building Safety certificate. The fair housing laws treat subleasing as renting, so you may not refuse consent for a discriminatory reason. We found no Commonwealth rule that makes a clause "self-defeating" by forfeiting a remedy. What to do: require written requests and written consent, answer promptly in writing, and make any approved subtenant sign an addendum.

title: Forwarding Legal Notices in the Northern Mariana Islands
bodyText: We found no Commonwealth statute, regulation or court rule that requires a tenant to forward to the landlord notices of legal proceedings affecting the property, or that voids a tenant's attornment (acknowledging someone else as landlord). Both are lease terms here: the library's "Notice of Proceedings Against the Property" clause ("tenant-forward-proceedings-ca") carries MP and is the one to use. It matters in the Commonwealth because notices about the property are often served or posted at the property itself: a contractor's mechanics' lien application is served on the owner and anyone with an interest in the property, and on Saipan a nuisance-abatement order is posted on the property when the owner's address can't be found. What to do: keep the clause, give the tenant a current address for forwarding papers, and keep your address on file with the Commonwealth Recorder so that official notices reach you directly.

title: Renter's Insurance in the Northern Mariana Islands
bodyText: We found no Commonwealth statute, regulation or court rule on renter's insurance in residential leases: nothing requires it, bars a lease from requiring it, caps the coverage you may require, or governs how a tenant's or landlord's insurance claims are handled between you. So the lease decides. The library's "Tenant's Property & Renter's Insurance" clause ("tenants-property-insurance-ks-oh-ca") carries MP; it is the version without a broad landlord disclaimer, because we assume you can't rely on a clause that excuses you from liability for your own negligence. Typhoon and flood risk is high in the islands, and the floodplain regulations note that National Flood Insurance Program coverage is available to renters for their contents. What to do: if you require renter's insurance, state the minimum liability amount in the lease, ask for proof each year, and tell tenants in writing that your property insurance does not cover their belongings.

title: Tenant Upkeep and Septic Systems in the Northern Mariana Islands
bodyText: Tenant upkeep: we found no Commonwealth statute, regulation or court rule listing a residential tenant's duties to keep the unit clean, avoid damage or make repairs. Those duties come from the lease: the library's "Tenant Maintenance & Cleanliness" clause ("tenant-maintenance") carries MP, and it keeps with you the conditions the law makes yours (we assume you owe a duty to keep the dwelling fit to live in). A tenant who breaches it can be given fifteen days' written notice to cure (if the lease is silent on the procedure), and damage beyond ordinary wear and tear can come out of the deposit. Septic systems: the Division of Environmental Quality's wastewater rules make maintenance of septic tanks, seepage pits and leaching fields the owner's responsibility, require the owner to have tanks emptied and cleaned as necessary by a licensed hauler, and advise inspection at least every three years. A lease may make the tenant avoid misuse (no grease, wipes or chemicals) and report backups, but keep pumping and repair with you. Wells: drilling a water well needs a DEQ drilling permit; if the unit relies on a private well or rain catchment, keep the system and water quality your responsibility. Public health and other officials may order an "owner or occupant" to clean or disinfect premises, and on Saipan both must keep exterior residential areas clean and sanitary. What to do: use the clause, list any special systems (septic, catchment tanks, generators) and what the tenant must and must not do with them, and schedule septic service yourself.

title: Tenant Repair Agreements in the Northern Mariana Islands
bodyText: We found no Commonwealth statute, regulation or court rule on agreements for a tenant to do repairs or maintenance: nothing requires them to be in a separate signed writing, to be supported by consideration, to be limited to single-family homes, or to be made in good faith, and no rule says which landlord duties may or may not be shifted. So a repair agreement is a contract term, subject to two cautious limits: we assume you owe a non-waivable duty to keep the dwelling fit to live in, and we treat the Consumer Protection Act as barring unconscionable terms, so don't shift structural, safety or habitability repairs to the tenant, and don't make the tenant pay for repairs to defects the tenant didn't cause. The library's "Tenant Maintenance and Minor Repair Agreement" clause ("tenant-repair-agreement-pr") carries MP; it keeps habitability and urgent repairs with you and says installed parts become your property. Repair work by anyone may need a building permit if it costs more than $3,000 or touches structure or exits, and if the building is ever declared unsafe, the Building Safety Official's order goes to owner, occupant and lessee alike. What to do: put any repair agreement in writing, list the tasks and any rent credit, and keep major systems with you.

title: Tenant Duties in the Northern Mariana Islands
bodyText: We found no Commonwealth statute, regulation or court rule that lists a residential tenant's duties the way a residential landlord-tenant act does elsewhere (keeping the unit clean and safe, disposing of waste, using fixtures reasonably, not damaging the premises, not disturbing neighbours). The only landlord-tenant chapter, the Holdover Tenancy Act, deals with notices and summary possession, and it leaves the parties free to create rights and duties in the rental agreement. So a tenant's duties are whatever the lease says. Use the library's tenant-duty clauses, which carry MP: "Tenant Maintenance & Cleanliness" ("tenant-maintenance"), "Prohibited Acts by Tenant" ("prohibited-acts-renter-wy") and "No Disturbance or Nuisance" ("no-disturbance"); see "edu-tenant-maintenance-mp", "edu-prohibited-acts-renter-mp" and "edu-disturbance-mp" for the public-law rules (septic care, Saipan exterior upkeep, vandalism, disturbing the peace) that apply to occupants anyway. Northern Marianas Housing Corporation voucher families have program obligations of their own. What to do: write every duty you rely on into the lease; a duty the lease doesn't state is hard to enforce.

title: Utility Accounts in the Northern Mariana Islands
bodyText: Who pays which utility is a lease term: the library's "Utilities Paid by Tenant" clause ("utilities-responsibility") carries MP. The Commonwealth Utilities Corporation (CUC) rules decide who CUC can bill. CUC bills the customer who applied for service at that location; it refuses new water service to an applicant who has unpaid CUC bills of their own, wherever incurred, but we found no rule letting CUC refuse service to a new tenant because of a former occupant's bill, or collect a tenant's bill from a landlord who is not the customer. Anyone who takes possession and uses water without applying is liable for the water used, so a tenant who moves in should open the account promptly. Residential customers have statutory protections: a one-month deposit, a thirty-day grace period after the due date, no disconnection on a Friday, during a billing dispute, or of all services when only one is unpaid. Unpaid utilities and eviction: no Commonwealth statute makes a tenant's unpaid utility bill a ground for removal, but if the lease makes paying utilities a tenant obligation, failing to pay is a non-rent breach; where the lease is silent on the procedure, serve fifteen days' written notice to cure or leave. Cautious course: don't treat utility charges as "rent" for the three-day rent notice unless the lease clearly makes them rent, and never shut off or interrupt utilities to force a tenant out; recover possession only through the Superior Court (the statutory route; we assume self-help is unlawful). What to do: name the account holder for each utility in the lease, require the tenant to open accounts before moving in, and ask for proof of payment with the "Evidence of Utility Payment" clause ("utility-payment-evidence").

title: Submetered Electricity in the Northern Mariana Islands
bodyText: We found no Commonwealth statute, regulation or court rule setting a procedure for a landlord who submeters electricity to interrupt a tenant's service for nonpayment, and no tariff or notice regime for landlord-submetered power. What CUC's electric rules do say: power CUC sells to a customer may not be resold to third parties, but a commercial customer may allocate the cost of electric power among tenants, and where tenants are metered the meters must be ANSI C-12.1 rated with cyclometer dials. CUC classes an apartment building used only for residential purposes as a residential customer, and the rule names only commercial customers as allowed to allocate, so whether a residential-class landlord may allocate by submeter is unsettled. Cautious course: if you pass electricity costs to tenants, charge only your actual CUC cost (no markup, which could look like resale), use compliant meters, show the readings and rate on each bill, and say in the lease how the charge is calculated; and never disconnect or interrupt a tenant's power yourself to collect a charge or force a move-out. Treat unpaid utility charges as a lease breach handled through notice and, if needed, the Superior Court. Ask CUC to confirm your building's classification before you set up submetering.

title: Proof of Utility Payment in the Northern Mariana Islands
bodyText: We found no Commonwealth statute, regulation or court rule on a landlord asking a tenant for proof that utility bills are paid, and none that limits such a request. It is a lease term: the library's "Evidence of Utility Payment" clause ("utility-payment-evidence") carries MP. It is useful in the Commonwealth because CUC's remedies for an unpaid bill run against the customer's own account and deposit, and CUC may cut off service to accounts more than 90 days past due that aren't being disputed, so a tenant's unpaid bill can leave your unit without power or water. See "edu-utilities-responsibility-mp" for the account and disconnection rules. What to do: keep the clause and, if a tenant falls behind, treat it as a lease breach handled by written notice rather than by any action of your own on the utility.

title: Utility Service Continuity in the Northern Mariana Islands
bodyText: We found no Commonwealth statute, regulation or court rule that makes a tenant keep utility service connected, or that sets a landlord's duty to keep utilities on, beyond the CUC rules that govern the utility's own disconnections. CUC must give residential customers a thirty-day grace period after the due date, may not disconnect on a Friday or during an active billing dispute, may not cut all services when only one is unpaid, and must cut off accounts more than 90 days past due unless they are being disputed. The library's "Utility Service Continuity" clause ("utility-service-continuity") carries MP and makes the tenant avoid interruptions of water, electricity, sewer and trash service. Cautious course: we assume you owe a duty to keep the dwelling fit to live in, and the summary possession procedure is the only route to recover possession, so don't interrupt utilities you control to collect money or to force a tenant out, and keep utilities in your name paid. Typhoon-related outages are common; the clause covers interruptions the tenant causes, not outages by the utility. What to do: keep the clause and follow "edu-utilities-responsibility-mp" on accounts and notice.

title: Smoke and Carbon Monoxide Alarms in the Northern Mariana Islands
bodyText: The Commonwealth has no smoke-alarm or carbon-monoxide-alarm statute of its own for rentals; it adopts the International Fire Code (IFC) by regulation, and the IFC sets the rules. The regulation adopts "the most up to date version" of the IFC. The 2024 edition was current until the 2027 edition was published in September 2026, and whether the regulation picks up the 2027 edition without new rulemaking is unsettled, so this row follows both where they differ. Smoke alarms (same in both editions): the IFC's chapter for existing buildings covers buildings built before the code was adopted, and requires existing residential (Group R) occupancies to have smoke alarms in the locations the code sets for dwellings: on the ceiling or wall outside each separate sleeping area near the bedrooms, in each room used for sleeping, and on each story of the dwelling unit, including basements (the 2027 edition adds sleeping lofts). You need not add alarms where the alarms the building code required when the building was built are already in place, or where alarms installed voluntarily met the rules in force when installed, or where fire-alarm-system smoke detectors substitute for them. In an existing building where no construction is taking place, alarms may be battery-only, and they need not be interconnected unless the building is undergoing alterations, repairs or construction. The fire code applies to existing conditions, and the Fire Prevention and Arson Investigation Division enforces it. Carbon monoxide: under the 2024 edition, existing buildings that contain a carbon-monoxide source or have an attached private garage need CO detection outside each separate sleeping area near the bedrooms, and inside a bedroom if the source is in that bedroom or its attached bathroom; battery-only CO alarms are allowed where the code at the time of construction didn't require CO detectors, and alarms that stop working or signal end of life must be replaced. The 2027 edition applies its CO section to existing buildings directly and frames dwelling-unit locations around "direct" and "forced-indirect" sources and an attached enclosed garage with a communicating opening. Cautious course covering both: wherever a unit has a fuel-burning appliance (such as a gas range, gas water heater or generator) or an attached garage, put a CO alarm outside each sleeping area near the bedrooms, and inside any bedroom that contains a fuel-burning appliance or opens to a bathroom that does; replace CO alarms that fail or reach end of life. Penalties: violating the Fire Safety Code carries a civil fine of $5,000 to $10,000 per violation (each ten days counts again), and anyone harmed by a violation may sue for damages and attorney's fees. What to do: check every unit at move-in, test alarms between tenancies, replace batteries and expired units, and ask the tenant in the lease to test monthly and report faults, which the library's "Smoke and Carbon Monoxide Detectors" clause ("detector-care-la") does.

title: Alternate Housing in the Northern Mariana Islands
bodyText: We found no Commonwealth statute, regulation or court rule that makes a private landlord provide or pay for alternate housing when a rental becomes unfit to live in, during repairs, or after a typhoon, whether or not the tenant asks. What happens to the lease and the rent after damage is set by the lease: see the casualty clause ("casualty-termination-mp"). Relocation help that does exist is governmental: the Commonwealth's relocation-assistance law gives relocation payments, advisory help and assurance of standard housing to people displaced by government land acquisition or government-supervised rehabilitation programs, and Northern Marianas Housing Corporation programs have their own relocation rules for assisted families. If the Building Safety Official orders a building vacated as unsafe, the order binds you and the tenant, and no rule we found requires you to house the tenant elsewhere. Cautious course: we assume you owe a duty to keep the dwelling fit to live in, so if the unit is unfit because of your failure to repair, expect a court to give the tenant a remedy such as rent abatement or ending the lease (Restatement not read; case law not searched). What to do: say in the lease what happens to rent while the unit can't be lived in, stop charging rent for any period the unit is ordered vacated, and refund prepaid rent and the deposit balance promptly if the lease ends.

title: Excluded Appliances in the Northern Mariana Islands
bodyText: We found no Commonwealth statute, regulation or court rule that presumes appliances left in a rental are supplied by the landlord, that lists essential-service appliances a lease can't exclude, or that sets how an exclusion must be worded. So a lease may say that items left at the property are not part of what is leased and that you won't repair them. The library's "Items Not Included" clause ("appliances-excluded-la") carries MP; it is optional and does not reach any defect that seriously affects health or safety (such as a gas appliance or water heater), any defect you knew or should have known of, or your liability for injury. Cautious course: we assume you owe a non-waivable duty to keep the dwelling fit to live in, we assume you can't rely on a clause excusing your own negligence, and we treat the Consumer Protection Act as requiring you to reveal known defects. So don't exclude anything the home needs to be fit to live in (water heating, a working toilet, safe wiring), tell the tenant of known defects in excluded items, and have the tenant initial the list. Excluded gas appliances and generators remain subject to the Fire Safety Code.

title: Included Appliances in the Northern Mariana Islands
bodyText: We found no Commonwealth statute, regulation or court rule on appliances a landlord includes with a rental: nothing lists required appliances, sets a repair deadline for them, or turns an agreed appliance into a statutory repair duty with its own remedy. The lease sets the duty: the library's "Appliances & Equipment Included" clause ("appliances-included") carries MP and lists the appliances you will maintain. Cautious course: we assume you owe a duty to keep the dwelling fit to live in, so repair listed appliances promptly, especially those tied to health and safety (water heaters, ranges, air conditioners where the unit depends on them in the tropical heat); keep gas appliances and generators in line with the Fire Safety Code; and if CUC requires electrical equipment at the service entrance for a residential connection, that falls on the owner or occupant. What to do: list each appliance in the lease, note its condition at move-in, and say who handles routine items such as filters.

title: Common-Area Lighting in the Northern Mariana Islands
bodyText: We found no Commonwealth statute, regulation or court rule that requires a landlord to light common areas of a residential building to a set standard, or that governs charging a tenant for common-area lights wired to the tenant's meter. Lighting, exits and other building-safety features of new and altered buildings come from the International Building Code and International Fire Code, which the Commonwealth adopts by reference and which are not in the materials this library was built from; apartment common areas are part of the Building Safety Division's annual inspection. CUC's electric rules let a commercial customer allocate the cost of electricity among tenants but bar resale (see "edu-utility-interruption-submeter-mp"). Cautious course: keep common-area lights on your own account; if any common light is on a tenant's meter, say so in the lease, credit the tenant for the cost, and don't add a charge; and keep stairways, walkways and exits lit and in safe repair, since we assume you owe a duty to keep the premises safe for tenants and their guests. On Saipan, commercial-property owners must keep walkways and steps in safe condition.

title: Rent After a Vacate Order in the Northern Mariana Islands
bodyText: We found no Commonwealth statute, regulation or court rule that expressly bars a landlord from collecting rent after a building is condemned or ordered vacated. What the law does say: the Building Safety Official may declare a building unsafe (including when it is unsanitary or unfit for human habitation), order the owner to repair, vacate or demolish it within up to thirty days, order immediate vacating when there is immediate danger, and post signs barring entry; the building may not be re-occupied until a new certificate of occupancy issues. The Fire Division may issue an order of closure under which premises "will not be used for habitation". Failing to get the annual certificate of compliance for an apartment or residential rental raises issues of non-habitability and leads to revocation of the occupancy permit. Cautious course: we assume you owe a duty to keep the dwelling fit to live in, and charging rent for a home the government has barred anyone from living in risks being treated as an unfair practice under the Consumer Protection Act (which we treat as reaching residential leasing). So stop charging rent from the date a vacate or closure order takes effect, refund any rent paid for the period after it, and refund the deposit balance within ten days after the tenant returns the property if the lease ends. Government land acquisitions are handled under the relocation-assistance law (see "edu-alt-housing-mp"). What to do: say in the lease that rent stops while a government order bars occupancy, and keep your certificate of compliance current.

title: Habitability Gaps in Northern Mariana Islands Law
bodyText: This row lists what Northern Mariana Islands law does not contain on habitability, so you know where the lease and the cautious course have to do the work. We found no Commonwealth statute, regulation or court rule that: (1) states a residential landlord's duty to keep a rental fit to live in or an implied warranty of habitability; (2) lists minimum standards for the inside of a private rental (water, hot water, power, plumbing, cooling, screens, locks); (3) sets repair deadlines; (4) lets a tenant repair and deduct, withhold rent or pay rent into escrow (only Northern Marianas Housing Corporation's own public-housing grievance rule uses an escrow); (5) lets a tenant end the lease for an unfit unit; or (6) bars a landlord from retaliating against a tenant who complains about conditions (the only housing anti-retaliation rule protects people who exercise fair housing rights). What does exist: the Building Safety Code (with the International Building Code adopted by reference), the annual certificate of compliance for apartments and residential rentals (failing to get it "raised issues of non-habitability"), the unsafe-building and vacate procedures, the Fire Safety Code, DEQ's septic and wastewater rules, and on Saipan the exterior maintenance standards of the blight act; voucher units must meet HUD Housing Quality Standards. Where no written law speaks, the courts apply the Restatements, which this library has not read. Cautious course: assume you owe a duty to keep the dwelling fit to live in, that a tenant may have remedies if you don't, that you may not retaliate against a tenant for lawful complaints, and that you can't rely on a lease clause waiving those rules or excusing your own negligence. What to do: keep your certificate of compliance current, fix health and safety problems promptly, answer repair requests in writing, and never raise rent, cut services or seek possession because a tenant complained.

title: Repair Requests and Approved Repairers in the Northern Mariana Islands
bodyText: We found no Commonwealth statute, regulation or court rule that lets a tenant hire a repairer at the landlord's cost, requires a landlord to name a repair contact or approved repairer, or sets how quickly a landlord must respond to a repair request. Because no Commonwealth statute gives tenants a repair-and-deduct right (any common-law remedy is unsettled; Restatement not read), a lease term naming your repair contact and requiring your written approval before any repair at your cost is lawful, and the optional "Repair Requests and Approved Repairers" clause ("designated-repairer-mp") does that. Cautious course: we assume you owe a duty to keep the dwelling fit to live in, so the clause keeps a narrow emergency exception: if a condition threatens health or safety and you can't be reached or don't respond in the stated time, the tenant may take reasonable steps to prevent further harm and you reimburse reasonable documented costs. Repairs over $3,000 or that touch structure or exits may need a building permit, and contractors working on the property should be licensed so that only they, not individual workers, can claim a mechanics' lien. What to do: give tenants a working repair contact, including during typhoon season, and answer every request in writing.

title: Disability Accommodations in the Northern Mariana Islands
bodyText: Both the Commonwealth Fair Housing Act and the federal Fair Housing Act require you to make reasonable accommodations in your rules, policies, practices and services when they may be necessary to give a person with a disability equal opportunity to use and enjoy a dwelling (for example an assistance animal in a no-pets building, a reserved accessible parking space, or a change in how rent is paid), and to allow reasonable modifications at the tenant's expense (see "edu-alterations-mp"). The rule covers the tenant, anyone who will live in the unit, and anyone associated with them. You need not rent to someone whose tenancy would be a direct threat to others' health or safety or would cause substantial physical damage to others' property. The Commonwealth act's small-landlord exemptions (an owner of no more than three single-family houses renting without a broker; an owner-occupied building of four units or fewer) do not reach the advertising ban, and the federal act has its own exemptions. We found no Commonwealth rule that requires the lease itself to state your right to condition a modification on restoration, or on a restoration deposit. The federal fair housing regulation fills in the details: where reasonable, you may condition permission on the tenant restoring the interior at the end of the tenancy (reasonable wear and tear excepted); you may not raise the usual security deposit for a tenant with a disability; where needed to make sure restoration money will be there, you may negotiate, as part of the restoration agreement, payments over a reasonable period into an interest-bearing escrow account, not more than the cost of restoration, with the interest going to the tenant; and you may ask for a reasonable description of the work and reasonable assurances that it will be done in a workmanlike manner with any required building permits. Restoration can't be required where it is unreasonable (for example narrowing a doorway that was widened). Coercing or interfering with someone for exercising these rights is itself unlawful. What to do: use the "Service and Assistance Animals" clause ("assistance-animal-accommodation"), which carries MP, answer requests promptly and in writing, ask only for the information you need to confirm a disability-related need that isn't obvious, and keep a record of each request.

title: Double Letting in the Northern Mariana Islands
bodyText: We found no Commonwealth statute, regulation or court rule on "double letting" (renting the same room or unit to two tenants for the same period) or setting a rent-abatement or other remedy when it happens. A landlord who promises the same unit to two people breaks a contract with at least one of them, and the general remedies for breach apply; if the tenant can't get possession on the start date, the library's "Possession Delay" clause ("possession-delay"), which carries MP, gives rent abatement and a right to cancel. Cautious course: we treat the Consumer Protection Act as reaching residential leasing, so advertising or promising a unit you have already let could be an unfair or deceptive practice, and accepting two deposits for one unit invites a claim. What to do: keep one booking record per unit, don't take a second application fee or deposit for a unit already promised, and refund promptly if you can't deliver. Hotel-style room rentals of under 90 days are hotel-occupancy-tax business, not residential leases.

title: Screening Property Staff in the Northern Mariana Islands
bodyText: We found no Commonwealth statute, regulation or court rule that requires a residential landlord or property manager to run background checks on employees who have keys to or enter tenants' homes, or that licenses property managers or real estate agents. Background checks appear in Commonwealth law only for other settings (child care, schools, gaming, firearms, government and foreign-worker employment). The fair housing laws do reach anyone acting for you: assume that a broker, agent or employee who discriminates exposes you too (the fair housing acts' text read for this row has no rule on an owner's liability for agents; case law not searched), and using a broker or agent ends the single-family-house exemption under the Commonwealth and federal fair housing acts. Cautious course: we assume you must take reasonable care for tenants' safety, so screen anyone who will hold keys or enter units (references, and a police clearance where lawful and relevant to the job), keep a key log, give notice before entering under the lease's entry clause, and train staff on fair housing. Employment-law limits on using criminal records were not reviewed for this row.

title: Habitability: Material Defects in the Northern Mariana Islands
bodyText: We found no Commonwealth statute, regulation or court rule that defines which defects are "material" to habitability or that ties any tenant remedy to how serious a defect is; there is no statutory habitability duty at all (see "edu-confirmed-absences-habitability-mp"). The closest written standards are the Building Safety rules: a building is unsafe if it is structurally unsafe, unsanitary, unfit for human habitation, lacks adequate exits, is a fire hazard or is electrically unsafe, and failing to get the annual certificate of compliance for a rental raises issues of non-habitability. Cautious course: treat any condition of that kind, and any loss of water, power, sanitation or security, as material and fix it promptly; treat cosmetic items as ordinary repairs under the lease.

title: Waiving Habitability Duties in the Northern Mariana Islands
bodyText: We found no Commonwealth statute, regulation or court rule that says which habitability duties a lease may or may not shift to a tenant, or that lets a lease waive a water or hot-water duty where the property has no well or utility water. Because the Commonwealth has no statutory habitability duty (see "edu-confirmed-absences-habitability-mp"), the question turns on the Restatement and case law, which this library has not read or searched. Cautious course: assume the core duty to keep the dwelling fit to live in can't be waived, and don't rely on a clause excusing your own negligence. Where a property depends on rain catchment or a private well rather than CUC water, the lease may describe the system and make the tenant use it carefully, but keep the supply, storage and water quality your responsibility; the septic system is the owner's to maintain by regulation. Disclose any known limits (for example seasonal shortages) before the lease is signed.

title: Habitability Presumptions in the Northern Mariana Islands
bodyText: We found no Commonwealth statute, regulation or court rule that creates a presumption about habitability (for example that a landlord who fails to repair within a set time acted in bad faith, that a tenant's complaint followed by a landlord action is retaliatory, or that a unit with a code violation is uninhabitable). See "edu-confirmed-absences-habitability-mp" for the full list of gaps. The written rules that come closest are administrative: failing to secure the annual certificate of compliance "raised issues of non-habitability" and leads to revocation of the occupancy permit. Cautious course: keep your certificate current and your repair records complete, because without statutory presumptions a dispute will turn on the evidence of what you knew and did.

title: Habitability Statements in Leases in the Northern Mariana Islands
bodyText: We found no Commonwealth statute, regulation or court rule that requires the lease itself to state that the landlord will deliver or keep the unit fit to live in, or that prescribes any habitability wording. The library's "Maintenance & Repairs" clause ("landlord-maintenance") carries MP and matches the cautious course. Two written rules to keep in view: the Building Safety Division's annual certificate of compliance for apartments and residential rentals must be posted in a conspicuous place, and we treat the Consumer Protection Act as barring a lease from misstating a tenant's rights, so don't describe the unit as fit or code-compliant unless it is, and don't state that the tenant has no repair rights. See "edu-confirmed-absences-habitability-mp".

title: Public Health Permits for Rentals in the Northern Mariana Islands
bodyText: We found no Commonwealth statute, regulation or court rule that makes a landlord give tenants a copy of health rules on request or refer tenants to a health office. But the Commonwealth's public-health sanitation law can reach rentals directly. The Sanitation Act makes it unlawful to operate "hotels, motels, and other room accommodations" without a valid sanitary permit from the Commonwealth Healthcare Corporation's environmental health office (the Bureau of Environmental Health), displayed in a conspicuous place; the statute defines a room accommodation as a structure with four or more guest rooms offering overnight (or hourly) accommodations for pay, while the environmental health regulations define it more broadly as any place for sleeping or sheltering for a fee, expressly including apartments, boarding houses and staff houses, and the fee schedule lists a $140 permit for each single house or room rental. Permit holders get a pre-operation inspection (which checks the business licence and certificate of occupancy), inspections about every six months, must allow inspectors access, and face a warning, then fines of up to $500 and up to $1,000 for later violations, or suspension. Whether an ordinary long-term lease of a house or apartment needs a sanitary permit is unsettled: the statute points to guest-room lodging, the regulation's wording is broader. Cautious course: if you rent rooms, run a boarding or staff house, rent short-term, or have four or more rentable rooms, get the sanitary permit; for other rentals, ask the environmental health office in writing whether a permit is needed and keep the answer. Keep the premises sanitary in any case: the Department of Public Health may order an owner or occupant to clean or disinfect premises, and an imminent health hazard can close a permitted establishment.

title: Heating and Cooling in the Northern Mariana Islands
bodyText: Heating does not arise in the Northern Mariana Islands: the islands are tropical, with no cold season, and we found no Commonwealth statute, regulation or court rule on heat, heating equipment or minimum indoor temperatures in rentals, so rules elsewhere about supplying heat or shifting it to the tenant have nothing to attach to. Cooling is the practical issue, and we also found no rule requiring a landlord to provide air conditioning or setting who pays for cooling. If the unit comes with air conditioners or ceiling fans, list them in the "Appliances & Equipment Included" clause ("appliances-included") and maintain them; see "edu-appliances-included-mp". If a building's single meter mixes residential and commercial use, CUC bills it as commercial, which affects cooling costs (see "edu-utility-interruption-submeter-mp"). Typhoon preparation (shutters, generators) is better covered in the lease's maintenance terms.

title: Tenant Remedies for Landlord Breach in the Northern Mariana Islands
bodyText: We found no Commonwealth statute, regulation or court rule that sets a residential tenant's remedies when the landlord breaches the lease or fails to keep the unit in repair: no statutory right to end the lease on notice, to repair and deduct, to withhold rent or pay it into escrow, or to recover a statutory penalty. A tenant's remedies come from the lease and general law: a suit for damages or other relief in the Superior Court (claims of $5,000 or less can go to small claims), and, cautiously, a claim under the Consumer Protection Act, which we treat as reaching residential leasing (actual damages, an equal additional amount for a wilful violation, and costs and attorney's fees). Where no written law speaks, the courts apply the Restatements, which this library has not read; expect them to recognise remedies such as rent abatement or termination for a serious failure to keep the dwelling fit to live in. The Holdover Tenancy Act's fee-shifting covers only actions under that Act (possession cases). Federal fair housing law and the Commonwealth Fair Housing Act give their own remedies for discrimination, and the Fire Safety Code and Building Safety Code give anyone injured by a code violation a damages action with attorney's fees. What to do: respond to every repair request and breach notice in writing, fix health and safety problems first, and give rent credits for periods the unit can't be used; the library's "Possession Delay" clause ("possession-delay") covers late delivery.

title: Landlord Maintenance Duties in the Northern Mariana Islands
bodyText: Northern Mariana Islands law has no residential landlord-tenant act listing a landlord's repair and maintenance duties; see "edu-confirmed-absences-habitability-mp" for what is missing (no statutory habitability warranty, interior standards, repair deadlines, tenant self-help or lease-ending remedy, and no rule on air conditioning as an essential service). The library's "Maintenance & Repairs" clause ("landlord-maintenance") carries MP and follows the cautious course. What written law does impose on owners: (1) the Building Safety Code makes it unlawful to use, occupy or maintain a building in violation of the code (civil penalties up to $10,000 a day or 1 percent of project value, crimes for wilful violations, and a damages action with attorney's fees for anyone harmed), and unsafe, unsanitary or unfit buildings may be ordered repaired, vacated or demolished, with the Commonwealth's costs becoming a lien on the land; (2) apartments and residential rentals need an annual Building Safety certificate of compliance, posted conspicuously; (3) the Fire Safety Code applies to all buildings, with fines of $5,000 to $10,000 per violation and a private damages action; (4) owners maintain septic tanks, seepage pits and leaching fields; (5) on Saipan, the Nuisance Abatement and Blighted Property Maintenance Act sets exterior standards and lets the Commonwealth abate a nuisance, charge the owner, hold the owner personally liable and record a lien on the property and on other property of the owner, after warning periods (90 days for residential owners). Cautious course: assume you owe a duty to keep the dwelling fit to live in that a lease can't waive, including at the start of the tenancy; repair promptly, especially anything affecting water, power, sanitation, security, structure or fire safety; and keep cooling equipment you supply in working order.

title: Shifting Maintenance Duties in the Northern Mariana Islands
bodyText: We found no Commonwealth minimum-standards statute that lets (or forbids) a rental agreement to shift a listed maintenance duty, such as common-area garbage removal, to the tenant, and no precondition a landlord must meet first. Because the Commonwealth has no statutory list of landlord duties (see "edu-landlord-maintenance-mp"), allocating routine tasks is a lease matter: see the "Tenant Maintenance & Cleanliness" clause ("tenant-maintenance"), the "Landscaping & Irrigation" clause ("landscaping-irrigation") and the "Tenant Maintenance and Minor Repair Agreement" clause ("tenant-repair-agreement-pr"), all of which carry MP. Two limits: public-law duties stay with whoever the law names, whatever the lease says between you (for example the owner's septic maintenance duty, and on Saipan the duty of "every owner or occupant, as applicable" to keep residential exterior areas clean and to remove dead trees, enforced against the owner of record); and, cautiously, a lease can't shift to the tenant the core duty to keep the dwelling fit to live in, or excuse you from liability for your own negligence. What to do: shift only routine, clearly described tasks (yard care, trash set-out, filter changes), supply what the tenant needs to do them, and check periodically that they are being done.

title: Facilities You Must Provide in the Northern Mariana Islands
bodyText: We found no Commonwealth statute, regulation or court rule that lists the facilities a private landlord must supply inside a rental home, such as a stove, refrigerator, hot water, screens, a mailbox, laundry or a pool, so the lease sets what you provide: list every facility, appliance and shared amenity in it. A few Commonwealth rules still reach you. Garbage: everyone, including owners of residential property, must keep trash and garbage only in suitable waste containers with tight-fitting lids kept closed, with enough capacity between collections, and must keep the area around the containers clean; the Bureau of Environmental Health can fine $100 per violation plus $50 a day. Annual certificate: apartments and residential rentals, including single-family houses, need a yearly Building Safety certificate of compliance, and not having one raises issues of non-habitability. Sewer and septic: a building on a septic system must connect to the public sewer when the utility's sewer rules or the environmental director require it, and septic maintenance is the owner's job (see "edu-tenant-maintenance-mp"). On Saipan, the blight law requires owners or occupants to keep exterior residential areas clean and free of junk. Cautious course: we assume you owe a duty to keep the dwelling fit to live in, so supply working plumbing, water, power and sanitation even if the lease is silent (see "edu-confirmed-absences-habitability-mp"). What to do: provide lidded trash containers (or require the tenant to in a single-family lease), keep your certificate current, and list every facility you supply and any you do not.

title: Promises to Repair in the Northern Mariana Islands
bodyText: We found no Commonwealth statute, regulation or court rule that requires your promise to clean, repair or improve a rental to be in writing, to carry a completion date, or to be made before the lease is signed. Whether an oral or pre-lease promise binds you is a question of contract law (case law not searched). Three Commonwealth rules make writing it down the safer course. A lease for more than one year must be a written instrument signed by you, and an agreement that by its terms can't be performed within a year is unenforceable unless it, or a note of it, is in writing and signed by the party to be charged. We treat the Consumer Protection Act as reaching residential leasing, and it makes it unlawful to represent that something has been supplied as previously represented when it has not, or to engage in any unfair or deceptive practice, so an unkept promise used to win a tenant can expose you to actual damages, equal extra damages for a wilful violation, and attorney's fees. And we assume you owe a duty to keep the dwelling fit to live in whatever you promised. What to do: list every promised cleaning, repair or improvement, with a completion date, in the lease or a signed addendum, and don't make oral promises you don't intend to keep.

title: Quiet Possession in the Northern Mariana Islands
bodyText: We found no Commonwealth statute that writes a covenant of quiet possession or quiet enjoyment into a residential lease. Where no written law speaks, Commonwealth courts apply the common law as stated in the Restatements, and the common law generally implies that covenant in a lease (Restatement not read; case law not searched), so assume your tenant has it: you must not yourself disturb the tenant's possession, and you answer for anyone with a better claim to the property (for example a lender or a co-owner) who disturbs it. Commonwealth statutes protect possession in other ways. Recover possession from a tenant only through the Superior Court (the summary possession procedure is the statutory route): no statute allows a lockout or other self-help, and we assume none is lawful (Restatement not read; case law not searched). Making an unlawful and unauthorized entry upon, or interfering with the peaceful use and enjoyment of, the property of another, and refusing to leave or stop when lawfully told to, is criminal trespass, punishable by up to six months in jail. And a condominium declarant converting a rental building must give tenants at least 60 days' notice before requiring them to leave. What to do: enter only as the lease's access terms allow, deal with neighbor disturbances through the lease (see "edu-disturbance-mp"), and recover possession only through the court.

title: Rent Collection and Repair Duties in the Northern Mariana Islands
bodyText: Some states say that whoever collects the rent keeps the landlord's repair duties, whatever a lease, assignment, deed or mortgage says. We found no Commonwealth statute, regulation or court rule like that, and no statutory habitability duty for it to protect (see "edu-confirmed-absences-habitability-mp"). Two Commonwealth rules follow control of the property instead. On Saipan, the blight law's maintenance duties fall on the "owner", defined to include anyone with charge, care or control of a dwelling, such as a trustee, a mortgagee in possession, an assignee of rents, a lessee in control of the building, or their authorized agent. And after a foreclosure sale, the purchaser is entitled to receive the rents from the tenant in possession until redemption. Cautious course: we assume a residential landlord owes a duty to keep the dwelling fit to live in (Restatement not read; case law not searched), so assume that duty stays with whoever acts as landlord and collects the rent, and that assigning the rents to a lender, or having a manager or master tenant collect them, doesn't let anyone collect rent free of it. What to do: if a manager or master tenant collects rent, make the management agreement require it to handle repairs and keep the building's certificate of compliance current, and tell the tenant in the lease who to contact for repairs.

title: Government Inspections of Rentals in the Northern Mariana Islands
bodyText: The Commonwealth does have a periodic rental inspection program. Every apartment (a set of rooms with a kitchen and bathroom in a larger building, rented for periods of more than a month) and every residential rental, including a single-family house, a bed and breakfast or an Airbnb-type rental, is a "commercial occupancy" that must have an annual Building Safety inspection and Certificate of Compliance. For a single-family rental, or a building of fewer than five apartments, the entire premises are inspected; for 5 to 12 units, all common areas and half the units; for more than 12, all common areas and 35 percent of the units. The fee ($70 for a residential rental; $70, $85 or $100 for apartments by size) is paid in advance, the certificate issues within five days of a successful inspection and must be posted in a conspicuous place, and you must schedule the renewal inspection 10 to 30 days before the certificate expires. Failing to secure the certificate raises issues of non-habitability and leads to revocation of the building's occupancy permit. Separately, the Building Safety Official and the fire officials may enter a building at reasonable times to inspect for code violations; for an occupied building the fire officials must show credentials and demand entry, and if entry is refused either may get a court warrant. We found no Commonwealth rule on whether a lease may authorize an inspector's entry. Because the tenant controls access to the unit, the optional "Annual Building Safety Inspection" clause ("rental-inspection-mp") has the tenant allow the annual inspection on notice. What to do: put the renewal date on your calendar, arrange the inspection with the tenant in advance, and post the certificate. If a tenant refuses access, ask in writing for a time that works rather than relying on an inspector to force entry.

title: No Repair Escrow or Exemption Notice in the Northern Mariana Islands
bodyText: Some states let a landlord with only a few units opt out of tenants' rent-escrow or repair remedies by giving a notice. Northern Mariana Islands law has no statutory rent escrow, repair-and-deduct or rent-withholding remedy for private rentals, so there is nothing to opt out of and no exemption notice to give. The only rent escrow we found is in the Northern Marianas Housing Corporation's own public-housing grievance rules: a public-housing tenant disputing rent must keep paying the monthly rent into an escrow account while a delayed hearing is pending. A tenant's complaint about conditions would instead reach you through the common law, which the Commonwealth's courts apply where no statute speaks (Restatement not read; case law not searched), for example as a defense or counterclaim when you sue for rent or possession. Cautious course: assume you owe a duty to keep the dwelling fit to live in and that a court could reduce the rent owed for a period when you didn't (see "edu-confirmed-absences-habitability-mp"). What to do: don't add an exemption or waiver notice to the lease; answer repair requests promptly and in writing.

title: Repair Notices in the Northern Mariana Islands
bodyText: We found no Commonwealth statute, regulation or court rule on how a tenant must tell you about needed repairs: no rule that the notice be written, no rule about lease terms that accept oral or electronic reports, and no tenant repair remedy or statutory defense that turns on whether you had written notice or simply knew of the problem. So the lease may set how repair requests are made, for example in writing to a named repair contact (the optional "Repair Requests and Approved Repairers" clause, "designated-repairer-mp", does this). Cautious course: we assume you owe a duty to keep the dwelling fit to live in (Restatement not read; case law not searched), and a court applying the common law may hold you responsible for a condition you actually knew about even if the tenant never sent a written request. So don't rely on a written-request term to avoid fixing a problem you know about, and accept urgent reports (water, power, gas, typhoon damage) by phone or text and follow up in writing. What to do: name the repair contact and the accepted methods (phone, text, e-mail, written notice) in the lease, log every report you receive however it arrives, and answer in writing.

title: Locks and Security Devices in the Northern Mariana Islands
bodyText: We found no Commonwealth statute, regulation or court rule that requires a residential landlord to install particular locks, deadbolts, window latches, peepholes or door viewers, or to rekey or change locks between tenants, and none that lets a tenant demand a lock change or install one. The building and fire codes the Commonwealth adopts by reference (the International Building Code and International Fire Code) govern doors and exits; their provisions on doors, locks and exits are not in the materials this library was built from, so check them with Building Safety before changing door hardware, and never fit a lock that keeps a door from opening from the inside without a key. One related rule: a person convicted of a domestic-violence crime can be ordered to repay the victim's cost of new or added locks or a home security system, which doesn't put a duty on you. Cautious course: a landlord who controls the locks may face negligence claims if a former tenant's key is used in a crime (Restatement not read; case law not searched), so give every exterior door a working lock and deadbolt, make windows lockable, and rekey or change the locks before each new tenant moves in. The library's "Keys" clause ("keys") carries MP and governs keys and lock changes during the tenancy. What to do: rekey at turnover, record which keys you hand over, and respond quickly to a tenant's safety request, including from a domestic-violence victim.

title: Staff in Housing for Older Persons in the Northern Mariana Islands
bodyText: We found no Commonwealth statute, regulation or court rule that requires a work card, licence or background check for staff of senior (55-plus or 62-plus) housing or of any other ordinary rental housing. The background checks Commonwealth law does require are tied to other settings, such as day care centers. If you run housing for older persons, the rules that matter are the fair housing exemptions. Both the Commonwealth Fair Housing Act and the federal Fair Housing Act exempt "housing for older persons" from their familial-status rules: housing in a qualifying government program for the elderly, housing intended for and solely occupied by people 62 or older, or housing intended and operated for occupancy by at least one person 55 or older per unit, with at least 80 percent of units so occupied and published procedures showing that intent. The Commonwealth act tells the Housing Corporation's Corporate Director to write regulations on the 55-plus test; we found none in the Administrative Code, so follow the federal criteria. Cautious course: Commonwealth consumer law also makes it an offense for a merchant to discriminate on the basis of age, and that law has no older-persons exemption; we treat landlords as covered, so take advice before limiting a property by age. If you screen staff who will hold keys to residents' units, apply the same screening to everyone in the role and keep the results confidential. What to do: keep a key-control log for staff and contractors, and document your older-persons eligibility if you claim the exemption.

title: Services and Utilities You Provide in the Northern Mariana Islands
bodyText: We found no Commonwealth statute, regulation or court rule that lists services or utilities a private landlord must provide (such as water, power, hot water, air conditioning or trash collection), or that sets a landlord's liability when a service is interrupted. Which services you supply is a lease term: the library's "Services and Utilities Provided" clause in its "services-utilities-provided-ks-oh" form carries MP (the base form, which adds a "Landlord is not liable" sentence, does not), and you list what you pay for in "Utilities Paid by Landlord" ("utilities-paid-by-landlord"). Public water and power come from the Commonwealth Utilities Corporation, whose own rules say it will use reasonable diligence to avoid interruptions but is not liable for an interruption or shortage, so outages after a typhoon are usually CUC's, not yours. Cautious course: we assume you owe a duty to keep the dwelling fit to live in (Restatement not read; case law not searched), so keep the services you agreed to supply running, restore them promptly after an outage you control (for example a building pump, water tank or generator), and never cut a service to pressure a tenant. See "edu-utilities-responsibility-mp" and "edu-utility-service-continuity-mp" for CUC accounts and disconnections. What to do: list every service you supply, say how backup systems (catchment, tanks, generators) are run and paid for, and say what happens to rent during a long outage you cause.

title: Stoves and Refrigerators in the Northern Mariana Islands
bodyText: We found no Commonwealth statute, regulation or court rule that requires a private residential landlord to supply a stove, range or refrigerator, or that sets who must repair one you do supply. The only appliance list we found is in the Office of the Public Auditor's personnel rules, which require government-owned or government-leased housing given to its own employees to come with a cooking range and refrigerator; that rule binds the agency's housing, not ordinary rentals (though if you lease a unit to that office for its staff, expect the lease to require them). So whether you supply a stove or refrigerator, and who repairs it, is a lease term: list supplied appliances in the "Appliances Included" clause ("appliances-included") and any you don't supply in "appliances-excluded-la", both of which carry MP (see "edu-appliances-included-mp"). Cautious course: we assume you owe a duty to keep the dwelling fit to live in, so repair a gas or electrical fault in an appliance you supplied promptly, whatever the lease says about routine care. What to do: list each appliance by type in the lease and say who repairs and replaces it.

title: Code Enforcement and Receivership in the Northern Mariana Islands
bodyText: We found no Commonwealth statute, regulation or court rule that lets a court or agency appoint a receiver to collect rents and repair a substandard rental. The receivers Commonwealth law mentions are for mortgage and deed-of-trust foreclosures and for court cases generally. Code enforcement instead runs through repair, vacate and demolition orders. Under the Building Safety Code, buildings that are structurally unsafe, lack adequate exits, are fire hazards or are otherwise dangerous to human life, or are used unsafely because of poor maintenance, dilapidation or disaster damage, are public nuisances to be corrected by repair, rehabilitation, demolition or removal. The Building Safety Official can order the owner to repair, vacate or demolish within up to thirty days, order immediate vacating and post the building against entry, and in an immediate danger of collapse may act at once, with the government's costs becoming a lien on the land (see "edu-condemned-premises-rent-bar-mp" for rent during a vacate order). On Saipan, the Nuisance Abatement and Blighted Property Maintenance Act lets the Zoning Administrator order an owner to abate a nuisance (residential owners get a 90-day warning before daily penalties start), and if the owner doesn't, the Commonwealth may abate it, charge the owner and record a lien on that and the owner's other property. What to do: answer any Building Safety or Zoning notice within its deadline, keep your annual certificate of compliance current, and tell tenants promptly if an order affects their occupancy.

title: Cable, Satellite and Antenna Access in the Northern Mariana Islands
bodyText: We found no Commonwealth statute, regulation or court rule on a tenant's access to cable television, satellite or internet service in a rental: nothing makes a landlord let a cable or telecom company into a building, bars a rent difference for subscribers, or limits exclusive service deals. The Public Utilities Commission regulates telecommunications and cable companies, not landlords. Federal law does reach you. The FCC's over-the-air reception devices rule prohibits any restriction, expressly including a lease provision, that impairs a tenant's installation, maintenance or use of a satellite dish or fixed-wireless antenna one meter or less in diameter, or a television broadcast antenna (and a supporting mast), on property within the tenant's exclusive use or control, such as a balcony or patio the tenant leases. The rule doesn't give a tenant the right to install on common areas, the roof or exterior walls you control. Typhoon safety is a legitimate concern, but the rule's safety exceptions are in a part of the federal regulation not in the materials this library was built from, so keep any safety rule narrow and don't let it stop the tenant from getting a usable signal. What to do: don't ban dishes outright; say in the lease that a tenant may install a qualifying dish or antenna only within the leased premises, must secure it against high winds, must not drill into walls or the roof without consent, and must remove it and repair any damage at move-out.

title: Tenant Repair Remedies in the Northern Mariana Islands
bodyText: We found no Commonwealth statute, regulation or court rule giving a residential tenant a remedy for a landlord's failure to repair: no repair-and-deduct, no rent withholding, no rent escrow (only the Housing Corporation's own public-housing grievance rule uses one), no statutory right to end the lease, and no statutory damages (see "edu-confirmed-absences-habitability-mp"). Where no written law speaks, Commonwealth courts apply the common law as stated in the Restatements, which this library did not read (case law not searched). How a repair complaint reaches you in practice: if you sue for possession under the Holdover Tenancy Act, the tenant must put every defense in an answer filed within five days after service and may include a counterclaim, which you must answer within five days; no other pleadings are allowed, and either side may ask for a jury. The tenant may also sue you separately. Separately, the Building Safety Official can order repairs, vacating or demolition of an unsafe or unfit building, and failing to keep your annual certificate of compliance raises issues of non-habitability. Cautious course: assume you owe a duty to keep the dwelling fit to live in and that a court could reduce the rent owed, award damages or let the tenant leave if you don't. What to do: fix health and safety problems promptly, answer repair requests in writing, and expect a condition complaint to come up as a defense or counterclaim in any rent or possession case.

title: Utilities You Pay in the Northern Mariana Islands
bodyText: We found no Commonwealth statute, regulation or court rule that requires you to pay any utility for a tenant or limits which ones you may include in the rent. Which utilities you pay is a lease term: list them in the library's "Utilities Paid by Landlord" clause ("utilities-paid-by-landlord"), which carries MP. If a utility stays in your name, you are the Commonwealth Utilities Corporation's customer and responsible for its bills (CUC's rules make the owner or operator of commercial premises the customer rather than the tenants), so an unpaid bill can lead to disconnection of your tenant's unit (see "edu-utilities-responsibility-mp" and "edu-utility-service-continuity-mp"). Two cautions. First, if utilities are included in the rent, a CUC rate rise doesn't let you raise the rent during a Governor's price freeze, when raising housing rentals is a felony (EO 2026-020 of Sept. 23, 2026 kept a freeze in effect for Rota; check the Governor's current orders to see whether it still is); a cap on what you pay is possible only as an agreed term set at signing ("utility-allowance-cap-co", see "edu-utility-allowance-cap-mp"). Second, for a Housing Corporation voucher unit, the rent to owner includes any utilities you provide under the lease, and the Corporation decides whether the total is reasonable. What to do: list every utility you pay, say whether any has a usage limit, keep accounts in your name paid on time, and give the tenant a contact for outages.

title: Utility Allowance Caps in the Northern Mariana Islands
bodyText: No Commonwealth statute or regulation bars a lease term under which you pay a utility up to a set monthly allowance and the tenant reimburses the excess, and the library's "utility-allowance-cap-co" clause carries MP. The Commonwealth Utilities Corporation's rules shape how you do it. Power CUC sells to a customer may not be resold to third parties, though a commercial customer may allocate the cost of electric power among tenants; and water may not be resold without the written approval of CUC's Executive Director. A residential-only apartment building on a single meter is classed as a residential customer, and a customer is commercial if its operation needs a business licence, so whether a particular landlord is a commercial customer allowed to allocate is unsettled (see "edu-utility-interruption-submeter-mp"). Cautious course: treat the reimbursement as passing on your actual CUC cost, never as a sale. Bill only the amount on the CUC bill above the allowance, with no markup or fee, show the tenant the bill, and set the allowance at signing. During a Governor's price freeze it is illegal to raise the price of housing rentals, so don't lower the allowance or add a utility charge while a freeze is in effect, and be prepared to absorb a CUC rate rise that hits during one (EO 2026-020 of Sept. 23, 2026 kept a freeze in effect for Rota; check the Governor's current orders to see whether it still is). What to do: name the utility and allowance in the clause, and ask CUC how your account is classed before you pass any electricity cost to tenants.

title: Shared Utility Bills in the Northern Mariana Islands
bodyText: We found no Commonwealth statute, regulation or court rule that makes unenforceable a lease term requiring a tenant to pay a share of utilities that are not separately metered to the unit, and none that prescribes how shared utilities must be split (by floor area, occupants or another ratio). What applies is the Commonwealth Utilities Corporation's rules: power may not be resold to third parties, though a commercial customer may allocate the cost of electric power among tenants, and water may not be resold without CUC's written approval. Because a split of a shared bill can look like resale, and whether a residential-class landlord may allocate power is unsettled, the cautious course is to pass on only your actual CUC cost, with no markup or administrative fee, divided by a formula stated in the lease, and to show tenants the CUC bill (see "edu-utility-allowance-cap-mp" and "edu-utility-interruption-submeter-mp"). We treat the Consumer Protection Act as reaching residential leasing, so a split that isn't disclosed before signing, or that charges more than the real cost, risks being an unfair or deceptive practice. Where you can, have CUC meter each unit separately and put accounts in tenants' names. What to do: if a utility is shared, say in the lease which one, how the tenant's share is calculated, when it is billed and how the tenant can see the bill.

title: Utility Shutoff Notices to Landlords in the Northern Mariana Islands
bodyText: We found no Commonwealth statute, regulation or court rule that lets a landlord authorize the Commonwealth Utilities Corporation to tell it about a tenant's pending disconnection, or that lets a tenant-customer name the landlord to receive copies of shutoff notices. CUC's statutory protections run to its customer: no disconnection before the disconnection date, during the thirty-day grace period after the due date, on a Friday or the last workday of the week, while the customer is actively disputing a bill, or of all services when only one is unpaid; the security deposit must first be applied to the past-due amount. None of these gives a notice right to a non-customer owner. So if a tenant holds the CUC account, you learn of trouble only through the tenant. What you can do by contract: the library's "Evidence of Utility Payment" clause ("utility-payment-evidence") carries MP and lets you ask for proof of payment, and you may ask the tenant, in a signed writing, to authorize CUC to tell you about a pending disconnection or to copy you on notices; whether CUC will honour such an authorization is up to CUC, so ask it first. What to do: if keeping utilities on matters (for example to protect the unit from mold or a pump failure), consider keeping the account in your name and passing on the cost under the lease (see "edu-utilities-paid-by-landlord-mp").

title: Utility Accounts in Your Name in the Northern Mariana Islands
bodyText: When the Commonwealth Utilities Corporation account for a rental is in your name, you are the customer and the bill is yours. We found no Commonwealth statute, regulation or court rule that protects tenants when a landlord-held account goes unpaid: nothing lets tenants pay CUC and deduct the payment from rent, gives tenants a right to a rent receiver, imposes damages for failing to identify tenants to CUC, requires CUC to notify each unit before a building-wide shutoff, or bars CUC from cutting a tenant's service for the landlord's unpaid bill. CUC's customer protections (grace period, no Friday shutoff, no shutoff during a billing dispute, deposit offset first) run to you as customer, and CUC must cut off accounts more than 90 days past due that aren't being disputed. CUC accounts can't be transferred: a new customer must apply. Cautious course: we assume you owe a duty to keep the dwelling fit to live in, and letting a landlord-held account lapse so that a tenant loses water or power risks a damages claim and, if used to push a tenant out, looks like self-help eviction, which no Commonwealth statute allows and which we assume is unlawful (recover possession only through the Superior Court; Restatement not read). What to do: pay landlord-held accounts on time, tell tenants promptly about any planned interruption, and if you want tenants to take over an account, have them apply to CUC in their own names before the start date (see "edu-utilities-paid-by-landlord-mp" and "edu-utilities-responsibility-mp").

title: Utility Shutoff Rules in the Northern Mariana Islands
bodyText: The Commonwealth has a utility shutoff statute, but it governs the Commonwealth Utilities Corporation, not landlords. For residential customers CUC must allow a thirty-day grace period after the due date and may not disconnect during it; may not disconnect on a Friday or the last workday of the week, before the disconnection date, while the customer is actively disputing a bill, or a customer receiving utility assistance because the assistance agency paid late; must first apply the customer's security deposit to the past-due amount; may not cut all services when only one is unpaid (and may not cut water for unpaid power); and must reconnect on payment, for a $25 reconnection fee. CUC is liable for reconnection fees and costs if it disconnects in violation of these rules. We found no Commonwealth rule that adds time or bars disconnection during a typhoon, other declared emergency, hot weather or a medical need; the Governor's emergency orders we could reach don't address utilities. Who benefits depends on whose name the account is in (see "edu-utilities-responsibility-mp" and "edu-utility-landlord-account-mp"). For you as landlord: there is no statute on a landlord cutting a tenant's utilities, but recover possession only through the Superior Court (the statutory route; we assume self-help is unlawful), so never shut off or interrupt a utility you control to collect money or force a move-out.
