What to do: if an account is in your name, pay it, and if a tenant faces a CUC shutoff, point them to these protections and to CUC.

title: Submetered Utility Billing in the Northern Mariana Islands
bodyText: We found no Commonwealth statute, regulation or court rule that requires a lease disclosure, a separate signed page, a type size, a regulator's authorization or billing limits (such as a late-fee cap) for submetered or landlord-billed utilities, and no unit-count thresholds for any such rule. What applies is the Commonwealth Utilities Corporation's rules: power CUC sells may not be resold to third parties, though a commercial customer may allocate the cost of electric power among tenants, and where tenants are metered the meters must meet the ANSI C12.1 standard with cyclometer dials; water may not be resold without CUC's written approval (see "edu-utility-interruption-submeter-mp" and "edu-utility-allowance-cap-mp"). We treat the Consumer Protection Act as reaching residential leasing, so an undisclosed or marked-up utility charge risks being an unfair or deceptive practice. Cautious course: if you submeter or bill any utility, disclose it in the lease before signing (which utility, how usage is measured, the rate, which is your actual CUC cost with no markup, the billing date and how disputes are handled), give the tenant each meter reading and the CUC bill on request, and don't add a utility charge mid-term or while a Governor's price freeze is in effect. Never disconnect a submetered service yourself. What to do: write the disclosure into the lease or a signed addendum and keep meter readings for each billing period.

title: Moving Utilities into the Tenant's Name in the Northern Mariana Islands
bodyText: We found no Commonwealth statute, regulation or court rule that lets a landlord cut off utilities still in the landlord's name when a tenant fails to transfer them, or that sets a deadline for a tenant to put utilities in the tenant's own name. The Commonwealth Utilities Corporation's rules do shape the move-in: accounts can't be transferred, so a tenant must apply for service in the tenant's own name; a person who takes possession and uses water without applying is liable for the water used, and if they don't apply when CUC tells them to and don't pay the accumulated bills, CUC may discontinue the water without further notice. Anyone who takes possession and uses a utility without applying also counts as a "customer" under the theft-of-utility-services law, which makes it a crime to reconnect a lawfully disconnected service or connect to the utility's property without its consent. Cautious course: don't cut off a utility yourself to force a transfer; ask CUC to close your account as of a date and let CUC handle the switch, because cutting service to a tenant in possession can look like self-help eviction, which no Commonwealth statute allows and which we assume is unlawful (recover possession only through the Superior Court; Restatement not read) and may breach your duty to keep the dwelling fit to live in. The library's "Utilities Paid by Tenant" clause ("utilities-responsibility") carries MP and makes the tenant open accounts. What to do: require the tenant to apply to CUC before the start date, give CUC a closing date for your account with notice to the tenant, and record the meter readings on move-in.

title: Lock Changes for Domestic Violence Victims in the Northern Mariana Islands
bodyText: We found no Commonwealth statute, regulation or court rule that requires a landlord to change locks for a victim of domestic violence, lets a victim change the locks without the landlord's consent, or sets who pays. Two Commonwealth rules bear on it. The Superior Court, on a petition for an order for protection, may at once and without notice remove and exclude the abuser from the petitioner's residence regardless of who owns it, order the abuser to stay away from it, and have police accompany the petitioner to recover belongings; after a hearing it may also order the abuser to pay the petitioner's rent and reimburse expenses such as repair or replacement of damaged property. And a person convicted of a domestic-violence crime can be ordered to repay the victim's cost of new or added locks or a home security system. Federal law protects victims in federally assisted housing (for example Housing Corporation vouchers and low-income housing tax credit units) from eviction because of the abuse. Cautious course: when a tenant shows you an order for protection that excludes another occupant, even a co-tenant on the lease, change or rekey the locks promptly at the victim's request, don't give the excluded person a key, and don't charge the victim more than your actual cost (seek it from the abuser instead). What to do: keep a copy of the order, follow its terms, and use the library's "Keys" clause ("keys") for lock changes.

title: Inspections in the Northern Mariana Islands
bodyText: We found no Commonwealth statute, regulation or court rule on a landlord's right to inspect a rented home: no required notice period, no limit on how often or when you may inspect, and no move-in or move-out inspection rule for private rentals. So inspections are a lease term: the library's "Inspection Rights" clause ("inspection-rights") carries MP and ties inspections to the lease's access terms ("landlords-access", which sets at least 24 hours' notice except in an emergency). One inspection is required by law: apartments and residential rentals need an annual Building Safety inspection for their certificate of compliance (see "edu-rental-inspection-mp" and the optional "rental-inspection-mp" clause). Housing Corporation voucher units also have the Corporation's own inspections. Cautious course: we assume a tenant has a right to quiet enjoyment (see "edu-quiet-possession-mp"), and entering without the tenant's consent outside what the lease allows risks a claim, so give the notice the lease promises, inspect at reasonable times and for a stated purpose, and don't inspect so often that it harasses the tenant. What to do: schedule routine inspections in writing, invite the tenant to attend, and record the condition with dated photos.

title: Key Control in the Northern Mariana Islands
bodyText: We found no Commonwealth statute, regulation or court rule that requires a landlord, at any size of complex, to adopt a key-control policy, to secure master keys, or to run background checks on employees or contractors who have access to units. The only key-control rules we found are for casinos. So key control is your own policy, and the lease's "Keys" clause ("keys") carries MP for keys you hand the tenant. Cautious course: you may face negligence claims if a staff member or a former tenant uses a key you controlled to enter a unit (Restatement not read; case law not searched), and entering a unit outside what the lease allows risks a claim for interfering with the tenant's possession. If you screen staff, Commonwealth consumer law bars a merchant from discriminating by race, color, creed, religion, sex, age, ethnic background, national origin, citizenship, or place of birth or residence; we treat that as reaching you, and employment-law rules on background checks were outside this library's search, so take advice before using criminal records in hiring. What to do: keep master keys locked and logged, issue keys to staff and contractors only for a stated job and get them back, rekey units between tenants (see "edu-security-devices-mp"), and enter only as the lease's access terms allow (see "edu-inspection-rights-mp").

title: Landlord Entry in the Northern Mariana Islands
bodyText: We found no Commonwealth statute, regulation or court rule on a landlord's entry into a rented home: no minimum notice period, no list of permitted purposes or hours, no rule that a repair request is consent to entry, no separate-document rule for showings or scheduled services, no right for the tenant to refuse consent, no statutory remedy for refused access or for unlawful or harassing entry, and no rule on landlord-initiated temporary relocation. So entry is a lease term. The library's "Landlord's Access" clause ("landlords-access") carries MP and gives reasonable access during business hours on at least 24 hours' notice except in an emergency; the optional "scheduled-services-entry-la" (regular services) and "showing-notice-la" (shorter notice for showings near the end of the term) clauses also carry MP. If a tenant refuses access the lease allows, that is a breach other than nonpayment: unless the lease sets its own procedure, serve fifteen days' written notice to cure or leave, by hand or by leaving it at the unit if the tenant is absent, and only the Superior Court can order the tenant out. Cautious course: we assume the tenant has a right to quiet enjoyment, and entering beyond what the lease allows, or so often that it harasses the tenant, risks a damages claim and possibly a trespass complaint. Government inspectors' entry is separate (see "edu-rental-inspection-mp"). What to do: give the notice the lease promises in writing, knock and announce, enter for the stated purpose only, and keep a log of entries.

title: Entry for Scheduled Services in the Northern Mariana Islands
bodyText: We found no Commonwealth statute, regulation or court rule on entry for regularly scheduled services (such as pest treatment, air-conditioning filter changes or generator checks): no rule that such entry needs its own notice, a conspicuous lease term or a separate document, and no general entry-notice statute for it to modify (see "edu-landlord-entry-mp"). So you may set a service schedule in the lease. The library's optional "Regularly Scheduled Services" clause ("scheduled-services-entry-la") carries MP: it lists each service and its schedule, sets the hours, and still requires advance notice of each visit and a knock before entry. If a building with several units under one owner is fumigated for termites, the pesticide applicator must inform all tenants of the project at least 14 days before it (the library's "pest-cooperation-pr" clause, which carries MP, covers the tenant's cooperation). Cautious course: we assume the tenant has a right to quiet enjoyment, so keep scheduled entries to the listed services, times and notice. What to do: fill in the clause's schedule, send a reminder before each visit, and log each entry.

title: Showing Notice in the Northern Mariana Islands
bodyText: Because the Commonwealth has no statute setting an entry-notice period (see "edu-landlord-entry-mp"), there is no statutory notice for a tenant to waive, and we found no rule requiring a waiver or a shorter showing notice to be in a separate signed document. The notice for showings is whatever the lease sets. The library's optional "Showing Notice" clause ("showing-notice-la") carries MP: during the last part of the term, or after either side gives notice to end the tenancy, it allows showings to prospective tenants or buyers on a shorter notice you fill in, only during stated hours, and leaves every other entry under the main access clause. Cautious course: we assume the tenant has a right to quiet enjoyment, so keep showings to reasonable hours and frequency, accompany prospects, and don't show the unit when the tenant has asked you not to without first trying to agree a time. What to do: fill in the clause's days, notice and hours, and confirm each showing in writing (a text message is enough if the lease says so).

title: Smart Locks and Electronic Access in the Northern Mariana Islands
bodyText: We found no Commonwealth statute, regulation or court rule on smart locks, app-based or keypad entry, key cards or fobs, or other electronic access systems in rental housing: nothing requires you to offer a physical key, limits the data such a system collects, or sets rules for entry logs, cameras or biometric readers at a rental. The Commonwealth Constitution protects individual privacy, but whether that reaches a private landlord is unsettled (case law not searched). So a smart-access system is a lease and policy matter. Cautious course: tell the tenant in the lease what system you use, what it records (entry times, codes, video), who can see the records and how long you keep them; give each tenant their own code or credential and cancel it at move-out; don't use entry logs or remote unlocking to enter beyond what the lease's access terms allow (see "edu-landlord-entry-mp"); keep a working mechanical override or backup for power outages and typhoons; and don't point cameras into a unit. What to do: add the system and its data practices to the lease or a signed addendum, and change codes between tenants (see "edu-security-devices-mp").

title: Property Left Behind in the Northern Mariana Islands
bodyText: We found no Commonwealth statute, regulation or court rule that governs personal property a residential tenant leaves behind in an ordinary dwelling: no notice-and-storage procedure, no deemed-abandonment test (such as days without power or unpaid rent), no lease legend that waives your duties, no separate notice when the tenancy ends, and no rule for a manufactured home on a rented lot. So the procedure is a lease term: the library's optional "Handling of Property Left Behind" clause ("abandoned-property-mp") sets written notice, at least 30 days to claim, safe storage at reasonable cost, and a commercially reasonable sale or disposal, and the tagged "surrender-end-of-term-ks-ne" and "tenant-death-contact-nh" clauses point to it. Three Commonwealth and federal rules still apply. Lodging houses: a hotel, inn, motel or lodging-house proprietor, or a person who lets rooms to lodgers for hire, has a lien on a tenant's property brought into the rooms for unpaid rent (work tools and uniforms exempt), may sell after 30 days' default, and may sell baggage left 60 days, but only at public auction after published notice for two successive weeks (or posted notice at least 10 days before in three public places), with notice to the owner and the surplus paid over to the government; if you let rooms to lodgers, follow those sections instead of the clause's sale terms. Vehicles: no one may abandon a vehicle on private property without the owner's or possessor's consent, and the Department of Public Safety removes a vehicle found on private property when the owner or person in lawful possession asks it to. Servicemembers: it is a federal crime to hold a servicemember's belongings or deposit to collect rent for the period after the servicemember lawfully ended the lease. Cautious course: never remove belongings while the tenant is in possession; recover possession only through the Superior Court, whose writ removes all persons. What to do: inventory and photograph what is left, send the clause's notice, store it safely, and keep records of any sale.

title: Abandonment and Re-letting in the Northern Mariana Islands
bodyText: We found no Commonwealth statute, regulation or court rule on what happens when a tenant abandons a rental before the term ends: no definition of abandonment, no rule that the lease ends on abandonment or on the landlord's failure to re-let, no statutory duty for a landlord to mitigate damages by re-letting, and no rule that the tenant stays liable for rent for the rest of the term. Those questions go to the common law the Commonwealth's courts apply where no statute speaks (Restatement not read; case law not searched), and the answer there is not settled for this library. The tagged "Default by Tenant" clause ("default-by-tenant") carries MP and promises reasonable efforts to mitigate "to the extent required by applicable law", and the fixed-term early-termination clause ("early-termination-ks") lets a tenant leave on notice for a stated fee. Cautious course: assume a court may expect you to mitigate. If a tenant leaves early, document the abandonment (unpaid rent, belongings removed, utilities closed, keys returned), recover possession lawfully (by the tenant's surrender, or through the Superior Court if the tenant may still claim possession), advertise and show the unit promptly at a reasonable rent, credit any rent you receive from a new tenant against what the old tenant owes, and refund the deposit balance within ten days after the property is returned. Belongings left behind are handled under "abandoned-property-mp". What to do: keep dated records of your re-letting efforts, since they are your proof if you sue for the lost rent.

title: Attorney Fees in the Northern Mariana Islands
bodyText: Northern Mariana Islands law has a two-way fee rule for possession cases: in any civil action under the Holdover Tenancy Act (the summary possession action for nonpayment, breach or holding over), the party who wins may recover reasonable court costs, including attorney's fees, from the party who loses, whether that is you or the tenant. The statute already runs both ways, so no reciprocity sentence is needed, and we found no Commonwealth statute that voids or caps a lease fee clause, limits fees to a percentage, or lists the fees a lease may charge for an eviction or collection case. The library's "Default by Tenant" clause ("default-by-tenant") carries MP and gives the prevailing party fees "to the extent permitted under applicable law", which covers suits outside the Holdover Tenancy Act (for example a suit only for unpaid rent or damage). Other fee rules: a tenant who wins a fair housing case may recover fees; a consumer who wins under the Consumer Protection Act may recover costs and fees (we treat it as reaching leasing); bounced-check claims carry their own fee range (see "edu-returned-payments-mp"); and a third-party debt collector may add fees only if the lease expressly authorizes them and they are legally chargeable (see "edu-collection-fee-mp"). In court, a fee claim is made by motion filed within 14 days after judgment unless a statute or order says otherwise. Cautious course: keep the lease's fee clause mutual, limit it to reasonable fees a court awards, and don't add fixed attorney or collection charges to a tenant's account before a court awards them. What to do: track your fees by task, and file the fee motion on time.

title: Fire and Typhoon Damage in the Northern Mariana Islands
bodyText: We found no Commonwealth statute, regulation or court rule that gives either party a right to end a residential lease, or that abates or reduces rent, after a fire, typhoon, earthquake or other casualty, and none on retrieving belongings from a damaged unit. What happens after a casualty is set by the lease and, where it is silent, by the common law the Commonwealth's courts apply (Restatement not read; case law not searched). The library's optional "Landlord Termination After Fire or Typhoon" clause ("casualty-termination-mp") lets you end the lease by written notice within 30 days when the home is substantially unusable (unless you caused the damage), stops rent from the casualty date for any period the tenant can't lawfully live there, reduces it for partial use, refunds prepaid rent, and keeps the tenant's own rights and liability for damage the tenant caused. Three Commonwealth rules often follow a typhoon. A typhoon condition or declared emergency can bring a Governor's price freeze, during which raising housing rent is a felony (EO 2026-020 of Sept. 23, 2026 kept one in effect for Rota; check the Governor's current orders). The Building Safety Official may order a damaged building vacated or repaired (see "edu-condemned-premises-rent-bar-mp" on rent during such an order). And the deposit balance is due within ten days after the property is returned if the lease ends. Cautious course: we assume you owe a duty to keep the dwelling fit to live in, so don't charge rent for a period the home can't be lived in, let the tenant retrieve belongings as soon as it is safe, and give written notice of your plans to repair or end the lease. What to do: use the clause, photograph the damage, and tell the tenant in writing within days what you will do.

title: Condominium Conversion in the Northern Mariana Islands
bodyText: If you convert a rental building into condominiums, the Commonwealth's Uniform Condominium Act gives your tenants rights. A "conversion condominium" is one containing any building that was occupied, in whole or part, by people other than purchasers before the declaration was recorded. As declarant you must give each tenant and subtenant in possession written notice of the conversion at least 60 days before you require them to leave, setting out generally their rights, hand-delivered to the unit or mailed to the unit or another address the tenant gave you. You can't require a tenant to leave on less than 30 days' notice except for nonpayment of rent, waste or conduct that disturbs other tenants, and you can't change the terms of the tenancy during that period. Failing to give the notice is a defense to your possession action, and the notice doesn't let you end a lease early in breach of its terms; a notice that states a move-out date also counts as a notice to vacate. For 30 days after the notice you must offer to sell each residential unit to the tenant who leases it, and for the next 60 days you may not offer it to anyone else on better terms. The Constitution limits who may buy: a person not of Northern Marianas descent can't acquire a freehold or a ground-floor condominium unit, though an interest above the first floor of a condominium building is exempt; check the tenant's eligibility before the offer. We found no rule requiring a conversion statement in the lease, a 90-day notice, or limits on converting rentals to hotel or short-term use, and municipal or zoning rules are outside this library. What to do: calendar the 60-day and 30-day periods, keep proof of delivery, and keep existing fixed-term leases running to their end.

title: Notice and Cure Before Eviction in the Northern Mariana Islands
bodyText: Northern Mariana Islands law has two notice-and-cure tracks, plus removal at the end of the term. Unpaid rent: you may start a possession case after serving a three-day written notice in the form the statute prescribes, demanding the rent or possession within 3 days, not counting Saturdays, Sundays and legal holidays, from delivery; serve it by handing the tenant a copy, or if the tenant is absent, by leaving a copy at the unit. Paying the rent within that time cures the default. The lease is not invited to change that form, period or service, and federal e-signature law doesn't validate an electronic eviction or cure notice for a primary residence, so deliver it on paper. Other material breaches (anything but rent): if the lease is silent, serve fifteen days' written notice requiring the tenant to cure the breach or give up possession, by hand or by leaving it at the unit if the tenant is absent; you may give longer. The lease may set its own cure period and notice method for these breaches, and the tagged "Default by Tenant" clause ("default-by-tenant") leaves the fifteen days in place. End of the term: a tenant who stays after a fixed term ends without your permission can be removed with no further notice, and a periodic tenancy ends on the written notice in the statute unless the lease sets different periods (year 60 days, quarter 30, month 15, week 7). No ground is "no-cure" except the end of the term, and we found no limit on how many times a tenant may cure. On a property with a federally backed mortgage or in a federal housing program, the federal 30-day notice to vacate also applies (see "edu-cares-act-notice"). Only the Superior Court can order a tenant out. What to do: use the statutory three-day form word for word, keep proof of delivery, and give the fifteen-day notice in writing describing the breach.

title: Tenant Default in the Northern Mariana Islands
bodyText: The library's "Default by Tenant" clause ("default-by-tenant") carries MP, and Northern Mariana Islands law fits it this way. Rent default: the statutory three-day written notice in the prescribed form, served by hand or, if the tenant is absent, left at the unit (see "edu-cure-and-eviction-grounds-mp"). Other breaches: the lease may set its own cure period and notice method; because the clause gives notice without a stated period, the statute's fifteen days' written notice to cure or leave applies. Ending the tenancy: the lease may let you end it for a tenant's breach, but recover possession only through the Superior Court (the summary possession action is the statutory route): no statute lets you terminate and retake the unit yourself, and we assume self-help is unlawful (Restatement not read). Money: the court enters a money judgment in the possession case only if your complaint expressly and specifically asks for money damages; a tenant who holds over after termination without your permission can be made to pay double the rent for the period of refusal (the statute says you 'may also recover' it; case law not searched; see "holdover-mp"); we found no treble-damages rule for holding over or rent default (a bounced rent check has its own treble-damages option; see "edu-returned-payments-mp"). Fees: the winner of a Holdover Tenancy Act action may recover reasonable costs and attorney's fees from the loser, in either direction (see "edu-attorney-fees-mp"). We found no statute requiring you to mitigate (the clause promises reasonable efforts "to the extent required by applicable law"; see "edu-abandonment-and-mitigation-mp"), no limit on how many times a tenant may cure, and no ban on lease collection charges other than the debt-collector rule (see "edu-collection-fee-mp"). What to do: name money damages in the complaint if you want them, and keep the notice, proof of service and ledger for court.

title: Typhoons and Declared Disasters in the Northern Mariana Islands
bodyText: We found no Commonwealth statute, regulation or court rule that ends a tenancy, suspends rent, or bars evictions after a declared typhoon, other natural disaster or emergency, or that sets what rent is owed while a home can't be reached. The Commonwealth's main disaster rule for landlords is the price freeze. When the Governor declares typhoon condition two, tropical storm condition one, or a state of significant emergency or major disaster, the Governor may declare a price freeze; while it lasts, it is illegal to raise housing rentals, including apartments and condos. Raising rent during a freeze is a felony (up to $10,000 or one year in prison) and carries a civil penalty of up to $2,500 per violation. A freeze declared on April 11, 2026, as Typhoon Sinlaku approached (EO 2026-005), was lifted for Saipan and Tinian on Sept. 23, 2026 but kept in effect for Rota after Super Typhoon Bavi (EO 2026-020); a freeze ends when the Governor rescinds it or the emergency declaration ends, so check the Governor's current executive orders before any increase. What happens to the lease after storm damage is otherwise set by the lease (see "edu-casualty-termination-mp" and the optional "casualty-termination-mp" clause) and the common law (Restatement not read; case law not searched). Cautious course: don't charge rent for a period the home can't lawfully or safely be lived in, don't raise rent or add charges during a freeze (including at renewal), and refund the deposit balance within ten days after the property is returned if the lease ends. What to do: keep tenants informed in writing after a storm, document damage, and check whether a freeze covers your island before changing rent.

title: Eviction Protection for Abuse Victims in the Northern Mariana Islands
bodyText: We found no Commonwealth statute, regulation or court rule that bars evicting a tenant because the tenant is a victim of domestic violence, sexual assault, dating violence or stalking, or that limits using abuse-related incidents (police calls, property damage, noise) against the victim. Federal law does for housing in a federal program, including Housing Corporation public housing and Section 8 vouchers and low-income housing tax credit properties: you may not deny, end assistance to, or evict a tenant because the tenant is or has been a victim, an incident of actual or threatened abuse isn't a serious or repeated lease violation by the victim or good cause to end the victim's tenancy, and you may not end the tenancy solely because of abuse-related crime by a household member or guest when the tenant is the victim; you may split the lease to remove the abuser while keeping the victim. In that federally assisted housing, if a tenant or applicant claims these protections you may, but need not, ask in writing for documentation; the person has 14 business days to provide it, and you may extend that. Acceptable documentation is any one of: the HUD-approved certification form; a statement signed by the person and by a victim service provider, attorney, medical professional or mental health professional who helped them, stating under penalty of perjury that the incident qualifies; a police, court or administrative agency record; or, at your discretion, the person's own statement or other evidence. If documents conflict you may require third-party documentation. Everything submitted, including the fact that someone is a victim, must be kept confidential and may not go into a shared database or be disclosed except with the person's written consent, for use in an eviction proceeding under the federal rules, or as otherwise required by law. You must give the HUD notice of rights, with the certification form, to applicants you admit or deny and with any eviction or termination notice. The federal programs must also have emergency transfer plans that let a threatened victim ask to move to another available, safe assisted unit (see "edu-dv-lease-termination-mp"). Commonwealth protection orders can also remove an abuser from the residence regardless of who owns or leases it (see "edu-dv-lockchange-mp"). Cautious course for any landlord: don't treat a victim's calls for help or the abuser's conduct as the victim's breach; act against the person who caused the harm; and if a court order excludes a co-tenant, follow it. The tagged "criminal-activity-ky" clause already excludes victims. What to do: train staff to recognise these situations, keep any information a tenant shares confidential (in covered housing that is a federal duty), and take advice before starting any case against a tenant who reports abuse.

title: Early Termination for Abuse Victims in the Northern Mariana Islands
bodyText: We found no Commonwealth statute, regulation or court rule that lets a victim of domestic violence, sexual assault, dating violence, stalking or trafficking end a lease early, that says whether one tenant's early termination ends the lease for co-tenants, or that gives a landlord a special right against an abuser left as the sole tenant. A victim who needs to leave depends on the lease (for example the fixed-term early-termination clause "early-termination-ks", which carries MP) or on your agreement. Related rules: a Commonwealth order for protection can remove and exclude the abuser from the residence regardless of who owns or leases it and, after a hearing, order the abuser to pay the petitioner's rent (see "edu-dv-lockchange-mp"); and housing assisted under a federal covered housing program (for example Housing Corporation public housing and vouchers, and low-income housing tax credit units) has federal victim protections against eviction (see "edu-dv-eviction-protection-mp"). Federal law gives no right to end a lease there either, but each federal program must have an emergency transfer plan: a tenant who expressly asks and reasonably believes they face imminent harm from further violence if they stay in the unit, or a sexual-assault victim whose assault happened on the premises within the previous 90 days, may transfer to another available and safe assisted unit, and the plan must keep the new unit's location from the abuser. Follow the program's plan and the Housing Corporation's procedures for those units. Cautious course: if a tenant shows you a protection order or other reliable evidence of abuse and asks to leave, agree in writing to release the tenant without an early-termination fee, refund the deposit balance within ten days after the property is returned, and keep the information confidential; you may continue the lease with any remaining co-tenant who wants to stay and qualifies. What to do: respond to such a request in writing within days, and don't disclose the tenant's new address to anyone.

title: Proof of Abuse for Lease Purposes in the Northern Mariana Islands
bodyText: Because the Commonwealth gives victims no statutory lease-termination or eviction protection of its own (see "edu-dv-lease-termination-mp" and "edu-dv-eviction-protection-mp"), we found no Commonwealth statute, regulation or court rule listing documents a tenant must give a landlord to prove domestic violence, sexual assault, dating violence or stalking (such as a protection order, police report or third-party statement). The most common document you will see is an order for protection from the Superior Court, which is served by the Department of Public Safety and entered in the Commonwealth's registry for orders for protection. Federal law sets a documentation rule only for housing assisted under a federal covered housing program (for example Housing Corporation public housing and vouchers, and low-income housing tax credit units). In that federally assisted housing, if a tenant or applicant claims these protections you may, but need not, ask in writing for documentation; the person has 14 business days to provide it, and you may extend that. Acceptable documentation is any one of: the HUD-approved certification form; a statement signed by the person and by a victim service provider, attorney, medical professional or mental health professional who helped them, stating under penalty of perjury that the incident qualifies; a police, court or administrative agency record; or, at your discretion, the person's own statement or other evidence. If documents conflict you may require third-party documentation. Everything submitted, including the fact that someone is a victim, must be kept confidential and may not go into a shared database or be disclosed except with the person's written consent, for use in an eviction proceeding under the federal rules, or as otherwise required by law. You must give the HUD notice of rights, with the certification form, to applicants you admit or deny and with any eviction or termination notice. Use the Housing Corporation's or the program's forms for those units. Cautious course for other rentals: if you agree to release or protect a tenant who reports abuse, accept any reasonable evidence (a protection order, a police report, or a written statement from a victim advocate, doctor or counselor), ask for no more than you need, keep it confidential and apart from the tenant file, and don't share it with the alleged abuser. What to do: write down what you accepted and why, and decide promptly.

title: Early Termination in the Northern Mariana Islands
bodyText: We found no Commonwealth statute, regulation or court rule that gives a residential tenant a right to end a lease early, caps an early-termination fee, requires the fee to be in a separate signed addendum, or defines abandonment. So early termination is a lease term: the library's "early-termination-ks" clause carries MP; it lets a tenant under a fixed term leave on 30 days' written notice for a stated fee, says the fee doesn't apply to month-to-month tenancies, and keeps the tenant's federal and other legal rights. Its "vacates or abandons" limb for you raises no Commonwealth conflict, because no statute defines abandonment; as a cautious course, still recover possession only by the tenant's surrender or through the Superior Court (no statute allows self-help). Federal law gives servicemembers a termination right that overrides the lease: a servicemember who enters military service after signing, or who gets permanent-change-of-station or deployment orders of at least 90 days, may end a residential lease by written notice with a copy of the orders; for monthly rent, termination takes effect 30 days after the next rent due date following delivery, rent is prorated to that date, and you may not charge an early-termination fee. Spouses and dependents have related rights on the servicemember's death or catastrophic injury. Cautious course: we treat the Consumer Protection Act as barring unconscionable terms, so keep any fee reasonable in relation to your likely loss from re-letting (one month's rent is common), don't also collect rent for the same period from a new tenant, and refund the deposit balance within ten days after the property is returned. What to do: fill in the clause's fee, and accept a servicemember's notice with orders without a fee.

title: Eminent Domain in the Northern Mariana Islands
bodyText: Only the government condemns property in the Northern Mariana Islands. The Constitution lets the Commonwealth take private property for a public purpose as provided by law, never without just compensation, and private land only if no suitable public land is available; the condemnation statute has the court fix a fair value, decide any ownership dispute, and state in the judgment the land or interest acquired and the compensation to be paid to the defendants. Federal takings are governed by the Covenant. We found no Commonwealth statute that ends or reduces the tenant's rent when the leased property is taken, or that lets the condemnation court cancel the lease, and none that divides the award between landlord and tenant. So the lease sets those terms: the tagged "Eminent Domain" clause ("eminent-domain-vi") carries MP. A tenant displaced by a Commonwealth land acquisition may also be entitled to relocation payments and help finding housing from the acquiring agency under the Commonwealth's relocation-assistance law (see "edu-alt-housing-mp"). Cautious course: if part of the property is taken, reduce the rent in proportion to the lost use, and if the home becomes unusable, end the lease and refund prepaid rent and the deposit balance within ten days after the property is returned. What to do: tell the tenant in writing as soon as you receive a condemnation notice, and name the tenant's interest if the government asks who holds interests in the land.

title: Entity Landlords in Court in the Northern Mariana Islands
bodyText: A court rule, not a statute, speaks to this in the Northern Mariana Islands. In small claims (claims of $5,000 or less, not counting interest, attorney's fees and costs), parties are encouraged to appear without lawyers, but no one who isn't an attorney licensed in the Commonwealth may represent another person or a corporation; an employee with first-hand knowledge of the facts may appear for the employer. So a corporate or LLC landlord may send a knowledgeable employee (such as its property manager on staff) to small claims, but not an outside agent or a member who isn't an employee unless that person is a licensed attorney. We found no Commonwealth statute or court rule that expressly lets a non-attorney appear for an entity in the Superior Court's ordinary civil cases, including the summary possession action under the Holdover Tenancy Act, and the usual rule elsewhere is that an entity must appear through a lawyer (case law not searched). Cautious course: if your landlord is a corporation, LLC, partnership or trust, file and appear in possession cases through a CNMI-licensed attorney; an individual owner may represent himself or herself. Remember that the winner of a Holdover Tenancy Act case may recover reasonable attorney's fees from the loser (see "edu-attorney-fees-mp"). What to do: line up counsel before you serve a three-day or fifteen-day notice if the owner is an entity.

title: Environmental Events and the Lease in the Northern Mariana Islands
bodyText: We found no Commonwealth statute, regulation or court rule that lets either party end a residential lease because of an environmental or public-health event, such as contamination, a chemical or fuel spill, sewage overflow, mold, volcanic activity or a government order to vacate. The related rules: the Building Safety Official may declare a building unsafe or unfit for human habitation and order it vacated (see "edu-condemned-premises-rent-bar-mp"); federal law requires lead-based paint disclosure for pre-1978 housing (the tagged "lead-based-paint" clause); and the Commonwealth gives no casualty termination right either (see "edu-casualty-termination-mp"). So an opt-in right to end the lease after such an event is a lease term. The library's optional "Landlord Termination After Fire or Typhoon" clause ("casualty-termination-mp") covers damage from fire, typhoon, earthquake "or other casualty"; if you want to cover non-physical events (for example a contamination order with no physical damage), add them expressly and give the tenant the same rent and refund protections. Cautious course: we assume you owe a duty to keep the dwelling fit to live in (Restatement not read; case law not searched), so don't charge rent for a period the home can't lawfully or safely be occupied, and refund prepaid rent and the deposit balance within ten days after the property is returned if the lease ends. What to do: tell tenants promptly in writing about any environmental order affecting the property and what you will do.

title: Stays of Eviction in the Northern Mariana Islands
bodyText: We found no Commonwealth statute or court rule that lets a court postpone a tenant's removal for hardship (illness, age, children, weather or inability to find housing). What does affect timing: under the civil rules, no execution may issue on a judgment, and no proceedings may be taken to enforce it, until 14 days after the judgment is entered, unless the court orders otherwise; the court may stay execution on terms while a motion for a new trial or relief from judgment is pending; and a tenant who appeals may get a stay by posting a supersedeas bond the court approves. The Holdover Tenancy Act itself sets five days to move for a new trial and 30 days to appeal, and if the tenant was served only by posting at the premises, at least five working days must pass after service before a judgment for final removal. Whether the 14-day rule applies to a summary possession judgment or is displaced by the Act's own timetable is unsettled (case law not searched); the cautious course is to wait 14 days after judgment before asking for the writ. After judgment the clerk issues a writ commanding the officer to remove all persons and put you in possession; only that officer, not you, carries it out. What to do: plan for at least two weeks between judgment and removal, and if the tenant asks for more time, consider a written move-out agreement rather than enforcement.

title: The Eviction Process in the Northern Mariana Islands
bodyText: The statutory route to recover possession of a private rental is the Holdover Tenancy Act's summary possession action in the Superior Court for the senatorial district where the property is (Saipan, Tinian or Rota), and no statute allows self-help; the Act doesn't apply to leases with the Commonwealth government or its agencies, and the court's mediation rules don't apply to these cases. Steps: serve the statutory notice (three days for rent, fifteen days to cure another breach if the lease is silent, none after a fixed term ends; see "edu-cure-and-eviction-grounds-mp"); file a complaint stating the facts and describing the premises, and ask expressly for money damages if you want a money judgment too; have the summons and complaint served under the court rules, and if the tenant can't be found after two attempts at least six hours apart, the officer may post them at the premises, in which case you give the clerk two extra copies and two stamped envelopes for mailing and must wait at least five working days after service before final judgment. The tenant must file every defense, and any counterclaim, in an answer within five days after service, and you answer a counterclaim within five days; no other pleadings are allowed, depositions may be taken but other discovery needs a court order, and either side may demand a jury within five days after the case is at issue. New-trial motions are due within five days after judgment and appeals within 30 days; the clerk then issues a writ directing the officer to remove all persons and put you in possession. Counting days: the court rules exclude intermediate Saturdays, Sundays and legal holidays from periods of 10 days or less unless the period is stated in calendar days, so expect the five-day deadlines to run on business days; the three-day rent notice excludes weekends and holidays by its own terms, and the cautious course is not to shorten the fifteen-day notice for weekends. The winner may recover reasonable costs and attorney's fees (see "edu-attorney-fees-mp"). We found no for-cause protection after a set tenancy length, no rent-into-court order during adjournments, no rent-affidavit condition on appeals, no bar on courts using required forms, no rules on private process servers' recordings, no shutdown continuance, and no lease-specific wage-attachment cap; a money judgment is collected through orders in aid of judgment, which must leave the tenant enough income and property for reasonable living needs (household goods and work tools are exempt). Federal law adds a 30-day notice to vacate for covered properties (see "edu-cares-act-notice") and protections for servicemembers. What to do: follow the steps in order, keep proof of every notice and service, and use an attorney if the landlord is an entity (see "edu-entity-landlord-court-representation-mp").

title: Eviction Records in the Northern Mariana Islands
bodyText: We found no Commonwealth statute or court rule that seals, expunges or removes from public indexes the record of an eviction (summary possession) case, whether the landlord won, lost or dismissed, and so no procedure for a landlord to object to sealing. The sealing and expungement rules we found are for criminal history, first-offense drug discharges, juvenile records, identity-theft victims and particular sealed documents a court orders. Court files in civil cases, including possession cases, are generally available through the clerk except for documents or cases the court has sealed. Using eviction records to screen applicants is not barred by any Commonwealth rule we found, but fair housing and consumer law still apply: don't screen on any Commonwealth or federal fair housing class, and apply the same criteria to every applicant. Cautious course: rely on the outcome of a case, not the mere filing, when screening, because a filed case may have been dismissed or settled. What to do: if you settle a possession case, put any agreement about dismissal or record handling in writing and file the dismissal promptly.

title: Service of Eviction Papers in the Northern Mariana Islands
bodyText: Northern Mariana Islands law gives the lease a role in eviction service in two places, and we found no address-confidentiality program that reroutes service for protected tenants. First, court papers: the summons and complaint are served under the court rules (personally, at the tenant's home with a resident adult, or on an agent the tenant has authorized by appointment to receive service). If the officer can't find the tenant after two attempts and posts the papers at the premises, you must give the clerk two extra copies and two stamped envelopes, one addressed to the address the tenant designated for notices in a written lease or other agreement (or, if none, the tenant's residential mailing address, if known) and one to the tenant's last known business address. So a notice address in the lease decides where the clerk mails. Second, pre-suit notices: for breaches other than rent, the lease may prescribe how notices are served; the three-day rent notice must still be handed to the tenant or, if the tenant is absent, left at the unit. Whether a tenant's appointment, in a landlord-drafted lease, of an agent to accept eviction papers would be upheld is unsettled (case law not searched), so don't rely on one. The optional "Tenant's Address for Notices and Court Papers" clause ("eviction-service-party-mp") records the tenant's designated address. The tagged "Tenant to Forward Notices of Proceedings" clause ("tenant-forward-proceedings-ca") covers papers about the property sent to the tenant. What to do: fill in a real mailing address (a P.O. box is common in the Commonwealth), and update it whenever the tenant tells you of a change.

title: Criminal Activity in the Northern Mariana Islands
bodyText: We found no Commonwealth statute that gives a landlord a fast-track eviction for violent or drug crime, makes any criminal ground "no-cure", requires a landlord to evict, authorizes or regulates a crime-free lease addendum, lets third parties (police, prosecutors, tenant groups) bring an eviction, or requires the lease to state a right to end it for criminal use. So removal for criminal activity runs through the ordinary route: it is a breach of the lease other than nonpayment, and unless the lease sets its own procedure you must serve fifteen days' written notice to cure or leave before going to the Superior Court. The library's optional "Criminal Activity" clause ("criminal-activity-ky") carries MP; it makes listed criminal activity a material breach under the lease's default terms and excludes a tenant or household member who is the victim. Commonwealth criminal law reaches owners in some cases: a person with possession or control of premises who knows they are used for prostitution and fails without lawful excuse to try to report, halt or abate it commits a crime; an owner, manager or lessor who knowingly permits a place to be used for illegal marijuana sales is guilty of a violation, and the building can be subject to a lien for the occupants' fines. Federal law bars a federally assisted landlord from denying or ending a tenancy solely because of domestic-violence-related crime by a household member or guest when the tenant is the victim; Housing Corporation public-housing and voucher rules have their own criminal-activity grounds. For Housing Corporation voucher (Section 8) units, federal rules require the lease to make drug-related criminal activity on or near the premises by a tenant, household member or guest grounds for ending the tenancy, and let the owner act on its own determination without an arrest or conviction, but only by court action. Marijuana in federally assisted housing: HUD's rules define a "drug" as a controlled substance under the federal Controlled Substances Act, and federal regulations list marijuana in Schedule I; the Commonwealth's Cannabis Act says it does not exempt anyone from federal law. So marijuana use, possession or growing that is legal under Commonwealth law is still drug-related criminal activity under HUD's definitions, and voucher leases must treat it that way (other federally assisted programs have their own lease rules, not reviewed here). Cautious course: act on reliable evidence (police reports, convictions, your own observation), not arrests alone, and apply the clause the same way to everyone. What to do: report suspected drug sales or prostitution to the police, give written notice under the lease, and keep records.

title: Drug-Free Lease Terms in the Northern Mariana Islands
bodyText: We found no Commonwealth statute or regulation that requires, authorizes or limits a drug-free housing addendum in a private lease, or that gives a landlord a special remedy for drug activity. A drug-free term is a lease term: the library's optional "Criminal Activity" clause ("criminal-activity-ky") carries MP and makes the illegal manufacture, sale, distribution or possession of controlled substances on the property a material breach, while protecting a tenant or household member who is a crime victim. Removal still runs through notice and the Superior Court (see "edu-criminal-activity-mp"). Marijuana: the Commonwealth's cannabis law expressly doesn't change landlord-tenant law, so the lease may ban marijuana use and growing even where they are legal, and an owner, manager or lessor who knowingly lets a place be used for illegal marijuana sales commits a violation (see "edu-smoking-policy-mp"). Housing Corporation public-housing and voucher units follow the Corporation's and HUD's own lease rules, which this library flags but doesn't restate. For Housing Corporation voucher (Section 8) units, federal rules require the lease to make drug-related criminal activity on or near the premises by a tenant, household member or guest grounds for ending the tenancy, and let the owner act on its own determination without an arrest or conviction, but only by court action. Marijuana in federally assisted housing: HUD's rules define a "drug" as a controlled substance under the federal Controlled Substances Act, and federal regulations list marijuana in Schedule I; the Commonwealth's Cannabis Act says it does not exempt anyone from federal law. So marijuana use, possession or growing that is legal under Commonwealth law is still drug-related criminal activity under HUD's definitions, and voucher leases must treat it that way (other federally assisted programs have their own lease rules, not reviewed here). What to do: if you want a drug-free term, use the clause rather than a separate addendum, say whether it covers marijuana, and apply it the same way to every tenant.

title: Eviction for Criminal Activity in the Northern Mariana Islands
bodyText: We found no Commonwealth statute or court rule that creates a faster or separate eviction procedure for drug, violent or other criminal activity, lets police, prosecutors or neighbors bring the case, or removes the tenant's right to notice. A tenant's criminal activity is handled as a lease breach other than rent: unless the lease sets its own procedure, you serve fifteen days' written notice to cure or leave, then use the Holdover Tenancy Act's summary possession action, which is already quick (answer within five days of service, limited discovery, new-trial motions within five days). The optional "Criminal Activity" clause ("criminal-activity-ky") carries MP and makes listed criminal activity a material breach (see "edu-criminal-activity-mp"). Where there is immediate danger, call the police; a protection order can remove an abuser from a home at once (see "edu-dv-lockchange-mp"). Federal rules protect tenants in federally assisted housing who are victims of the crime (see "edu-dv-eviction-protection-mp"). For Housing Corporation voucher (Section 8) units, federal rules require the lease to make drug-related criminal activity on or near the premises by a tenant, household member or guest grounds for ending the tenancy, and let the owner act on its own determination without an arrest or conviction, but only by court action. Cautious course: never lock out or remove a tenant yourself, however serious the conduct; possession comes only through the court. What to do: document the conduct (police report numbers, dates, witnesses), serve the written notice, and file promptly.

title: Foreclosure of a Rental in the Northern Mariana Islands
bodyText: If the rental is mortgaged and the lender forecloses, the mortgage can be foreclosed only through the court remedies in the Real Estate Mortgage Law. A deed of trust is different: under the Deed of Trust Act (its stated purpose is financing by the United States through the Farmers Home Administration or other federal agencies such as HUD and the VA) it may allow a nonjudicial sale by the trustee at public auction after notices to the borrower, with no right of redemption, and people holding possession through the borrower must give up possession before the sale date (subject to the federal tenant protections below). The lender's complaint must name everyone who has an interest in the property that ranks below the mortgage, which can include a tenant whose lease is recorded; a person whose interest wasn't on record when the case began need not be named and is bound by the judgment. After a court-ordered mortgage sale (not a deed-of-trust sale), the owner has 12 months to redeem the property, and from the sale until redemption the buyer at the sale is entitled to collect the rent (or the value of use and occupation) from the tenant in possession. So once a sale happens, the tenant's rent goes to the buyer, not to you. Recording matters for priority: apart from a lease for one year or less, an unrecorded lease isn't valid against a later good-faith buyer or mortgagee who records first. We found no Commonwealth statute, regulation or court rule that requires you to tell tenants about a pending foreclosure, says in terms that a lease stays in force against the buyer (a court-ordered sale doesn't affect the rights of holders of prior recorded encumbrances, which may include a lease recorded before the mortgage; unsettled, case law not searched), or gives tenants a set notice period before the buyer may seek possession; the buyer would still have to go to court to remove a tenant (the summary possession procedure is the statutory route; no statute allows self-help, and we assume it is unlawful). Federal law fills that gap. Under the federal Protecting Tenants at Foreclosure Act, whoever takes the property through a foreclosure of a dwelling takes it subject to the rights of a bona fide tenant: the new owner must give the tenant a notice to vacate at least 90 days before it takes effect, and a tenant with a bona fide lease made before the notice of foreclosure may stay until the lease term ends, unless the new owner sells the unit to a buyer who will live in it as a primary residence, in which case the 90-day notice still applies. A month-to-month or other periodic tenant also gets the 90 days, far more than the Commonwealth's 15-day monthly notice, and the buyer would still have to go to court if the tenant stays. A lease or tenancy is bona fide only if the tenant isn't the borrower or the borrower's child, spouse or parent, it was an arm's-length deal, and the rent isn't substantially below market (unless it is reduced by a subsidy). The federal Act treats the date of the notice of foreclosure as the date complete title passes under a court's order or under the mortgage or deed of trust; after a court-ordered mortgage sale in the Commonwealth the deed to the buyer issues only after the 12-month redemption period runs out, and until then the buyer collects the rent, while after a deed-of-trust trustee's sale the trustee gives the buyer a deed once the price is paid, with no redemption period. Subsidized tenancies keep their own termination rules. If the property has a federally backed mortgage, the CARES Act 30-day notice to vacate can also apply (see "edu-cares-act-notice"). What to do: if a foreclosure case is filed, tell your tenants in writing (and tell the lender or buyer which tenancies are bona fide), tell them who to pay rent to after any sale, account for their security deposits, and for any lease over one year, sign it before a notary and record it.

title: Redeeming a Tenancy After Default in the Northern Mariana Islands
bodyText: When a tenant falls behind on rent, Northern Mariana Islands law gives the tenant one statutory chance to keep the tenancy: your written three-day notice must demand payment of the rent or possession of the premises within 3 days (not counting Saturdays, Sundays and legal holidays), so a tenant who pays the full amount demanded within that time has met the notice. We found no Commonwealth statute, regulation or court rule that lets a tenant undo the forfeiture later, for example by paying the arrears and costs after the notice period has run, before trial, after judgment or before the writ is carried out, and none that makes you accept a late payment once the notice has expired. The 12-month redemption period in the Real Estate Mortgage Law applies to property sold on foreclosure of a mortgage, not to a lease. Whether a court could still relieve a tenant from forfeiture as a matter of fairness is a common-law question we have not resolved. Cautious course: decide before you take money. If you accept payment of the rent you sued or gave notice for, assume the court may treat the default as cured or waived for that rent (see "edu-waiver-by-acceptance-mp"); if you want to keep the case going, don't accept it, or agree with the tenant in writing (or in a court-approved settlement) on what the payment does.

title: Lease Guarantors in the Northern Mariana Islands
bodyText: Northern Mariana Islands law requires a guaranty to be in writing: a promise to answer for another person's debt or default is invalid unless it, or a note or memo of it, is in writing and signed by the guarantor (or the guarantor's agent). Having the guarantor sign the lease itself, as the library's optional guaranty clause "guaranty-as" does, meets that rule. We found no Commonwealth statute, regulation or court rule that limits a lease guarantor to the original term, that requires a guaranty to state a maximum amount or an end date, or that caps a deposit or prepayment you take from a guarantor (there is no Commonwealth cap on security deposits at all; see "edu-security-deposit-cap-mp"). So what the guarantor owes after the first term depends on what the guaranty says. Because a court may read a guaranty narrowly in the guarantor's favor (Restatement not read; case law not searched), say plainly whether it covers renewals, extensions and a month-to-month continuation, and state a maximum dollar amount; "guaranty-as" makes you choose both. Cautious course: treat anything a guarantor pays you to secure the lease as a security deposit and refund the balance within ten days after the property is returned, less proper deductions (the deposit statute doesn't say whether a guarantor's payment counts). Don't require a guarantor from some applicants and not others on the basis of race, color, religion, sex, familial status, marital status, disability or national origin, and, as a cautious course, age, citizenship, ethnic background or place of birth or residence; apply one written income or credit standard to everyone.

title: Tenant Holdover in the Northern Mariana Islands
bodyText: If a tenant stays after the lease has ended without your permission, Northern Mariana Islands law lets you seek removal through the Superior Court's summary possession procedure and also recover double the rent for the period during which the tenant refuses to give up possession. The court enters a money judgment in a possession case only if your complaint expressly and specifically asks for money damages, so ask for the double rent in the complaint. When a written lease for a fixed term expires and the tenant stays on without a new written lease, the tenant is a tenant at sufferance; your acceptance of rent does not by itself renew the lease. If you give written consent to the tenant staying, the tenancy becomes a periodic one that follows the rent period (month to month if rent is monthly), which either side can end on written notice (at least 15 days before the end of a monthly period unless the lease sets another period). The library's "holdover-mp" clause states these rules: double the Monthly Rent, prorated by the day, in place of (not on top of) the regular rent for those days, removal only through the court, and a month-to-month continuation on 15 days' notice if you consent in writing. We found no other Commonwealth statute, outside the Holdover Tenancy Act, that sets a different holdover measure for private residential leases. The Act doesn't apply to a lease where the CNMI government, its agencies or instrumentalities is a party; leases of public land, airport and port space and government office leases carry their own holdover terms. Prevailing-party court costs and attorney's fees are recoverable in a case under the Act.

title: Holdover Rates in the Northern Mariana Islands
bodyText: Northern Mariana Islands law sets the holdover measure itself: if a tenant stays after the lease has ended without your permission, you may recover double the rent for the period during which the tenant refuses to give up possession. We found no Commonwealth statute, regulation or court rule that caps a holdover rate written into a lease (such as a percentage of the daily rent), or that sets a lower cap for subsidized units. The library doesn't offer a separate stipulated holdover rate for the Commonwealth: the "holdover-mp" clause uses the statutory double rent, prorated by the day, in place of the regular rent for those days, and you should not add a second holdover charge on top of it. If you write a different figure into a lease anyway, keep it at or below double the rent, because a larger figure could be attacked as a penalty or an unconscionable term under the Consumer Protection Act, which we treat as reaching residential leasing. During a Governor's price freeze, don't present the holdover amount as a rent increase. Ask for the double rent specifically in your court complaint.

title: Exemption Waivers in the Northern Mariana Islands
bodyText: If you win a money judgment against a tenant, Northern Mariana Islands law protects some of the tenant's property from attachment and execution: necessary household furniture, cooking and eating utensils, clothing, bedding and four months' household provisions; the tools and equipment the tenant needs for his or her usual occupation; and interests in land (a court may order some land sold only if the debtor keeps enough to support the household). Other laws protect particular income, such as workers' compensation, which by statute can't be waived, and Commonwealth retirement-fund benefits. The Commonwealth has no homestead exemption in the sense used in some states for a debtor's home. We found no Commonwealth statute, regulation or court rule that lets a tenant waive these exemptions in a lease, or that sets the words a waiver must use, and none that expressly forbids a waiver of the general exemptions either. Cautious course: don't put an exemption waiver in the lease. A court could refuse to enforce it, and a clause suggesting the tenant has given up protections the law provides could be attacked under the Consumer Protection Act as misstating the tenant's rights or as unconscionable. Collect a judgment only through the court's writ and the officer who levies it, and leave exempt property alone.

title: Early Termination for Illness or Care in the Northern Mariana Islands
bodyText: We found no Commonwealth statute, regulation or court rule that lets a residential tenant end a lease early because of age, illness or disability, or because the tenant must move into a nursing home, assisted living or other care facility. So unless the lease gives that right, a tenant who leaves early for those reasons is treated like any other tenant who ends a fixed term early; a month-to-month tenant can end the tenancy on the ordinary written notice. Two cautions. First, a request from a tenant with a disability to be released early, or to end on shorter notice, may be a request for a reasonable accommodation in your rules, policies or practices under fair housing law; consider it in good faith rather than refusing automatically (see "edu-disability-accommodation-mp"). Second, federal law gives servicemembers, and the spouse or dependent of a servicemember who dies in service, their own termination rights (see "edu-servicemember-rights-mp"). If you want to offer a medical or care-facility release, put it in the lease or a written addendum, with the notice and proof you will accept, and apply it to every tenant on the same terms.

title: Landlord Liens in the Northern Mariana Islands
bodyText: We found no Commonwealth statute giving an ordinary residential landlord a lien on a tenant's belongings for unpaid rent, and no procedure for distress (seizing a tenant's goods for rent), whether by the landlord or through the court. The one exception is narrow: a hotel, inn, motel or lodging-house proprietor, or a person who lets rooms to lodgers for hire, has a lien on property a guest, boarder or tenant brings into the rooms for unpaid lodging and rent (tools of the trade and required work uniforms are exempt), may keep that property until paid, and may sell it after 30 days' default only at a public auction after published or posted notice. If you let rooms to lodgers, follow those sections; whether they reach an ordinary house or apartment lease is doubtful, so don't rely on them for one. The Commonwealth's secured-transactions law doesn't apply to a landlord's lien, and we found no rule on a lien written into a residential lease. Cautious course: don't put a lien-and-seizure clause in the lease, and never take, hold or sell a tenant's belongings to collect rent while the tenant is in possession; regain possession only through the court (the cautious course; no statute allows self-help), and household goods, clothing, bedding, provisions and tools of the trade are exempt from execution even on a judgment. Federal law makes it a crime to seize or hold the belongings or deposit of a servicemember who has lawfully ended a lease, to satisfy rent for the period after termination. To collect unpaid rent, sue for it (in the possession case or separately) and enforce the judgment through the court's writ. Property left behind after the tenant moves out is handled under "abandoned-property-mp".

title: Landlord Remedies After Default in the Northern Mariana Islands
bodyText: When a tenant defaults, Northern Mariana Islands law gives you two kinds of remedy, which you can pursue together. Possession: you file a summary possession complaint in the Superior Court in the senatorial district where the property is; the tenant has five days after service to answer, and after judgment the court issues a writ for an officer to remove the occupants and put you in possession. Money: in the same case the court will also enter a money judgment for rent and other amounts owed, but only if your complaint expressly and specifically asks for money damages; you can also recover double the rent for any period the tenant refuses to leave after the tenancy has ended without your permission, and the winning side may recover reasonable court costs and attorney's fees. You can instead, or later, sue for money alone in an ordinary civil action, including for rent that fell due before the lease ended. A claim of $5,000 or less (not counting interest, attorney's fees and costs) can go through the Superior Court's small claims procedure, which is informal and designed for parties without lawyers. Court-annexed mediation rules don't apply to Holdover Tenancy Act cases. We found no Commonwealth statute that says whether ending the lease cuts off rent for the rest of the term, or that requires you to re-rent to reduce your losses. Cautious course: after a tenant leaves early, make reasonable efforts to re-rent, credit what you receive against what the tenant owes, and claim only your actual losses. Sue within six years of when the claim arises (see "edu-limitation-of-actions-mp").

title: Rent Acceleration in the Northern Mariana Islands
bodyText: Some leases let the landlord declare all the rent for the rest of the term due at once if the tenant defaults ("rent acceleration"). We found no Commonwealth statute that bars a residential lease from doing so; the Commonwealth's acceleration statutes cover mortgages and commercial paper, not leases. But the library doesn't offer an acceleration clause for the Northern Mariana Islands, and the cautious course is not to use one. A clause that makes all future rent due immediately, especially if you also take back the property or don't credit rent from re-renting, could be attacked as a penalty or as an unconscionable term under the Consumer Protection Act, which we treat as reaching residential leasing, and the common-law limits on acceleration haven't been reviewed. If a tenant defaults or leaves early, recover your actual losses instead: rent as it falls due (or in a lump sum at the end of the term), less what you receive from re-renting after reasonable efforts, plus the costs the lease and the law allow. If a lease you are using already has an acceleration term, get legal advice before relying on it.

title: Landlord Self-Cure of Tenant Breach in the Northern Mariana Islands
bodyText: We found no Commonwealth statute, regulation or court rule that gives a residential landlord the right to fix a tenant's breach (for example, unrepaired tenant damage or uncleared trash) and charge the tenant the cost, and none that forbids it. So the right exists only if the lease gives it. The library's optional "landlord-self-cure-as" clause does: after written notice and a reasonable time to fix the problem (sooner in an emergency), you may do the work, entering only as the lease allows and peaceably, and bill the tenant the reasonable cost on an itemized statement. Keep that cost separate from rent. In the Northern Mariana Islands the three-day notice that can lead to removal is for a default in paying rent, so don't label repair costs "rent" to bring them within that notice; for an unpaid repair bill or other breach, use the lease's default terms or, if the lease is silent, a 15-day written notice to cure or leave. Never use a self-cure right to change the locks, remove the tenant's belongings or shut off utilities; recover possession only through the court (the statutory route; we assume self-help is unlawful). Don't use it for repairs that are your own duty as landlord (keeping the home fit to live in).

title: Liquidated Damages in the Northern Mariana Islands
bodyText: We found no Commonwealth statute, regulation or court rule that governs liquidated damages in a residential lease, such as a fixed early-termination fee or a set charge for breaking the lease, and no consumer-protection regulation that expressly allows or forbids keeping an agreed amount when a tenant breaches. The Commonwealth's Uniform Commercial Code has a liquidated-damages rule, but only for sales of goods: there, an agreed amount must be reasonable in light of the anticipated or actual harm, and an unreasonably large amount is void as a penalty. Courts often apply the same idea to other contracts, so treat it as the likely test for a lease too. Cautious course: if the lease sets an amount for a tenant's breach, such as the early-termination fee in the library's "early-termination-ks" clause, keep it to a reasonable estimate of your real loss (for example, about a month's rent to cover turnover and vacancy), don't add it on top of collecting the same lost rent separately, and don't apply it where the law gives the tenant a right to leave. In particular, federal law bars an early termination charge when a servicemember lawfully ends a lease under the Servicemembers Civil Relief Act. A fee far above any likely loss could be attacked as a penalty or as an unconscionable term under the Consumer Protection Act, which we treat as reaching residential leasing. Money you hold to secure the tenant's performance is a security deposit, refundable within ten days after the property is returned, less proper deductions.

title: Lockouts for Unpaid Rent in the Northern Mariana Islands
bodyText: No. We found no Commonwealth statute, regulation or court rule that lets a residential landlord lock out a tenant who is behind on rent, even with advance notice, an opt-in lease clause or key access on request. The Holdover Tenancy Act sets the route for removing a tenant who doesn't pay: a written three-day notice demanding the rent or possession, then a summary possession case in the Superior Court, and, if you win, a writ under which an officer removes the occupants and puts you in possession. The Act was passed to give landlords a prompt court procedure, and nothing in it authorizes a landlord to change the locks or exclude a tenant without a court order. Cautious course: don't put a lockout clause in the lease and never change the locks, remove doors or belongings, or cut off utilities to force a tenant out for unpaid rent; serve the three-day notice and file in court (see "edu-self-help-eviction-mp").

title: Minors as Tenants and Defendants in the Northern Mariana Islands
bodyText: In the Northern Mariana Islands a person becomes an adult at 18, so anyone 18 or older can sign a lease in his or her own name; there is no higher age of majority and no special rule for 18-to-20-year-olds. A person under 18 generally can't be bound by a contract, so don't make a minor a tenant on the lease; have a parent or other adult sign as tenant (or as guarantor), and list the minor as an occupant. We found no Commonwealth statute or court rule that bars naming a minor in a possession case. But a minor party must act through a guardian, next friend or guardian ad litem, the court must appoint a guardian ad litem or make another protective order for an unrepresented minor, and a minor is served through the guardian ad litem. So name the adult tenants as defendants. The Holdover Tenancy Act lets the court remove the tenant together with those holding under the tenant, and the writ directs the officer to remove all persons from the premises, so a minor occupant normally leaves with the household without being sued. Don't refuse to rent to, or set different terms for, a household because it includes children (familial status is protected), and, as a cautious course, don't turn away an adult applicant because of age.

title: Notice for Unpaid Rent in the Northern Mariana Islands
bodyText: Before you can have a tenant removed for unpaid rent, Northern Mariana Islands law requires a written three-day notice demanding payment of the rent or possession of the premises. The notice must be in substantially the statutory form: it states the amount of rent owed, the address of the premises, that you demand payment or possession within 3 days (not counting Saturdays, Sundays and legal holidays) from the date of delivery, the deadline date, and your name, address and telephone number. Use the statutory wording; the printed form ends with "19__", so write the full current year. Serve it by handing a copy to the tenant or, if the tenant is not at the property, by leaving a copy there. Mailing, e-mail or text alone isn't a method the statute provides, and federal e-signature law doesn't validate an electronic notice of default or eviction for a primary residence, so serve on paper. The lease can't stand in for the notice, waive it or shorten it: the law requires the notice to be served after the rent is unpaid, and it doesn't invite the lease to change the form, period or service. We found no Commonwealth rule requiring an agency form or information sheet with the notice, a mediation step, a payment-plan offer, registered or certified mail, or limiting how often a tenant may cure by paying; accept full payment made within the three days. If the property is a federally covered property under the CARES Act, the tenant can't be required to leave until 30 days after a notice to vacate (see "edu-cares-act-notice"). For the demand rules generally see "edu-rent-demand-bar-mp"; for notice fees see "edu-notice-service-fee-mp".
