title: Notice Service Fees in the Northern Mariana Islands
bodyText: We found no Commonwealth statute, regulation or court rule that allows, bans or caps a fee charged to a tenant for preparing or serving a notice (such as the three-day notice for unpaid rent or a notice to cure). There is no Commonwealth list of permitted rental fees. Cautious course: don't charge one. A fee for a notice the law requires you to give before going to court looks like a penalty, and it can confuse the notice itself: the three-day notice states the sum owed "for the rent and use of the premises", so don't fold a notice fee, late fee or other charge into that amount. If you do use a notice fee anyway, it must be listed in the lease's fee section (see "fees-and-charges-vi"), be a modest charge tied to your real cost, and never be the only reason for a default or eviction. Your actual costs of a court case are handled differently: in a case under the Holdover Tenancy Act the winning party may recover reasonable court costs, including attorney's fees, from the losing party, as the court awards.

title: Waiving or Shortening Notices in the Northern Mariana Islands
bodyText: Northern Mariana Islands law lets the lease change some notices but not others. Ending a periodic tenancy: the statutory notice periods (at least 7 days before the end of a weekly period, 15 days for month to month, 30 days for quarter to quarter and 60 days for year to year) apply "unless otherwise agreed", so the lease may set a different period. Breaches other than unpaid rent: the 15-day written notice to cure or leave, and its hand-delivery service rule, apply only when the lease is silent or oral, so the lease may set its own cure period and method of serving notice. Unpaid rent: the three-day written notice demanding the rent or possession, in substantially the statutory form and served by hand or, if the tenant is absent, left at the premises, is not something the lease is invited to change; don't shorten it, waive it or replace it with lease language. The end of a fixed term needs no notice: a tenant who stays after the term without your permission can be removed. Cautious course: even where the lease may vary a notice, don't write a waiver of notice or a period so short that a tenant can't realistically respond, and make any change apply to both sides; a one-sided waiver could be attacked as unconscionable under the Consumer Protection Act. Federal notices, such as the CARES Act 30-day notice for covered properties, apply regardless of the lease. See "edu-termination-notice-mp" for the periodic-tenancy choices and "edu-nonpayment-notice-mp" for the rent notice.

title: Nuisance Liability for Rentals in the Northern Mariana Islands
bodyText: Several Northern Mariana Islands laws can make you answer for a nuisance at your rental, even one your tenant causes. Criminal nuisance: anyone who, by an act or by neglecting a legal duty, maintains or allows a place to exist in a condition that is a hazard to, or otherwise harms, the health, comfort, safety, property, or peace, quiet and privacy of others commits an offense once he or she knows of the condition or has been notified of it (up to six months in jail). Cannabis: a place where marijuana is sold, made or kept for sale in violation of Commonwealth law, or where people gather to use it unlawfully, is a common nuisance, and an owner, manager or lessor who knowingly suffers or permits it commits a violation; an owner who knowingly lets premises be used that way can face a lien on the building for the occupants' fines and costs. Building safety: unsafe buildings are public nuisances, a violation of the building safety code is a public nuisance in itself, and anyone harmed may sue the violator for damages, litigation costs and attorney's fees. On Saipan, the local Nuisance Abatement and Blighted Property Maintenance Act lets the Zoning Administrator order the owner (which can include a person in control of a dwelling or a long-term lessee) to abate conditions such as accumulated trash, pests, junk vehicles, overgrown vegetation, unsecured vacant buildings, or a property not occupied by the owner that provides a site for drug activity; if the owner doesn't, the Commonwealth may abate it, charge the owner, and record a lien. Check Tinian and Rota local law too. We found no Commonwealth rule creating a nuisance receivership over rents, a building-closure order with a motion to cancel the lease, a neighbors' suit to close a building, a requirement that the lease summarize a criminal statute, or a rule making the landlord a necessary party to an abatement-by-eviction case. What to do: act promptly on written complaints; use the lease's criminal-activity and default terms ("criminal-activity-ky") to end a tenancy for illegal activity, through the court; and keep records of what you did once you learned of a problem.

title: Possession Bonds in the Northern Mariana Islands
bodyText: We found no Commonwealth statute, regulation or court rule that provides an end-of-term possession bond, a bond with a confessed judgment for possession, or any other bond a tenant must post to keep or give up possession of a residence. Northern Mariana Islands law doesn't set up a confession-of-judgment procedure for leases either; the only confessed-judgment mention we found is in the commercial paper rules, which say a term authorizing a confession of judgment on an unpaid instrument doesn't affect whether the instrument is negotiable. In a possession case, the bonds and deposits that do exist are court-procedure ones: a party demanding a jury when a special venire must be summoned deposits the jury fees, and a party who appeals can seek a stay by posting a supersedeas bond. Cautious course: don't put a confession of judgment or a warrant of attorney in a residential lease. Recover possession at the end of the term through the summary possession case, and secure performance with the security deposit and, if needed, a guarantor.

title: Delayed Move-In in the Northern Mariana Islands
bodyText: We found no Commonwealth statute, regulation or court rule on what happens when a landlord can't deliver possession on the start date (for example, because the prior tenant hasn't left or repairs aren't finished), and none requiring a landlord to provide alternate housing during the delay. So the lease decides. The library's "possession-delay" clause, which carries MP for the Northern Mariana Islands, says the lease stays in force, the tenant owes no rent until possession is delivered, and if possession isn't delivered within 30 days after the start date the tenant may cancel by written notice and get back everything paid. If a prior tenant is holding over, you are the one with the remedy: a tenant who stays after the term without your permission can be removed through the Superior Court's summary possession procedure, and you may recover double the rent for the period of refusal. For alternate housing when a home becomes unfit after the tenancy starts, see "edu-alt-housing-mp"; for damage from a typhoon or fire, see "casualty-termination-mp". What to do: tell the new tenant in writing as soon as you know of a delay, don't collect rent for days the tenant can't move in, and refund promptly if the tenant cancels.

title: Property and Pets After Eviction in the Northern Mariana Islands
bodyText: When you win a possession case, the court clerk issues a writ commanding the officer to remove all persons from the premises and put you in possession. Northern Mariana Islands law says nothing more about the tenant's belongings or animals at that point. We found no Commonwealth statute, regulation or court rule that sets a landlord's duty to store, inventory or give notice about belongings left after a writ is carried out, a rule for pets left behind, a statutory immunity for landlords when the writ is executed, a separate ejectment procedure with a warehouse option, or a special crime for staying or returning after a writ. So the lease's procedure governs: the library's "abandoned-property-mp" clause applies once the tenant has been removed under a writ, with written notice, safe storage, a claim period of at least the days you choose (not less than 30), sale only on commercially reasonable terms, and vehicles handled by notifying the Department of Public Safety. Animals: a person who knowingly abandons an animal in his or her care commits animal cruelty, and someone who cruelly neglects an animal under his or her control does too, so if a pet is left behind, give it food, water and shelter and contact the tenant and local animal control promptly; don't release it to the street. If a former tenant comes back after removal and refuses to leave when lawfully told to, that can be criminal trespass (up to six months), so call the police rather than using force.

title: Unlawful Use of Rental Premises in the Northern Mariana Islands
bodyText: We found no Commonwealth statute that makes a residential lease void, or ends it automatically, because the premises are used for an unlawful purpose such as gambling, prostitution or drug dealing. Criminal and nuisance laws still reach the landlord who knows: an owner, manager or lessor who knowingly suffers or permits a place to be used for selling, making or unlawfully using marijuana commits a violation, and the building can face a lien for the occupants' fines; a person who knowingly operates or assists in operating a house of prostitution, or otherwise aids prostitution, commits the crime of promoting prostitution; and anyone who knowingly allows a place to stay in a condition hazardous to others' health or safety maintains a criminal nuisance. So the lease, not a statute, gives you the right to end the tenancy for illegal use. Use the residential-use and criminal-activity terms ("residential-use-only", "criminal-activity-ky") and the default terms, and remove the tenant through the summary possession case; for a breach other than unpaid rent, give the cure-or-quit notice the lease sets (or 15 days' written notice if the lease is silent). Don't treat a household member who is the victim of the crime as the wrongdoer: in federally covered housing, criminal activity relating to domestic violence against the tenant can't be the basis to evict the victim.

title: Tenant Defenses and Rent Deposits in Possession Cases in the Northern Mariana Islands
bodyText: In a Northern Mariana Islands summary possession case, the tenant must put all defenses of law or fact in an answer filed within five days after being served, and may include a counterclaim; if it does, you must answer the counterclaim, with all your defenses, within five days after it is served. No other pleadings are allowed, and defensive motions are heard before trial. We found no Commonwealth statute, regulation or court rule that requires a tenant to pay rent into court (or into the court registry) to raise a defense or counterclaim, to get a jury trial, or to obtain a continuance, and no rent-escrow procedure for repair disputes. The only deposit in the Act is jury fees: a party who demands a jury, when a special jury panel must be summoned, deposits the jury fees with the clerk. We also found no rule making any particular counterclaim mandatory in a possession case beyond the court's general civil rules. What to do: expect a tenant to raise conditions or other claims in the answer, keep your repair records and rent ledger ready, answer any counterclaim within five days, and ask the court for a prompt trial; if you want rent protected while the case is pending, you can ask the court, but no statute gives it to you automatically.

title: Rental Application Misstatements in the Northern Mariana Islands
bodyText: We found no Commonwealth statute that gives a landlord a special right to end a lease because the tenant lied on the rental application. A false application is handled as a breach of the lease if the lease says so: the library's Northern Mariana Islands clause "rental-application-accuracy-mp" makes materially false or misleading application information a material breach. For a breach other than unpaid rent, you must give written notice to cure or leave as the lease provides or, if the lease is silent, 15 days' written notice, and then remove the tenant only through the court. Some records the applicant may lawfully leave out. Under Northern Mariana Islands law, a person whose first-offense drug-possession case was discharged and expunged can't be held to have made a false statement for failing to mention the arrest, charge or trial in answer to any inquiry; a person whose juvenile record was expunged may answer as if the proceedings never happened; and a person whose conviction was set aside after successful probation isn't treated as convicted of that crime for any purpose. So don't treat an applicant's "no" about such a record as a misrepresentation, and don't base a breach on it. That clause excludes both information you weren't permitted to request or consider and answers the applicant was entitled by law to give. Ask screening questions the same way for every applicant, and don't ask about or act on race, color, religion, sex, familial status, marital status, disability or national origin (or, as a cautious course, age, citizenship or place of birth).

title: Ending a Lease Over Repair Costs in the Northern Mariana Islands
bodyText: We found no Commonwealth statute, regulation or court rule that lets a landlord (or a tenant) end a residential lease because repairs would cost more than a set amount or a share of the property's value, and none that limits repair-and-deduct or other tenant repair remedies by cost. The repair-cost thresholds that do exist serve other purposes: flood-zone building rules treat repairs costing 50 percent or more of a structure's value as a substantial improvement that must meet current standards, and Housing Corporation rehabilitation programs refuse homes whose rehabilitation would cost more than their after-repair value. So unless the lease says otherwise, you can't end a fixed-term lease early just because repairs are expensive; a month-to-month tenancy can be ended on ordinary written notice. For damage from a typhoon, fire or other casualty, the optional "casualty-termination-mp" clause lets you end the lease after substantial damage, with rent abated. Remember that you remain responsible, as a cautious course, for keeping the home fit to live in, and a unit that fails its annual Building Safety inspection raises habitability issues; if a unit isn't worth repairing, end the tenancy lawfully rather than leaving the tenant in an unsafe home.

title: Seasonal and Short-Term Rentals in the Northern Mariana Islands
bodyText: We found no Commonwealth statute, regulation or court rule that creates a special category of seasonal or vacation tenancy, such as one that ends automatically at the end of a season without notice or is exempt from the usual removal procedure. The Holdover Tenancy Act applies to "any tenancy" of houses, buildings or land, so a short or seasonal rental is treated like any other: a fixed term ends on its stated date, and an occupant who stays on without your permission must be removed through the Superior Court. If you rent by the week or month with no fixed end date, it is a periodic tenancy ended by written notice (7 days before the end of a weekly period, 15 days for monthly) unless the agreement sets another period. So state the exact end date in a seasonal agreement. Short stays bring other duties. An occupant who stays less than 90 consecutive days in a room or unit, including an apartment, condominium or private residence, is a transient occupant subject to the 15% hotel occupancy tax, which you must collect and pay over monthly (see "edu-rent-tax-mp"). Residential rentals, including Airbnb and similar short-term rentals, need the annual Building Safety Certificate of Compliance. Check zoning and local rules for short-term rentals in your senatorial district.

title: Self-Help Eviction in the Northern Mariana Islands
bodyText: The statutory way for a landlord to take back a rental from a tenant who won't leave is the summary possession case in the Superior Court under the Holdover Tenancy Act, ending in a writ under which an officer removes the occupants. We found no statute, regulation or court rule that allows self-help, such as changing the locks, removing doors or windows, taking the tenant's belongings, or shutting off water or power to force a tenant out. We also found no Commonwealth statute written specifically against landlord self-help, no special lockout or utility-shutoff offense, and no statutory money remedy for a tenant who is ousted. That doesn't make self-help safe. General laws can reach it: interfering with the peaceful use and enjoyment of another's property and refusing to stop when told can be criminal trespass; compelling someone to give up a legal right through threats can be criminal coercion; tampering with another's property so as to interrupt the supply of water or power can be criminal mischief; and a tenant can sue for breach of the lease and of the covenant of quiet possession, which courts generally imply (see "edu-quiet-possession-mp"). The library's lease terms reflect this: the self-cure option ("landlord-self-cure-as") forbids changing locks, removing belongings or shutting off utilities, and the left-behind-property clause ("abandoned-property-mp") applies only after the tenant has moved out or been removed under a writ. What to do: serve the proper notice (three days for unpaid rent; the lease's cure notice or 15 days for other breaches; the periodic-tenancy notice to end a month-to-month tenancy), file the possession case, and let the officer carry out the writ.

title: Servicemember Lease Rights in the Northern Mariana Islands
bodyText: Federal law, the Servicemembers Civil Relief Act, applies in the Northern Mariana Islands (it defines "State" to include a commonwealth). We found no Commonwealth statute that adds to it or narrows it: no local servicemember lease-termination right, no protection for Guard members on Commonwealth orders, no shortened military notice for periodic tenancies, and no rule on deciding servicemember applications. Under the federal Act, a servicemember tenant may end a residential lease if the lease was signed before entering military service, or if, while in service, the servicemember receives orders for a permanent change of station or to deploy for at least 90 days (or a stop-movement order of 30 days or more after signing on such orders). The tenant ends the lease by delivering written notice and a copy of the military orders to you or your agent, by hand, private carrier, return-receipt mail, or electronic means you've designated. For a lease with monthly rent, termination takes effect 30 days after the next rent due date following delivery of the notice. Rent owed for the period before termination is prorated. You may not charge an early termination fee, but the tenant still owes taxes, other lease obligations and reasonable charges for excess wear. Rent paid in advance for the period after termination must be refunded within 30 days. Ending the lease also ends any dependent's obligation under it. The spouse or dependent of a tenant who dies in military service may end the lease within one year after the death, and a tenant who suffers a catastrophic injury or illness during service has a similar one-year right. Knowingly seizing or holding a servicemember's belongings or security deposit to satisfy rent for the period after a lawful termination is a federal crime. Two more federal rules apply in a possession case. First, except by court order, you may not evict a servicemember, or a servicemember's dependents, during military service from a home whose monthly rent is at or below a federal ceiling ($2,400 in 2003, adjusted each year for housing inflation; the Defense Department publishes the current figure in the Federal Register each year); if a servicemember whose ability to pay is materially affected by military service asks, the court must stay the case for 90 days (or a longer or shorter time if justice requires) or adjust the lease, and knowingly taking part in an eviction that breaks this rule is a federal crime. Second, before the court enters a judgment for you in a case covered by the federal default-judgment rule (typically when the tenant doesn't appear), you must file an affidavit, or a statement signed under penalty of perjury, stating whether the tenant is in military service with facts supporting it, or that you can't determine it; if the tenant is in military service the court can't enter judgment until it appoints an attorney for the tenant, and if it can't tell, it may require you to post a bond. Check a tenant's military status before filing.

title: Ending a Tenancy Without Cause in the Northern Mariana Islands
bodyText: Northern Mariana Islands law doesn't require you to have a reason ("good cause" or "just cause") to end an ordinary private residential tenancy. A fixed-term lease ends when its term ends, and if the tenant stays on without your permission you may ask the Superior Court to remove the tenant. A month-to-month or other periodic tenancy can be ended by either side, without stating a reason, by written notice given before the end of a rental period: at least 15 days for month to month, 7 days for week to week, 30 days for quarter to quarter and 60 days for year to year, unless the lease sets a different period. We found no Commonwealth statute, regulation or court rule that requires good cause to end or refuse to renew a private tenancy, whether for all rentals or for a group such as long-term tenants, older or disabled tenants, mobile home parks or tenants in their first year, and no rule requiring government officials to attend a removal. There are exceptions to watch for. If the unit is in a federally assisted program (for example a Housing Choice Voucher or project-based voucher unit administered by the Northern Marianas Housing Corporation, or public housing), the program rules and the tenancy addendum limit when and how you may end the tenancy: in a voucher unit, during the lease term you may end the tenancy only for a serious or repeated lease violation, a violation of law connected with the occupancy, or other good cause, you must give the tenant written notice of the grounds and give the Housing Corporation a copy of any eviction notice, and you may evict only by court action. Federal law also bars evicting a tenant in covered housing because the tenant is a victim of domestic violence, dating violence, sexual assault or stalking. If you convert a building to a condominium, you must give each tenant 60 days' notice of the conversion and can't require a tenant to leave on less than 30 days' notice except for nonpayment of rent, waste or conduct that disturbs other tenants. And never end a tenancy for a discriminatory reason or to retaliate against a tenant for a lawful complaint. Even when no reason is needed, regain possession through the court (the Holdover Tenancy Act's summary possession procedure), not by changing locks or removing belongings; that is our cautious course, since self-help is a common-law question (Restatement not read; case law not searched).

title: Late Benefit or Voucher Payments in the Northern Mariana Islands
bodyText: We found no Commonwealth statute or court rule that gives a tenant a defense, a continuance or reinstatement in a possession case because a Social Security check, other government benefit or a voucher payment arrived late. One program rule does protect assisted tenants: in the Northern Marianas Housing Corporation's voucher programs, the family isn't responsible for the part of the rent covered by the housing assistance payment, and you may not terminate the tenancy of an assisted family because the Housing Corporation hasn't paid its share. Your remedy for a late or missing assistance payment is against the Housing Corporation under the payment contract, not the tenant. For the tenant's own share, and for tenants whose income arrives late, the ordinary rules apply: a three-day written notice demanding the rent or possession, and full payment within those three days meets the notice. Practical course: when a tenant tells you a benefit payment is late, consider agreeing in writing to a short extension, which the law allows, rather than filing; and never count the assistance agency's share as the tenant's unpaid rent.

title: Retaliation Against Tenants in the Northern Mariana Islands
bodyText: We found no Commonwealth statute that generally bars a residential landlord from retaliating against a tenant, for example by raising rent, cutting services or ending a tenancy because the tenant complained about conditions, contacted a government agency or joined a tenants' group, and no statutory presumption of retaliation. Two specific laws do apply. The Commonwealth Fair Housing Act makes it unlawful to coerce, intimidate, threaten or interfere with anyone because he or she exercised, or helped another person exercise, fair housing rights; federal fair housing law, which applies in the Commonwealth, has the same protection. And the Commonwealth's smoke-free air law bars retaliating against an employee or customer who exercises rights under it or reports a violation; whether a tenant counts as a "customer" is unsettled, so treat it as reaching tenants who report smoking violations. We found no Commonwealth bill of rights for older adults or people with disabilities, and no long-term-care ombudsman law, that reaches a landlord's reprisals. Cautious course: assume the common law protects a tenant from retaliation for lawful complaints about conditions or for using legal rights (Restatement not read; case law not searched). Don't end a tenancy, refuse to renew, raise rent or reduce services soon after a tenant's complaint, request for repairs, report to Building Safety, Environmental Quality or the Housing Corporation, or a fair housing complaint, unless you have a documented, independent reason that you would have acted on anyway, and keep records of it.

title: Owner Move-In Terminations in the Northern Mariana Islands
bodyText: We found no Commonwealth statute, regulation or court rule that gives a landlord the right to end a lease early so that the owner or a family member can move in, or that sets a minimum ownership period, notice or relocation payment for doing so. So for a fixed-term lease, the right exists only if the lease reserves it; a lease that is silent leaves you bound to the full term. The library's optional "owner-occupancy-termination-ar" clause reserves it for a fixed term: you name who will move in, give written notice of at least the period you choose (not less than 30 days) ending on the last day of a monthly rental period, refund any rent paid for later periods, and regain possession only through the court if the tenant doesn't leave. A month-to-month or other periodic tenancy can be ended by either side on the ordinary written notice without any reason, so no reservation is needed there (see "edu-for-cause-eviction-mp"). Exceptions: in a Housing Choice Voucher unit you may not end the tenancy for personal or family use during the initial lease term; in a project-based voucher unit administered by the Northern Marianas Housing Corporation, wanting the unit for personal or family use isn't good cause to end the tenancy; and a condominium declarant converting a building may not end a lease in violation of its terms. Use the right honestly: if you end a tenancy for owner occupancy and then re-rent instead, the tenant may claim you breached the lease or acted in bad faith.

title: Tenant Early Termination Rights in the Northern Mariana Islands
bodyText: We found no Commonwealth statute that gives a residential tenant a right to end a lease early because the landlord made a fraudulent misrepresentation, and no rule that makes a landlord forfeit accrued rent or other money for leaving a prescribed statement out of the lease. The tenant's statutory early-termination rights in the Northern Mariana Islands come from federal law: servicemembers (and a spouse or dependent after a servicemember's death in service, or after a catastrophic service injury or illness that leaves the servicemember unable to manage his or her own affairs) may end a lease under the Servicemembers Civil Relief Act (see "edu-servicemember-rights-mp"). A tenant who was misled still has remedies. Because we treat the Consumer Protection Act as reaching residential leasing, a tenant harmed by an unfair or deceptive practice, such as a false statement about the unit, may sue in the Superior Court for legal or equitable relief the court orders (which can include undoing the lease), actual damages, an equal amount more for a wilful violation, and attorney's fees; and under general contract law a lease induced by fraud can generally be rescinded (Restatement not read; case law not searched). What to do: describe the unit, its condition, the fees and the included services accurately, in writing, and correct any mistake as soon as you learn of it. If a tenant asks to leave because of something you misstated, consider agreeing to a written release rather than holding the tenant to the term.

title: End of the Lease Term in the Northern Mariana Islands
bodyText: In the Northern Mariana Islands the end of a fixed term does end the tenancy: there is no good-cause renewal rule that keeps a tenant in possession after the term. A tenant who stays after the expiration of the term without your permission can be removed through the Superior Court's summary possession procedure without any further notice, and can be charged double rent for the period of refusal once the tenancy has ended. When a written lease for a fixed term expires and the tenant holds over without a new written lease, the tenant is a tenant at sufferance; accepting rent doesn't renew the term, but your written consent turns the holdover into a periodic tenancy (month to month if rent is monthly). The library's end-of-term clause for the Commonwealth is "surrender-end-of-term-ks-ne": the tenant surrenders possession and returns the keys at the end of the term, leaves the property in its starting condition except ordinary wear and tear, and any property left behind is handled under "abandoned-property-mp". Exceptions: in a project-based voucher unit, refusing to renew without good cause has program consequences (the Housing Corporation gives the family a tenant-based voucher and removes the unit from the contract), and voucher and condominium-conversion rules limit terminations during the term (see "edu-for-cause-eviction-mp"). Cautious course: a short written reminder before the term ends is good practice, and after the term don't accept rent without stating in writing whether you consent to the tenant staying.

title: Tenancy at Will in the Northern Mariana Islands
bodyText: Northern Mariana Islands law uses "tenancy at will" in one place, and gives it a specific meaning. When a written lease for a fixed term expires and the tenant stays on without a new written lease, the tenant is a tenant at sufferance, and accepting rent doesn't renew the term. If you give written consent to the tenant staying, the tenancy becomes a "tenancy at will as described in" the rule on duration: that is, a periodic tenancy measured by the rent period, month to month if rent is paid monthly, week to week if weekly, and so on. Likewise, when a rental agreement says nothing about how long the tenancy lasts, its length follows the rent period. So in practice a tenancy at will is ended the same way as any periodic tenancy: by written notice before the end of a rental period, at least 7 days for weekly, 15 days for monthly, 30 days for quarterly and 60 days for yearly, unless the agreement sets another period. We found no separate Commonwealth rule for an at-will tenancy that can be ended at any moment, or for a tenant at sufferance's notice. What to do: if you let a tenant stay after the term, put your consent and the terms in writing (the library's "holdover-mp" clause does this: a month-to-month continuation on 15 days' notice), and if you don't consent, say so in writing and don't let accepted payments suggest otherwise.

title: Tenant Bankruptcy in the Northern Mariana Islands
bodyText: Bankruptcy is federal law; Northern Mariana Islands law adds nothing specific (we found no Commonwealth statute, regulation or court rule on a tenant's bankruptcy, on lease clauses that make bankruptcy a default, or on collecting rent or seeking possession from a bankrupt tenant). Under the federal Bankruptcy Code, a tenant's bankruptcy filing automatically stays most actions against the tenant: starting or continuing a court case, including a possession case, or any action to recover a claim that arose before the filing; enforcing a judgment obtained before the filing; and any act to obtain possession of property of the bankruptcy estate or to exercise control over it, which can include the tenant's lease. There are two exceptions for a tenant's home. The stay doesn't stop you from continuing an eviction if you obtained a judgment for possession before the bankruptcy petition was filed, and it doesn't stop an eviction based on the tenant's endangering the property or illegally using (or allowing the use of) a controlled substance there in the 30 days before, if you file with the bankruptcy court and serve on the tenant a certification under penalty of perjury. Each exception is subject to further conditions in the Code that we haven't reviewed and that can give the tenant a chance to object or cure, so don't act on them without advice. In a chapter 7 case, if the trustee doesn't assume or reject the residential lease within 60 days after the order for relief (or a longer time the court sets within those 60 days), the lease is deemed rejected. What to do: when you learn a tenant has filed, stop collection and eviction steps, including serving or acting on a three-day notice, filing or pursuing a possession case and carrying out a writ, unless an exception clearly applies, and get legal advice before going further. Don't treat the filing itself as a default or rely on a lease clause that ends the lease because the tenant files; keep recording rent paid after the filing as your advisor directs.

title: Tenant-Caused Damage in the Northern Mariana Islands
bodyText: We found no Commonwealth statute that sets a tenant's liability for damage to the rental, and no statutory casualty or untenantable-premises termination right (for either side) that a tenant's fault could affect. There is also no rent-escrow or repair-withholding statute, and no list of void lease terms limiting whose acts a tenant answers for. So the lease and general law govern. The library's optional "tenant-caused-damage-nm" clause makes the tenant liable for the reasonable repair cost and your other actual damages when damage results from the deliberate or negligent act of the tenant, a household member or another person on the premises with the tenant's consent, including lost rent while repairs are made (for no longer than the remaining term, less rent you receive), and requires you to make reasonable efforts to repair and re-rent. The optional casualty clause "casualty-termination-mp" lets you end the lease after a casualty but doesn't release the tenant from liability for damage the tenant's side caused. You may deduct the cost of tenant-caused damage beyond ordinary wear and tear from the security deposit, refunding the balance within ten days after the property is returned. For a tenant with a disability who made an approved modification, you may require restoration of the interior only where reasonable, with reasonable wear and tear excepted. What to do: document the unit's condition at move-in and move-out, keep repair invoices, and bill or deduct only actual, reasonable costs.

title: Death of a Tenant in the Northern Mariana Islands
bodyText: We found no Commonwealth statute that ends a residential lease when the tenant dies, gives the family a right to end it, or protects a household from removal after a tenant's death; and no rule letting the lease name a person with authority over the tenant's belongings, deposit or animals, or an affidavit procedure for a landlord to clear a unit. So, unless the lease says otherwise, assume the lease continues after a tenant's death: rent keeps accruing against the tenant's estate, and the lease can be ended by agreement with the personal representative or as the lease and the ordinary notice rules allow. A co-tenant who signed the lease remains bound and entitled to stay. Belongings belong to the estate. Release them only to the court-appointed personal representative or to a person a court order names. Northern Mariana Islands probate law has a simplified court procedure for an estate whose personal property is worth no more than $5,000 above the family's exempt property: the surviving spouse, an adult child, a parent, a sibling, the eldest brother of the decedent's mother or the head of the lineage (or, after 90 days, a creditor) may petition the court for an order transferring the property. When the tenant was domiciled in the Commonwealth, the surviving spouse (or, if there is none, the children jointly) is entitled to the household furniture, furnishings, appliances and personal effects ahead of creditors. The library's optional contact clause ("tenant-death-contact-nh") lets the tenant name someone for you to contact, without giving that person a right to occupy or remove property; property left at the unit is then handled under "abandoned-property-mp", which has you hold a deceased tenant's property for the personal representative or those legally entitled and not sell or dispose of it without their consent or a court order. If the tenant was a servicemember who died in military service, the spouse or a dependent may end the lease within one year after the death (see "edu-servicemember-rights-mp").

title: Ending a Periodic Tenancy in the Northern Mariana Islands
bodyText: Unless the lease says otherwise, Northern Mariana Islands law lets either you or the tenant end a periodic tenancy by written notice given before the end of a rental period: at least 7 days for a week-to-week tenancy, 15 days for month to month, 30 days for quarter to quarter and 60 days for year to year. The notice must be in writing; the statute sets no particular delivery method. A tenancy with no stated length follows the rent period (monthly rent makes it month to month). Because these periods apply "unless otherwise agreed", the lease may set its own period. The library's optional "termination-notice-mp" clause lets you choose one, never shorter than the statutory period for that kind of tenancy and the same for both sides; if you don't use it, the statutory periods apply. If you use it, its period also replaces the 15 days stated for a month-to-month continuation in the holdover clause ("holdover-mp"). No notice is needed to end a fixed term: it ends on its date, and a tenant who stays without your permission can be removed. These notices are separate from the three-day notice for unpaid rent (which the lease can't change) and the cure-or-quit notice for other breaches (which the lease may set, or 15 days if it is silent). We found no Commonwealth rule requiring a termination notice to advise of extension rights for older, disabled or other tenants, a tenant end-of-term notice requirement, a payment-plan offer before a nonpayment case, or a lengthened pay-or-quit period; the Holdover Tenancy Act has not been amended since 1997. Federal limits can lengthen these notices: on a CARES Act covered property a tenant can't be required to vacate until 30 days after a notice to vacate (see "edu-cares-act-notice"), and voucher units have their own rules. What to do: give the notice on paper, deliver it in a way you can prove (by hand, or as the lease's notice terms provide), date it, and make sure it arrives at least the required number of days before the last day of a rental period.

title: Removing Squatters and Unauthorized Occupants in the Northern Mariana Islands
bodyText: We found no Commonwealth statute, regulation or court rule that sets up a fast procedure, outside an eviction case, for removing squatters or other people who were never tenants, whether by police on an owner's affidavit, by a sworn complaint to an officer, or by an ex parte court order; and no special squatting offense or penalty for wrongful use of such a procedure. Two routes exist. Criminal trespass: a person who makes an unlawful and unauthorized entry on another's property, or interferes with its peaceful use, and refuses to leave promptly after being lawfully told to, commits trespass (up to six months). If someone with no right to be there refuses to leave when you tell them, call the Department of Public Safety; its fee schedule lists an $80 service call for matters such as squatters. Civil action: you can sue in the Superior Court to recover possession. The Holdover Tenancy Act's summary procedure reaches a tenant and those holding under the tenant (assigns, subtenants, legal representatives), so a subtenant or assignee who stays after your tenant leaves can be named with the tenant; whether a guest who never held under the tenancy can be is unsettled (case law not searched), so ask the court case to cover all occupants or bring an ordinary civil action. Be careful with anyone who may claim a tenancy, such as a former tenant, a person the tenant let move in, or someone who has paid you rent: don't treat them as trespassers, and use the court case instead, because a mistaken lockout or removal can expose you to liability. Never use force.

title: Paying to Stop an Eviction in the Northern Mariana Islands
bodyText: We found no Commonwealth statute, regulation or court rule that lets a tenant redeem the tenancy after the three-day notice has run, for example by paying everything owed up to a set time before the writ is carried out, and none that stops a possession writ once a money judgment is paid. We also found no rule prescribing reservation wording you must use to accept a partial payment without waiving the default, and none requiring you to accept payment from a charity, government program or other third party, or barring you from limiting payment methods for such payments. The only statutory chance to pay is within the three-day notice period: a tenant who pays the full rent demanded within 3 days (not counting weekends and legal holidays) has met the notice. For a money judgment, an execution sale doesn't go ahead if the judgment, interest and the costs of the levy are paid before the sale. Cautious course: decide your policy before money arrives. If you accept full payment of the rent you gave notice for, assume the default is cured. If you accept a partial payment and want to keep your remedies, say so in writing when you accept it (for example, "accepted as partial payment only; Landlord does not waive the default or the notice"), apply it as the lease provides, and don't rely on that statement alone if you keep accepting payments over time (see "edu-waiver-by-acceptance-mp"). Accepting rent assistance paid on the tenant's behalf is usually the practical course. See also "edu-forfeiture-redemption-mp".

title: Accepting Rent After a Default in the Northern Mariana Islands
bodyText: Northern Mariana Islands law has one statutory rule on accepting rent: when a written lease for a fixed term has expired and the tenant stays on without a new written lease, your mere acceptance of rent does not renew the term; the tenant remains a tenant at sufferance unless you give written consent to the tenant staying, which turns the holdover into a periodic tenancy. We found no Commonwealth statute on whether accepting rent after a default, a three-day notice or a cure notice, or during a possession case, waives the default or the notice, and no rule on lease "non-waiver" clauses. Cautious course: assume that accepting the full rent you demanded cures that rent default, and that accepting rent with knowledge of another breach, especially repeatedly, may be treated as waiving that breach or as consenting to the tenancy continuing. If you mean to go on with a notice or case, either refuse the payment or accept it only with a written statement, given at the time, that you accept it without waiving the default, the notice or your right to possession, and keep a copy. After a fixed term ends, don't accept rent without saying in writing whether you consent to the tenant staying. A lease non-waiver clause helps but may not overcome a pattern of conduct; don't rely on it alone. See also "edu-redemption-mp".

title: Notice Delivery Methods in the Northern Mariana Islands
bodyText: Northern Mariana Islands landlord-tenant law doesn't use an "actual notice" standard; it sets specific methods for some notices and leaves others to the lease. Three-day notice for unpaid rent: hand delivery to the tenant or, if the tenant is absent, leaving a copy at the premises. The lease isn't invited to add other methods, so don't rely on a text or e-mail for it. Notice to cure or quit for other breaches: the statute's hand-delivery rule applies only in the absence of a lease provision prescribing the method for serving notices, so the lease may set the method. Notice to end a periodic tenancy: it must be written; the statute sets no delivery method. Federal e-signature law lets the parties use electronic records for many purposes, but it doesn't validate an electronic notice of default, eviction or the right to cure under a rental agreement for a primary residence, and it doesn't require anyone to accept electronic records. So any notice that can lead to removal should go on paper by an accepted method; e-mail or text can be an extra copy. The library's optional "electronic-notice-ma" clause follows this: routine communications and notices the law doesn't require to be delivered a particular way may go by e-mail, but notices to the tenant of nonpayment, default, termination, eviction or the right to cure don't. We found no Commonwealth rule that allows or forbids text-message notice by agreement.

title: Lease Addenda in the Northern Mariana Islands
bodyText: We found no Commonwealth statute or regulation that requires a separate optional addendum (such as a nonstandard-provisions form) to control over a private residential lease, or that otherwise ranks addenda against the lease. One addendum must control by federal rule: in a Housing Choice Voucher tenancy, the HUD-prescribed tenancy addendum must be added word for word to your lease, the tenant may enforce it against you, and its terms prevail over any other lease provision; the Housing Corporation's project-based voucher rules say the same. Federal lead-based paint rules also require a disclosure for pre-1978 housing, which goes with the lease. The library's "addendum-precedence" clause, which carries MP for the Northern Mariana Islands, says the lease controls over an addendum except that any disclosure, notice or addendum the law requires, or that the law says controls, prevails. That fits both rules above. What to do: for a voucher unit, attach the tenancy addendum unchanged; for any addendum you write yourself, make sure it doesn't contradict the lease, or say expressly which term controls.

title: Telling Tenants About Proceedings in the Northern Mariana Islands
bodyText: We found no Commonwealth statute or regulation that requires a residential landlord to tell tenants about a lawsuit, foreclosure, condemnation, code-enforcement order or other proceeding that could affect their tenancy. Some proceedings reach tenants directly instead. When the Building Safety Official finds a building unsafe, the official notifies the owner, occupant, lessee, mortgagee and others with an interest, in writing by personal service or certified mail, and may order the occupants to vacate; occupants may appear at the hearing. A condominium declarant converting a building must give each tenant notice of the conversion at least 60 days before requiring them to leave. An applicator seeking a permit for a termite fumigation of a single-owner complex with multiple units must inform all tenants at least 14 days before the fumigation. And in a mortgage foreclosure, a tenant whose lease is recorded may be named in the case, and after the sale the buyer collects the rent (see "edu-foreclosure-mp"). Cautious course: tell your tenants promptly in writing of any proceeding you know will affect their possession or rent (a foreclosure filing, a condemnation, an unsafe-building or vacate order, a pending sale with a move-out date), what it means for them, and who to pay rent to. Concealing it could be attacked as an unfair or deceptive practice.

title: Automatic Lease Renewal in the Northern Mariana Islands
bodyText: We found no Commonwealth consumer-contract statute on automatic renewals (no bold-type, opt-in or pre-renewal notice requirement) that reaches a residential lease. Without a renewal clause, a fixed-term lease doesn't renew itself: if the tenant stays after the term without a new written lease, accepting rent doesn't renew the term, and only your written consent turns the holdover into a periodic tenancy. If you use an automatic-renewal clause, keep three Commonwealth rules in mind. A lease (including renewals) for more than one year must be a signed written instrument, and as a cautious course should be notarized and recorded. Renewal rights that could carry the total term, including renewals, beyond 55 years run into the constitutional land-alienation limit for a tenant who isn't of Northern Marianas descent. And any rent increase at renewal can't take effect while a Governor's price freeze is in effect. Cautious course: state the renewal term, any rent change and how either side can stop the renewal in plain words near the signature, and remind the tenant in writing before the renewal date; a buried renewal could be attacked as unfair or deceptive under the Consumer Protection Act.

title: Arbitration Clauses in the Northern Mariana Islands
bodyText: We found no Commonwealth arbitration act and no statute or court rule that specifically allows, limits or forbids a binding arbitration clause in a residential lease, or says which claims (such as possession cases or personal-injury claims) must stay in court. The Commonwealth's court mediation rules don't apply to cases under the Holdover Tenancy Act, and they say nothing in them prevents parties from choosing other forms of dispute resolution, including binding arbitration. Federal arbitration law may apply to some leases; it was not reviewed here. Cautious course: don't make binding arbitration a standard lease term. If you offer it, make it optional and mutual, keep possession cases (the summary possession procedure in the Superior Court) and small claims in court, don't use it to limit a tenant's fair housing, consumer-protection or personal-injury claims or remedies, and split or pay the arbitration costs so the tenant isn't priced out. A one-sided clause could be attacked as unconscionable under the Consumer Protection Act. The library's optional informal dispute-resolution clause ("informal-dispute-resolution-or") already keeps possession actions out of its process. The library now offers an optional clause, `arbitration-agreement`, built on these limits: money claims only, with possession, small claims, security-deposit, injury and emergency claims kept in court, every remedy and the right to a lawyer kept, the arbitration fees above a court filing fee paid by you, a 30-day opt-out for the tenant, and separate initials from both of you.

title: Other Rules the Northern Mariana Islands Does Not Have
bodyText: Rules found in some other places for which we found no Commonwealth statute, regulation or court rule, each explained in its own row: no good-cause requirement to end a private tenancy ("edu-for-cause-eviction-mp"); no general anti-retaliation law ("edu-retaliation-mp"); no lockout or other self-help eviction right ("edu-lockout-for-rent-delinquency-mp", "edu-self-help-eviction-mp"); no residential landlord's lien or distress for rent ("edu-landlord-lien-mp"); no possession bond or confessed judgment ("edu-possession-bond-mp"); no notice-service fee rule ("edu-notice-service-fee-mp"); no rent-into-court requirement ("edu-rent-into-court-counterclaim-mp"); no post-notice redemption right ("edu-redemption-mp", "edu-forfeiture-redemption-mp"); no continuance when a benefit payment is late ("edu-social-security-defense-mp"); no early termination for illness or a care-facility move ("edu-infirmity-termination-mp") or for landlord misrepresentation ("edu-statutory-early-termination-mp"); no right to end a lease because repairs cost too much ("edu-repair-cost-termination-mp"); no seasonal-tenancy regime ("edu-seasonal-tenancy-mp"); no Commonwealth servicemember lease law beyond federal law ("edu-servicemember-rights-mp"); no owner move-in rule ("edu-owner-move-in-reservation-mp"); no consumer auto-renewal rule ("edu-automatic-renewal-mp"); no arbitration act ("edu-binding-arbitration-mp"); no tenant-death lease rule ("edu-tenant-death-mp"). We also found no Commonwealth rule setting type size, bold print, plain-language standards or blank-space rules for residential leases, or requiring you to give the tenant a copy of the signed lease (type-size and plain-language rules exist only for other contracts, such as self-storage and car-rental agreements). Give every tenant a signed copy anyway. Where no written law speaks, Commonwealth courts apply the common law as stated in the Restatements, which this library hasn't read; each row gives the cautious course.

title: Checked Across All of Northern Mariana Islands Law
bodyText: Three points checked across all of Northern Mariana Islands law, not only the Holdover Tenancy Act. (1) Squatters: there is no fast removal outside the courts; report criminal trespass to the Department of Public Safety or sue for possession ("edu-unauthorized-occupant-removal-mp"). (2) Rent receipts: no landlord-specific receipt rule, but the Sales Receipt Act requires a receipt from anyone receiving gross revenue from a sale, which may reach rent received in a business; give a written receipt for every payment, especially cash ("edu-rent-receipts-mp"). (3) Registration before eviction: we found no landlord-registration requirement and no rule that a landlord without a business licence can't bring a possession case, although every business must hold a business licence. But a landlord that is a foreign (off-island) corporation, limited liability company or limited liability partnership transacting business in the Commonwealth may not maintain a court proceeding until it has its certificate of authority or statement of foreign qualification; for a corporation, the statute lets the court stay the case until it does. For a foreign limited liability company the statute settles the question: owning income-producing real property in the Commonwealth is transacting business, and while it lacks a certificate of authority it is treated as having appointed the Registrar of Corporations as its agent for service of process (4 CMC §§ 4933(b), 4938). For a corporation, merely owning property is not transacting business, so whether renting it out is remains unsettled (4 CMC §§ 4641(b)(9), 4642). Either way, a foreign entity landlord should register before filing.

title: Domestic Violence Law Citations Current in the Northern Mariana Islands
bodyText: Northern Mariana Islands landlord-tenant law (the Holdover Tenancy Act) doesn't refer to the domestic violence laws at all, so there is no cross-reference that could have gone stale. The protection-order law is current and sits in the Domestic and Family Violence Prevention Act in Title 8 of the Code. The Superior Court may, even without notice to the abuser, remove and exclude the abuser from the victim's residence regardless of who owns it, order the abuser to stay away, and order who keeps personal effects, with police standing by; after a hearing it may also order the abuser to pay rent or the mortgage on the victim's residence where the abuser has a duty of support. Criminal and bail laws can also bar contact and order restitution, including a victim's costs of changing locks. If a tenant shows you a protection order excluding a household member, respect it: don't let the excluded person back in or give that person a key, even if he or she is on the lease, and cooperate with police serving or enforcing it. If the tenant asks you to change the locks so the order can be enforced, do so promptly (the Commonwealth has no statute requiring it, but it is the cautious course). The Commonwealth has no statute giving a victim a right to end a lease early ("edu-statutory-early-termination-mp"); in federally assisted housing, the Violence Against Women Act protects victims from eviction because of the abuse and lets you remove only the abuser.

title: Electronic Signatures on Leases in the Northern Mariana Islands
bodyText: The Commonwealth has no electronic-transactions act of its own, so the federal E-SIGN Act governs electronic signatures on leases in the Northern Mariana Islands (it defines "State" to include the territories and possessions) for any transaction in or affecting interstate or foreign commerce; whether every local lease is one is not settled here (case law not searched), so treat it as applying but keep the paper-notice limits below. Under it, a lease or signature can't be denied legal effect just because it is electronic, and the Act itself doesn't require anyone to agree to use electronic records. The library's "electronic-signatures" clause, which carries MP for the Commonwealth, records both parties' consent to sign electronically. Two limits. First, E-SIGN doesn't validate an electronic notice of default, eviction or the right to cure under a rental agreement for a primary residence, so serve those notices on paper: the three-day rent notice by hand delivery or, if the tenant is absent, by leaving a copy at the premises (see "edu-actual-notice-method-mp"). There is no Commonwealth rule that adds to or narrows this exclusion. Second, a lease for more than one year must be a signed written instrument, which an electronic signature can satisfy, but as a cautious course such a lease should also be acknowledged before a notary and recorded with the Commonwealth Recorder; the Recorder's Office may accept electronic recording under its rules, so check what it accepts for acknowledgment before relying on an e-signed copy. Keep a complete copy of the signed lease that both parties can print and store, and give the tenant one.

title: Emergency Contacts for Northern Mariana Islands Tenants
bodyText: We found no Commonwealth statute, regulation or court rule that requires you to give tenants an emergency or 24-hour contact number, or to collect an emergency contact from each tenant, and none that says what a named contact may do. Emergency-contact rules in Commonwealth law apply only to child-care centers and schools. You may ask for one. The library's optional "tenant-death-contact-nh" clause does so: naming a contact gives that person no right to occupy the property or remove the tenant's belongings, and if the tenant dies you deal with the personal representative or heirs (see "edu-tenant-death-mp"). Good practice: give tenants a way to reach you or your manager for emergencies such as fire, flooding, typhoon damage or a loss of water or power, and post or send it in writing; and handle any contact information you collect privately.

title: Energy Usage Data in the Northern Mariana Islands
bodyText: We found no Commonwealth statute, regulation or court rule that requires energy benchmarking of residential buildings, or that governs a lease term letting the Commonwealth Utilities Corporation release a tenant's electricity or water usage data to you. If the tenant holds the utility account, the usage records are the tenant's account information: ask the tenant to share them, or include an optional lease term in which the tenant authorizes the utility to give you usage data for the unit for building-management purposes, and get the utility's own authorization form signed if it has one. Don't make access a condition you enforce by default or eviction. If you hold the account and bill the tenant for utilities, keep the meter and billing records and share them with the tenant on request.

title: Changing the Lease in the Northern Mariana Islands
bodyText: We found no Commonwealth statute, regulation or court rule that lets a landlord amend an existing lease by written notice so that it complies with a new law, and none that sets rules for an "entire agreement" (integration) clause in a lease. So the lease decides how it can be changed. The library's "entire-agreement" clause, which carries MP for the Northern Mariana Islands, says the Lease and its addenda are the whole agreement and can be changed only in a writing signed by all parties (its "as applicable law permits Landlord to change it by written notice" limb has nothing to attach to here). Two Commonwealth rules matter. A lease for more than one year, and any surrender of it, must be a written instrument signed by the party granting or surrendering it, and an agreement that can't be performed within a year must be in writing and signed; a signed lease and signed amendments meet both. The Holdover Tenancy Act leaves the parties free to add rights and duties by agreement. If a new law changes what a lease may say and reaches existing leases, it applies whatever the lease says (whether it reaches existing leases depends on the new law's own terms; Commonwealth acts often carry a savings clause for rights already acquired under contract); you can't add a term mid-lease without the tenant's signature, but in a month-to-month or other periodic tenancy you can end the tenancy by the required written notice and offer a new lease (see "edu-term-change-notice-mp"). What to do: put every change in a written amendment signed by you and every tenant, and keep the signed copy with the lease.

title: Governing Law in the Northern Mariana Islands
bodyText: The Northern Mariana Islands is a Commonwealth in political union with the United States, not a state, so the library uses the Northern Mariana Islands clause "governing-law-mp", which names the laws of the Commonwealth and applicable federal law, in place of the shared "State of" wording. What governs your lease: the Commonwealth Code and regulations; federal laws that apply here under the Covenant or by their own terms (for example, fair housing and lead-paint disclosure); and, where no written law or local customary law speaks, the common law as stated in the American Law Institute's Restatements, which Commonwealth courts apply as the rules of decision. We found no Commonwealth statute on choice-of-law clauses in leases. A possession case must be filed in the Superior Court in the senatorial district where the property is (Rota; Tinian and Aguiguan; or Saipan and the islands north of it), and each district may have local laws (for example, Saipan's blight-maintenance law) that we flag but have not reviewed. What to do: use "governing-law-mp", and check local law for the island where the property is.

title: Settling Disputes Before Court in the Northern Mariana Islands
bodyText: We found no Commonwealth statute, regulation or court rule that governs a lease term requiring the parties to try to settle a dispute informally before going to court, and no general arbitration statute. So such a term is a contract choice. The library's "informal-dispute-resolution-or" clause, which carries MP for the Northern Mariana Islands, asks each side to give written notice and offer to meet within 10 days before suing, and it leaves out possession actions and does not delay any notice, deadline or remedy the law gives. That carve-out matters here: the Holdover Tenancy Act's summary possession case is meant to be fast, and the court's mediation rules expressly don't apply to it. Other civil cases in the Superior Court (for example, a suit for unpaid rent or damage outside a possession case, or a tenant's deposit claim) are ordered to non-binding mediation unless the court finds good cause to skip it; small claims and family cases are excluded. If a tenant files a fair housing complaint with the Northern Marianas Housing Corporation, the Corporate Director must, to the extent feasible, try conciliation, and a conciliation agreement may provide for binding arbitration. Northern Marianas Housing Corporation public-housing tenants have their own grievance procedure, which we flag but have not reviewed. What to do: if you use the clause, keep possession cases outside it, and expect court-ordered mediation in other lawsuits.

title: Landlord Registration and Licences in the Northern Mariana Islands
bodyText: We found no Commonwealth statute or regulation that makes a residential landlord register with a rental registry, county assessor or similar office as a condition of renting, none that requires an owner living off-island to hire a licensed local broker or manager, and no real estate broker or property-manager licensing law. Three Commonwealth permits can still reach you. Business licence: before engaging in or continuing in a business, a person must get a licence from the Department of Finance for each line of business at each location ($100 a year); for tax purposes "business" normally means any regular and continuous activity carried on for profit, so whether an owner renting a single home needs one is a judgment call. Cautious course: if you rent regularly for profit, get a licence. Annual certificate: every apartment and residential rental, including a single-family house, needs a yearly Building Safety inspection and Certificate of Compliance (see "edu-rental-inspection-mp" and the optional clause "rental-inspection-mp"). Sanitary permit: the Bureau of Environmental Health's permit for room accommodations can reach some rentals (see "edu-health-district-rental-rules-mp"). If you rent to a Housing Choice Voucher family, the Northern Marianas Housing Corporation keeps its own approved-landlord registry, which we flag but have not reviewed. If you own through a corporation or limited liability company formed outside the Commonwealth, it also needs a certificate of authority from the Registrar of Corporations, and until it has one it can't bring a possession case (4 CMC §§ 4642, 4933(b), 4938; see "edu-nonresident-owner-agent-mp"). What to do: get the business licence if you rent as a business, keep the Building Safety certificate current, and ask the environmental health office in writing whether your rental needs a sanitary permit.

title: Completing Every Blank in the Northern Mariana Islands
bodyText: We found no Commonwealth statute, regulation or court rule that requires every blank in a written lease to be filled in before signing, or that treats an unfilled blank as a breach by the landlord. The only "no blanks" rule we found is for licensed lenders, who may not take a note or promise to pay with blanks left to be filled in after it is signed; it does not reach leases. Still, a blank can cost you: where the lease is silent the Holdover Tenancy Act's defaults apply (for example, 15 days' written notice to cure a non-rent breach) and a court may read an unclear term against the party who drafted it (Restatement not read; case law not searched). What to do: before anyone signs, fill in every blank or write "none" or "N/A", have every party initial any handwritten change, and give each tenant a complete signed copy.

title: What a Lease Must Contain in the Northern Mariana Islands
bodyText: The Northern Mariana Islands has no residential landlord-tenant act listing what a lease must contain; we found no Commonwealth statute or regulation that prescribes the contents of a private residential lease. What the law does require: (1) Lead paint (federal): for housing built before 1978, the lease must include, within it or attached, the federal Lead Warning Statement, your disclosure of known lead-based paint or hazards, a list of records given, the tenant's acknowledgment and signatures (the library's "lead-based-paint" clause carries MP for the Northern Mariana Islands); short leases of 100 days or less with no renewal, and housing certified lead-free, are excluded. (2) Housing Choice Voucher tenancies (federal): the lease must be written and signed, name the owner and tenant, identify the unit, state the term, the monthly rent to owner and who supplies which utilities and appliances, and include the HUD tenancy addendum word for word, which prevails over the rest of the lease (see "edu-addendum-precedence-mp"). (3) A lease for more than one year must be a signed written instrument; and no lease, with renewal rights, may give a person not of Northern Marianas descent more than 55 years. Useful but optional: an address the tenant designates for notices (see "eviction-service-party-mp"), your own cure period and notice method for non-rent breaches, and any change to the default termination notice periods, all of which the Holdover Tenancy Act lets the lease set. What to do: use the library's lease, add the lead and voucher pieces where they apply, and get every party's signature.

title: Giving the Tenant a Copy in the Northern Mariana Islands
bodyText: We found no Commonwealth statute, regulation or court rule that requires a landlord, broker or property manager to give the tenant a copy of the lease, and none that makes failure to give a copy a defense to enforcing the lease. The Commonwealth has no real estate broker licensing law that would impose such a duty. Tenants often need their copy anyway: Commonwealth programs such as food assistance and some business and residency applications ask for a copy of the lease or rental agreement. If the tenant has a Housing Choice Voucher, any agreed change to the lease must be in writing and you must give the housing agency a copy right away. The library's optional clause "lease-copy-receipt-hi", which carries MP for the Northern Mariana Islands, has the tenant acknowledge receiving a copy of the lease and its rules and commits you to deliver a fully signed copy promptly. What to do: give every tenant a complete signed copy of the lease and any addenda, and keep your own signed original.

title: Initialing Lease Terms in the Northern Mariana Islands
bodyText: We found no Commonwealth statute, regulation or court rule that requires a residential tenant to initial particular lease provisions, or that requires any residential lease term to be printed in boldface, capitals or a minimum type size. The Commonwealth's initialing and conspicuous-print rules are for other kinds of contracts: self-service storage rental agreements, motor vehicle rental damage waivers, and some sale-of-goods forms under the Uniform Commercial Code. The closest landlord-side rule is the bad-check statute: to claim treble damages on a bounced rent check, your written demand must carry a conspicuous prescribed notice (see "edu-returned-payments-mp"). What to do: although initials aren't required, having the tenant initial each page and any term that is unusual or that limits the tenant's rights (for example, a fee, a waiver or an optional clause) is good evidence that the tenant saw it, and avoids a later claim that a term was hidden.

title: Long Leases: Formalities in the Northern Mariana Islands
bodyText: A residential lease for more than one year has formalities in the Northern Mariana Islands, though no seal is required. (1) Writing and signature: it must be a written instrument signed by the landlord granting it, or by the landlord's agent if the agent's authority is itself in writing; an agreement that can't be performed within a year must also be signed by the party to be held to it (so have every tenant sign too). (2) Spouse's consent: if you are married and your spouse has any legal or equitable interest in the property, you need your spouse's written consent to lease it for more than one year; without it, the lease can be undone at your spouse's option, and your spouse may sue the tenant as well as you. (3) Notary and recording: a lease for more than one year that is recorded must first be acknowledged before a notary, and an unrecorded lease over one year is not good against a later good-faith buyer or mortgagee who pays value without notice of it and records first; whether the tenant must record it is unsettled, so the cautious course is to sign before a notary and record it (see "edu-statute-of-frauds-lease-term-mp"). (4) Maximum term: a lease, counting renewal rights, of more than 55 years is a long-term interest only persons of Northern Marianas descent may acquire, and a transaction that violates this is void; a new lease that both sides agree to (not through a tenant's option), made close to the end of the old one, starting after it ends and itself within 55 years, is not counted as a renewal right. What to do: for any lease over one year, have every owner (and any owner's spouse) sign or consent in writing, use a written authority for any agent, notarize, record, and keep the total term with options at 55 years or less.

title: Lease Print Size in the Northern Mariana Islands
bodyText: We found no Commonwealth statute, regulation or court rule that sets a minimum type size for a residential lease, or that limits the use of a lease printed in small type as evidence. The Commonwealth's type-size rules are for other documents: self-service storage rental agreements (10-point), motor vehicle rental agreements and advertising, insurance policies, notary fee schedules, and product warning labels. For pre-1978 housing, the federal lead disclosure must be in the language of the lease but has no type-size rule in the saved text. What to do: no size is required, but print the lease in a readable size (at least 10-point is a sensible floor, matching the Commonwealth's rules for other consumer contracts) so no one can claim a term was hidden in fine print.

title: Off-Island Owners in the Northern Mariana Islands
bodyText: We found no Commonwealth statute, regulation or court rule that requires an owner living outside the Northern Mariana Islands to appoint a local agent, name an agent in the lease, or file an agent designation before suing a tenant, and no such rule hidden in nuisance, blight or receivership law (Saipan's blight regulations make banks and lenders post property-management contact information on foreclosed and vacant properties, which doesn't reach a landlord renting to a tenant). Two general rules do reach an off-island owner. First, if you own through a corporation or limited liability company formed outside the Commonwealth, it needs a certificate of authority from the Registrar of Corporations naming an agent in the Commonwealth. A foreign limited liability company that owns income-producing real property here is transacting business; without the certificate it can't bring a possession case and is treated as having appointed the Registrar as its agent for service of process. A foreign corporation transacting business without one can't maintain a case and is liable for a civil penalty of $100 a day, up to $5,000 a year (4 CMC §§ 4641, 4642, 4647, 4932, 4933(b), 4938). Second, whoever you are, holding or owning real property in the Commonwealth submits you to its courts on claims arising from it, and if you can't be found here a tenant can serve you by leaving the papers with the Attorney General and delivering them to you personally or by certified or registered mail (7 CMC §§ 1102, 1104(a)). In practice an off-island owner still needs someone local: the three-day notice demanding rent must give the landlord's name, address and telephone number and must be hand-delivered or left at the home, and a possession case is filed in the Superior Court on the island where the property is (an entity landlord should appear through a CNMI-licensed attorney; see "edu-entity-landlord-court-representation-mp"). Tax: a nonresident alien or foreign corporation is generally subject to the Northern Marianas Territorial Income Tax only on income sourced in the Commonwealth (the source rules were not reviewed, but assume rent from Commonwealth property is Commonwealth-source); whether a tenant or manager must withhold tax from rent paid to a nonresident owner turns on the territorial income tax's withholding provisions, which we have not reviewed. What to do: if you live off-island, give tenants the name, address and phone of a local manager or contact in the lease, arrange for someone on-island to deliver notices, and ask the Division of Revenue and Taxation or a tax adviser about withholding and filing on your rental income.

title: Delivering Notices in the Northern Mariana Islands
bodyText: How each notice is delivered in the Northern Mariana Islands is covered in "edu-actual-notice-method-mp": the three-day rent notice must be hand-delivered or, if the tenant is absent, left at the premises; for a notice to cure other breaches the lease may set the method (hand delivery or leaving a copy applies only if the lease is silent); a notice ending a periodic tenancy must be written but has no set method; and federal e-signature law does not validate an electronic notice of default, eviction or the right to cure for a primary residence. Points that answer the other questions: (1) Who serves: the rent notice is served by the person entitled to the rent (you or your agent); no sheriff, marshal or process server is required for any pre-suit notice. The court summons and complaint, by contrast, are served under the court rules. (2) Lease-agreed methods: if your lease prescribes a method for serving notices, that method governs cure-or-quit notices, so follow your own lease exactly. (3) E-mail by agreement: there is no Commonwealth electronic-transactions act and no Commonwealth rule on e-mail or text notice; the library's optional "electronic-notice-ma" clause allows e-mail only for routine notices and keeps nonpayment, default, termination, eviction and cure notices on paper. Federal e-signature law sets conditions before any notice the law requires to be in writing can go to a tenant electronically: the tenant must first receive a clear and conspicuous statement of the right to paper copies and to withdraw consent, plus a statement of the hardware and software needed, and must then consent electronically in a way that shows the tenant can open the format you will use; notices of default, eviction or the right to cure for a primary residence stay excluded even with consent. A servicemember ending a lease under federal law may deliver the notice to you by hand, carrier, return-receipt mail or electronic means you designate. (4) Counting days: the landlord-tenant statutes don't define "days"; the three-day rent notice excludes Saturdays, Sundays and legal holidays by its own text, and the court's time rule (exclude the trigger day; for periods of 10 days or less, skip weekends and holidays unless the period says "calendar days") applies to any applicable statute, so whether it stretches other notice periods is unsettled. Cautious course: count generously and give extra days.
