What to do: deliver every legally significant notice on paper by hand (or leave it at the home if the tenant is out), keep a dated record, and send an e-mail copy if you like.

title: While a Notice to Vacate Is Pending in the Northern Mariana Islands
bodyText: We found no general Commonwealth statute that limits what a landlord may do to the unit or the tenancy while a notice to vacate is running, such as a ban on alterations that make the unit unlivable. One rule applies in a condominium conversion: a declarant converting a building must give tenants at least 60 days' notice before requiring them to vacate, may not require a tenant to vacate on less than 30 days' notice except for nonpayment of rent, waste or disturbing other tenants, and may not alter the terms of the tenancy during that period; failure to give the notice is a defense to a possession case (see "edu-conversion-notice-mp"). Otherwise, the tenancy and the lease stay in force until the notice period ends, so your duties continue: under the cautious course we take, you owe a duty to keep the dwelling fit to live in and must not retaliate against a tenant (see "edu-retaliation-mp"), and any removal must go through the Superior Court, not by making the unit unusable (see "edu-self-help-eviction-mp"). What to do: while a notice to vacate is pending, keep services and repairs going, schedule any renovation work for after the tenant leaves, and don't change rent or other terms.

title: Notices in the Northern Mariana Islands
bodyText: The library's shared "notices" clause carries MP for the Northern Mariana Islands: notices go to the addresses in the lease (or an updated address given in writing), and where the law requires a particular method, form, timing or content for a notice, the law controls. In the Commonwealth that means: the three-day notice demanding rent must be in substantially the statutory form and be hand-delivered or left at the premises if the tenant is absent; a notice to cure a non-rent breach follows the lease's method if the lease sets one; and a notice ending a periodic tenancy must be in writing. Details are in "edu-notice-delivery-methods-mp", "edu-actual-notice-method-mp" and "edu-nonpayment-notice-mp". The tenant's notice address also matters in court: if a summons must be posted at the property, the clerk mails copies to the address the tenant designated for notices in a written lease (if none, the tenant's residential mailing address), so consider the optional "eviction-service-party-mp" clause. What to do: put both parties' notice addresses in the lease, update them in writing, and follow the statutory method for every notice that can lead to removal.

title: Lease Choices the Law Leaves to You in the Northern Mariana Islands
bodyText: With no residential landlord-tenant act, Northern Mariana Islands law leaves most lease terms to the parties: the Holdover Tenancy Act says nothing in it impairs the parties' right to create additional rights and duties in a rental agreement. A few statutory defaults apply only if the lease doesn't change them, so these are true choices for your lease: (1) rent is payable without demand, at the start of each period, and is apportioned day by day "unless otherwise agreed"; (2) a periodic tenancy ends on written notice of 60 days (year to year), 30 (quarter), 15 (month to month) or 7 (week to week) before the end of a period "unless otherwise agreed", so the lease may set a different period (for example, 30 days for a monthly tenancy); (3) for a material non-rent breach, the 15-day cure-or-quit notice and hand-delivery method apply only when the lease is silent, so the lease may set its own cure period and notice method; and (4) the tenant may designate an address for notices in a written lease, which the court clerk then uses (see "eviction-service-party-mp"). Things to treat as fixed whatever the lease says (the statutes don't invite the lease to vary them; for some, such as the court-only route and fees, this is our cautious reading, case law not searched): the three-day rent notice's form, period and service; the ten-day deposit refund; the court-only possession process; either side's ability to recover reasonable court costs and attorney's fees if it wins a Holdover Tenancy Act case; fair housing rules; and a Governor's price freeze on rent. Optional clauses in the library for the Commonwealth open "[Optional.]" and are never defaults. What to do: decide each of the four choices above deliberately and write it into the lease; otherwise the statutory default governs.

title: Size Thresholds for Landlords in the Northern Mariana Islands
bodyText: A few Northern Mariana Islands rules turn on how many homes or units you own or rent, and none gives a small landlord a general exemption from landlord duties. Fair housing (Commonwealth Fair Housing Act and federal Fair Housing Act): the main discrimination rules don't apply to (1) a single-family house rented by a private individual owner who owns no more than three such houses, but only if every condition is met together: no real estate broker or agent and no rental services of anyone in the business of renting dwellings are used, and no discriminatory advertisement is published; or (2) rooms or units in a building of no more than four families where the owner lives in one of the units. A person is "in the business" of renting (and so can't count as an unassisted owner) after three or more rental transactions as principal in 12 months, or by owning a dwelling for five or more families. Even exempt owners may never publish a discriminatory advertisement, and the Commonwealth's anti-discrimination rule for merchants has no small-owner exemption (cautious course: treat it as reaching you). Accessibility design rules apply to "covered multifamily dwellings": buildings of four or more units with an elevator, and ground-floor units in other buildings of four or more units. Building Safety: the annual inspection covers the entire premises of a single-family rental or a building of fewer than five apartments, all common areas and half the units for 5 to 12, and all common areas and 35 percent of the units for more than 12 (see "edu-rental-inspection-mp"). Sanitary permits: the statute's room-accommodation definition starts at four guest rooms (see "edu-health-district-rental-rules-mp"). What to do: read each exemption's conditions together, and assume fair housing and the merchant rule apply unless you clearly meet every condition.

title: Renter's Insurance in the Northern Mariana Islands
bodyText: We found no Commonwealth statute or regulation on renter's insurance in residential leases: nothing requires or forbids a lease term making the tenant carry renter's insurance, nothing lets the tenant pick the carrier or limits force-placed coverage and fees, and nothing requires a written notice that your insurance won't cover the tenant's belongings or a flood-zone or renter's-insurance notice before signing. So a renter's-insurance requirement is a contract term. The library's "tenants-property-insurance-ks-oh-ca" clause, which carries MP for the Northern Mariana Islands, tells the tenant your insurance doesn't cover the tenant's property and requires renter's insurance with liability coverage of at least the amount the lease states, without a clause excusing you from your own negligence (the library doesn't use that disclaimer here; see "edu-tenants-property-insurance-mp"). If you require insurance, don't insist on a particular insurer or agent, and don't add a charge for buying coverage on the tenant's behalf unless the lease clearly provides for it; under the cautious reading of the Consumer Protection Act, a term that misstates the tenant's rights or is one-sided can be challenged. What to do: if you want renter's insurance, put the requirement and the minimum in the lease, let the tenant choose the insurer, and ask for proof of coverage at move-in and each renewal.

title: Selling or Changing Management in the Northern Mariana Islands
bodyText: We found no Commonwealth statute, regulation or court rule that requires a landlord to tell tenants when the property is sold or a new manager takes over, releases a selling landlord once notice is given, makes a buyer liable for deposits by statute, requires a tenant estoppel certificate, governs showings to buyers, or deals with a receiver rejecting a residential lease. Deposits on sale are covered in "edu-security-deposit-on-sale-mp" (cautious course: transfer every deposit to the buyer and tell tenants who holds it), and foreclosure in "edu-foreclosure-mp". What the law does say: (1) Recording: apart from a lease of one year or less, an unrecorded lease isn't valid against a later good-faith buyer or mortgagee who records first, so a long lease should be notarized and recorded to bind a buyer. (2) Lead paint (federal): selling pre-1978 housing triggers the federal disclosure to the buyer. (3) Fair housing: the discrimination rules apply to sales as well as rentals. (4) Condominium conversion: special notice and purchase-offer rules protect tenants (see "edu-conversion-notice-mp"). (5) If you hold the property under your own lease (common in the Commonwealth, where many owners lease land from a person of Northern Marianas descent), you can't give a tenant more than you hold: keep the residential lease term inside your own lease term, and tell the tenant if your ground lease ends first (Restatement not read; case law not searched). For showings, the tagged "showing-notice-la" and "landlords-access" clauses set the contract terms. What to do: on a sale or management change, tell every tenant in writing the new owner's or manager's name, address and phone and where to pay rent, transfer the deposits and lease files, and have the buyer sign on to the leases.

title: Which Rules Apply in the Northern Mariana Islands
bodyText: Scope in the Northern Mariana Islands is simple because there is no residential landlord-tenant act. The Holdover Tenancy Act (the summary possession procedure and its notice rules) covers any tenancy of houses, buildings, lands or tenements, residential or commercial, of any length, but not a lease to which the CNMI government or one of its agencies or instrumentalities is a party; it took effect August 1, 1997. A person who never was a tenant (for example, a squatter) appears to be outside it on its terms, so plan on an ordinary civil case to remove one (our reading; case law not searched). We found no mobile home park act, no farm-tenancy carve-out, no long-lease exclusion, no population or census line and no rule gated by lease date apart from effective dates (the deposit-refund law dates from 2005). Land rules matter more: leases of public land are made by the Department of Public Lands under their own law, and rights under a homestead permit can't be sold, assigned, leased or encumbered before the deed issues, so don't rent a homestead lot that is still under permit. A lease (with renewals) longer than 55 years is restricted by Article XII. Local law differs by senatorial district: Saipan has a zoning law and a blight-maintenance law, and Tinian and Rota have their own local laws; we flag these but haven't reviewed them. Northern Marianas Housing Corporation public housing and voucher tenancies follow their own federal and corporation rules. What to do: confirm who owns the land and under what title before you lease, and check the local law of the island where the property is.

title: Invalid Terms and Severability in the Northern Mariana Islands
bodyText: The library's shared "severability" clause carries MP for the Northern Mariana Islands, and here it does real work. Most Commonwealth rules that reach a lease knock out only the offending term (for example, a clause in a lease, licence or permit granting exclusive rights for fiber-optic networks is void and unenforceable, and, in a credit sale or lease of consumer goods or services, an agreement cutting off the consumer's defenses against an assignee has no force), so the rest of the lease stands. Two rules can reach the whole transaction. First, Article XII: a land transaction that gives a person not of Northern Marianas descent a permanent or long-term interest (for example, a lease over 55 years with renewals, or a purchase option on freehold land) is void; but by statute a court must enforce the remaining provisions if it can do so without unjust enrichment or prejudice, and if the agreement says its provisions are severable, the court must conclusively presume the valid provisions can be enforced and enforce them. Second, a lease of more than one year of real property in which the landlord's spouse has an interest, signed without the spouse's written consent, is voidable at that spouse's option (see "edu-lease-term-limitation-mp"). What to do: keep the severability clause in every lease, keep options and renewals within Article XII's limits, and get any spouse's written consent for a lease over one year.

title: Writing and Recording Leases in the Northern Mariana Islands
bodyText: The Northern Mariana Islands' writing threshold for leases is one year. A lease for a term of one year or less may be oral (the Holdover Tenancy Act expressly covers oral agreements). A lease for more than one year, and any assignment or surrender of one, must be made by a written instrument signed by the party creating, assigning or surrendering it (or by that party's agent authorized in writing); separately, an agreement that by its terms can't be performed within a year is invalid unless signed by the party to be charged. The same one-year line is a recording line: an unrecorded interest other than a lease of one year or less isn't valid against a later good-faith buyer or mortgagee who records first; a document to be recorded must be acknowledged before a notary; and a statute says a written real property interest "shall be recorded" by the party receiving it, with a fine up to $10,000 for a knowing and wilful violation. Whether that recording duty reaches an ordinary residential lease over one year is unsettled; the Legislature's findings say all real property interests should be written, identified and recorded, so the cautious course is to notarize and record any lease over one year (the tenant is the receiving party; cooperate with the recording). There is no separate long-lease exclusion; the outer limit is Article XII's 55 years including renewals (see "edu-lease-term-limitation-mp"). The writing rules don't apply to a partida (a customary family land division). What to do: put every lease, extension, assignment or early surrender of a lease over one year in writing signed by the parties, and notarize and record it.

title: Prescribed Forms in the Northern Mariana Islands
bodyText: There is no statutory residential lease form in the Northern Mariana Islands, and no prescribed statement of condition or rental application. The law prescribes text only for side documents: (1) the three-day notice demanding rent, which must contain a statement "in substantially the following form" set out in the Holdover Tenancy Act (amount owed, address of the premises, demand for payment or possession within 3 days excluding Saturdays, Sundays and legal holidays, the deadline date, and your name, address and phone; the printed form says "19__", so write the full year; see "edu-nonpayment-notice-mp"); (2) the written demand on a bounced check, which must carry a conspicuous notice substantially in the statutory words if you want treble damages and the statutory attorney's fees (see "edu-returned-payments-mp"); (3) for pre-1978 housing, the federal Lead Warning Statement, which must appear in the lease or an attachment in the exact federal wording; and (4) for a Housing Choice Voucher tenancy, the HUD tenancy addendum, added word for word to your lease. What to do: copy these texts exactly from the current statute or federal form each time, and don't paraphrase them.

title: Online Tenant Portals in the Northern Mariana Islands
bodyText: We found no Commonwealth statute, regulation or court rule on tenant portals: nothing bars or regulates a lease term requiring rent payments, requests or signatures through an online portal, and the Commonwealth has no electronic-transactions act (so no statutory right to opt out of electronic dealings). Payment methods are a contract choice (see "edu-acceptable-payment-methods-mp"). Federal e-signature law makes electronic signatures and records valid in transactions affecting interstate commerce, but it doesn't require anyone to agree to use or accept electronic records, so a tenant who never agreed to the portal can't be forced to sign or receive documents electronically. For information the law requires to be given in writing, delivery through a portal counts only if the tenant first received a clear and conspicuous statement of the right to paper copies and to withdraw consent and a statement of the hardware and software needed, and then consented electronically in a way that shows the tenant can access the portal's format. It also doesn't validate an electronic notice of default, eviction or the right to cure for a primary residence. Cautious course: if you use a portal, get the tenant's agreement to it in the lease, keep a paper or e-mail alternative for a tenant who can't use it, state any portal or card fee in the lease, and keep notices that can lead to removal on paper by the statutory method (see "edu-notice-delivery-methods-mp").

title: Tenant Records and Data in the Northern Mariana Islands
bodyText: We found no Commonwealth statute, regulation or court rule that requires a landlord to keep a rent ledger, give a tenant a ledger or payment history on request, attach one to a nonpayment notice, or answer a tenant's records request. Nor did we find a Commonwealth data-security or breach-notification law: nothing requires a written information-security program or notice to applicants or tenants if their Social Security numbers or bank details are exposed. The Commonwealth's Identity Theft Act makes it a crime to use or traffic in another person's identifying information for fraud, and gives victims a civil claim against a convicted offender, but it puts no safeguarding duty on businesses. Federal law adds one records-related duty: if you deny an application or take other adverse action against an applicant based even partly on a consumer (credit or tenant-screening) report, you must give the applicant the federal adverse-action notice (the reporting agency's name, address and phone, a statement that the agency didn't make the decision, and the applicant's rights to a free report and to dispute it); the federal law's definition of "State" includes U.S. territories. Federal law also governs disposal: anyone who possesses consumer information derived from consumer reports (such as screening and credit reports on applicants) for a business purpose must dispose of it by reasonable measures that protect against unauthorized access or use, for example burning, pulverizing or shredding papers, or destroying or erasing electronic media, so the information can't practicably be read or reconstructed, or using a vetted record-destruction company. Rent records still matter in court: in a nonpayment case you must prove the rent owed, and claims can be brought for years after the tenancy (see "edu-limitation-of-actions-mp"). What to do: keep an accurate ledger for every tenant and give a copy on request, store applications and ID numbers securely, shred or erase screening reports and applications when no longer needed, and use the federal adverse-action notice whenever a screening report affects your decision.

title: Tenant's Insurance and Your Repairs in the Northern Mariana Islands
bodyText: Renter's insurance in the Northern Mariana Islands is covered in "edu-tenant-insurance-claims-mp" and "edu-renters-insurance-rules-mp": no Commonwealth statute or regulation requires, bars or limits it, so the lease decides. On the specific question of shifting repairs: we found no Commonwealth rule that forbids a lease from making a tenant claim on the tenant's own renter's insurance for repairs that are the landlord's responsibility, and no rule on subrogation between a landlord's and a tenant's insurers (the only insurer-subrogation waiver we found is the condominium association's policy, which must waive subrogation against unit owners). Even so, under the cautious course we take, you owe a duty to keep the dwelling fit to live in, and you can't rely on a lease term that pushes that duty, or liability for your own negligence, onto the tenant or the tenant's insurer. That is why the library uses "tenants-property-insurance-ks-oh-ca" for the Commonwealth (renter's insurance required, no landlord disclaimer) rather than the shared version with a "Landlord is not liable" sentence. What to do: insure the building yourself, pay for repairs that are yours to make whatever insurance the tenant carries, and use the tenant's policy only for the tenant's own belongings and liability.

title: Changing Terms of a Periodic Tenancy in the Northern Mariana Islands
bodyText: We found no Commonwealth statute or regulation on changing the terms of a month-to-month or other periodic tenancy: no special notice period for a change in terms, none for raising a fee the lease already provides, and no rule treating a change as a termination. Because a lease term can't be changed without the tenant's agreement (see "edu-entire-agreement-mp"), the lawful route for a change the tenant won't sign is to end the periodic tenancy by the written notice the law requires (unless the lease sets another period: at least 15 days before the end of a monthly period, 7 days for weekly, 30 for quarterly, 60 for yearly) and offer a new tenancy on the new terms starting with the next period. Cautious course: give any change in rent, fees or rules in writing at least that far ahead, make it effective on the first day of a new rental period, and treat a fee increase like a rent increase (see "edu-rent-increase-notice-mp"). A fixed-term lease can change mid-term only as it provides. Never raise rent or rent-like charges while a Governor's price freeze is in effect for your island. What to do: put any change in a written notice or amendment, give at least the termination notice period before it takes effect, and keep proof of delivery.

title: No Sunset on Tenant Laws in the Northern Mariana Islands
bodyText: We found no sunset or dated repeal clause on any Northern Mariana Islands law that protects tenants or governs renting: the Holdover Tenancy Act (in force since August 1, 1997, with no later amendment printed), the security-deposit refund law, the Commonwealth Fair Housing Act and the Consumer Protection Act have no expiry date. The one time-limited tenant protection is event-based, not dated: a Governor's price freeze on rents lasts until the Governor rescinds it or the emergency or disaster declaration ends, and it can be continued for one island (as on Rota under EO 2026-020 of September 23, 2026; that freeze rests on the Typhoon Bavi emergency declaration, which ends after thirty days unless renewed, and we could not confirm whether it was still in effect on October 23, 2026). What to do: treat these rules as permanent, and check the Governor's current declarations before raising rent after a typhoon or other emergency.

title: Lease Language and Translation in the Northern Mariana Islands
bodyText: We found no Commonwealth statute, regulation or court rule that requires a residential lease to be translated, or provided in the language in which it was advertised or negotiated, and no prescribed type size or verbatim lease text tied to language. The Constitution makes Chamorro, Carolinian and English the official languages, but its language clause lets the Legislature require only government proceedings and documents to be in at least one of the three; it doesn't reach private leases, and we found no rule on which language version of a law prevails if two texts differ. Two rules still bear on language: (1) for pre-1978 housing, the federal lead disclosure must be in the language of the lease (for example, a lease in Chinese or Korean needs the lead elements in that language); and (2) a tenant's limited English can matter if a term is challenged as unconscionable (the Condominium Act lists a party's "inability to understand the language of the agreement" as a factor, and under the cautious reading of the Consumer Protection Act an unconscionable term is unlawful). Fair housing law forbids treating applicants differently because of national origin, so don't refuse to rent because someone needs a translation. What to do: if you negotiate in another language, give the tenant a translation or an interpreter at signing, say in the lease which version controls, and put the lead disclosure in the lease's language.

title: Notices That Must Be in Writing in the Northern Mariana Islands
bodyText: Northern Mariana Islands law requires writing for the notices and consents that matter most: (1) ending a periodic tenancy (week to week, month to month, quarter to quarter, year to year) takes written notice by either party; (2) the three-day notice demanding unpaid rent or possession must be in writing in the statutory form; (3) the notice to cure a non-rent breach or give up possession must be written (15 days unless the lease sets its own rule); (4) if a fixed-term lease ends and you let the tenant stay, only your written consent turns the holdover into a periodic tenancy (accepting rent alone doesn't renew the term); (5) a surrender or assignment of a lease for more than one year must be by signed written instrument; (6) to claim treble damages or the statutory fees on a bounced check you must send a written demand; and (7) for a Housing Choice Voucher tenancy, termination during the term needs a written notice of grounds, with a copy of any eviction notice to the housing agency. A servicemember ending a lease under federal law gives you written notice with a copy of the orders. We found no Commonwealth rule requiring other routine notices (for example, entry or repair notices) to be written, so the lease decides; the library's leases use written notice throughout. Federal e-signature law also sets conditions before a notice the law requires to be in writing (for example, a notice ending a month-to-month tenancy) can be sent electronically to a tenant instead of on paper: the tenant must first get a clear and conspicuous statement of the right to paper copies and to withdraw consent, and a statement of the hardware and software needed, and must then consent electronically in a way that shows the tenant can open the format you will use; even then, notices of default, eviction or the right to cure for a primary residence are excluded. What to do: put every notice in writing, date it, keep a copy and record how and when it was delivered (see "edu-notice-delivery-methods-mp").

title: Tenant Animals Left Without Care in the Northern Mariana Islands
bodyText: We found no Commonwealth statute or regulation that lets a landlord enter a rental to care for, feed or remove a tenant's animal when the tenant is away, hospitalized or detained. Animal-welfare law (PL 21-31, 2020) works through public officers instead: it is a crime for a person to abandon or cruelly neglect an animal in that person's keeping (failing to provide necessary food, water, shelter or protection from bad weather); a police officer or a Mayor's Office animal control officer who has probable cause may enter premises with a search warrant and impound the animal; and the Mayor's animal control office may capture animals found abandoned, unattended, emaciated or in severe bad health. Be careful acting on your own: taking, leading away or confining a pet with intent to deprive the owner is the crime of theft of a pet. The library's optional "animal-care-access-vi" clause, which carries MP for the Northern Mariana Islands, has the tenant name an emergency caretaker and lets you admit that person (or ask an animal warden, a peace officer or a shelter to take charge) after trying to reach the tenant. What to do: if an animal seems abandoned, try to reach the tenant and the named caretaker, and if you can't, call the Department of Public Safety or the Mayor's animal control office rather than removing the animal yourself.

title: Assistance Animals in the Northern Mariana Islands
bodyText: In the Northern Mariana Islands the right to an assistance animal in housing comes from fair housing law, not from a separate animal statute: both the Commonwealth Fair Housing Act and the federal Fair Housing Act make it discrimination to refuse a reasonable accommodation in rules, policies or practices that a person with a disability needs for equal opportunity to use and enjoy a dwelling, and a no-pets rule is the classic example: the federal fair housing regulation's own illustration is that refusing to let a blind applicant live in a no-pets building with a seeing-eye dog is unlawful. Details, including who is covered, the direct-threat limit and the small-landlord exemptions, are in "edu-disability-accommodation-mp". Points specific to animals: we found no Commonwealth statute that separately protects trained service dogs or guide dogs in housing, defines emotional-support animals, sets documentation standards or limits the species, makes it a crime to misrepresent an animal as a service animal, or gives a landlord immunity for injuries a permitted assistance animal causes. So the fair-housing accommodation test governs every assistance animal, trained or not. The library's "assistance-animal-accommodation" clause carries MP for the Northern Mariana Islands: an assistance animal isn't a pet, no pet deposit, pet rent or pet fee, documentation only when the disability or need isn't apparent, the tenant stays responsible for damage, and the animal may be refused only for a direct threat or substantial damage that can't be reduced by another accommodation. What to do: use that clause, decide each request individually and in writing, and don't charge pet fees or require pet insurance for an assistance animal (the tagged "pet-insurance-requirement" clause already exempts it).

title: Pet Information Sheets in the Northern Mariana Islands
bodyText: We found no Commonwealth statute, regulation or court rule that requires a landlord to give a tenant a government fact sheet about pets and eviction (or any pet-related information sheet), whether or not you know the tenant has a dog or cat. The only pamphlet a landlord must hand over by law is the federal lead-hazard information pamphlet for housing built before 1978 (see the tagged "lead-based-paint" clause). What to do: nothing is required for pets; it is good practice to put your pet rules, any pet deposit and pet rent, and what happens to an animal if the tenant can't care for it (the optional "animal-care-access-vi" clause) in the lease so the tenant has them in writing.

title: Pet Deposits and Fees in the Northern Mariana Islands
bodyText: We found no Commonwealth statute or regulation on pet deposits, pet fees or pet rent, and no statutory definition of "security deposit" for rentals. The deposit-refund law applies to any business that requires security deposits as a condition of renting and makes it refund the balance within ten days after the property is returned (see "edu-security-deposit-return-mp"). A refundable pet deposit is money held as a condition of the rental to secure performance, so the cautious course is to treat it as part of the security deposit: refund the balance within ten days with the rest of the deposit. The library's "pet-policy-or" clause, which carries MP for the Northern Mariana Islands, does this (the pet deposit is a security deposit; monthly pet rent is part of the Rent). There is no cap on deposits, so no rule asks whether a pet deposit counts toward a cap (see "edu-security-deposit-cap-mp"). A nonrefundable one-time pet fee isn't prohibited, but state it in the lease by name and amount (see "edu-nonrefundable-deposit-notice-mp"). Don't charge a pet deposit, pet fee or pet rent for an assistance animal: fair housing law requires a reasonable accommodation, and we treat waiving pet charges as part of it (see "edu-assistance-animal-accommodation-mp"). What to do: label each pet charge in the lease as a refundable deposit, a one-time fee or monthly pet rent, return any refundable pet deposit with the security deposit within ten days, and waive pet charges for assistance animals.

title: Pet Liability Insurance in the Northern Mariana Islands
bodyText: We found no Commonwealth statute or regulation that requires, bars or limits a lease term making a tenant carry liability insurance for a pet, and no breed-specific rule. So it's a contract choice. The library's "pet-insurance-requirement" clause carries MP for the Northern Mariana Islands: a tenant with an approved pet keeps renter's insurance that covers pet liability and names you as an interested party on request, and the requirement doesn't apply to an assistance animal (fair housing law; see "edu-assistance-animal-accommodation-mp"). Local rules show why the coverage is worth having: on Rota a dog's owner is liable for damages when the dog bites someone in a public place or lawfully on private property, and Saipan's dog-control regulations let officers immediately impound a vicious animal (one that bites or attempts to bite without provocation). These are senatorial-district rules that we flag but haven't fully reviewed. What to do: if you require pet liability insurance, state the minimum in the lease, ask for proof at move-in and renewal, and never require it for an assistance animal.

title: Pet Policies in the Northern Mariana Islands
bodyText: We found no Commonwealth statute or regulation on pet policies in private rentals: no right for senior or other tenants to keep a pet, no limit on pet rules, no list of permitted entry purposes, and no rule on whether pet rent is rent. So your pet policy is a contract term, within three limits. (1) Assistance animals are not pets, and fair housing law requires a reasonable accommodation (see "edu-assistance-animal-accommodation-mp"). (2) Pet deposits: treat a refundable pet deposit as part of the security deposit and refund it within ten days (see "edu-pet-fees-mp"); the library's "pet-policy-or" clause, which carries MP for the Northern Mariana Islands, also makes monthly pet rent part of the Rent. (3) Removing an animal: no statute lets a landlord seize or remove a tenant's animal, the statutory route to recover possession of the home is the Superior Court (no statute allows self-help, and we assume it is unlawful), and taking, leading away or confining a pet with intent to deprive the owner is the crime of theft of a pet. Abandoned or neglected animals are for the police or the Mayor's animal control office, which may impound them (see "edu-animal-care-access-mp"). That is why the library does not use the shared pet clause that lets a landlord enter and remove a pet "without liability"; "pet-policy-or" instead lets you revoke approval of a dangerous or nuisance pet by written notice, which you then enforce as a lease breach (15-day cure notice unless the lease sets another). What to do: name each approved pet in the lease, enforce pet rules by written notice, and call the authorities rather than removing an animal yourself.

title: Penalties for Refusing an Assistance Animal in the Northern Mariana Islands
bodyText: We found no Commonwealth statute that makes it a crime for a landlord to refuse a service or assistance animal, and no guide-dog or hearing-dog law that requires landlords to waive lease restrictions. The Penal Code's definition of "public accommodation" covers transient lodging, food and fuel sellers, recreation and public transport; it doesn't reach a residential rental building, and we found no offense that uses it for animal access. The consequences of refusing an assistance animal are civil, under fair housing law: a refused reasonable accommodation is a discriminatory housing practice under both the Commonwealth and federal Fair Housing Acts (the federal regulation's own example is refusing a blind applicant's seeing-eye dog under a no-pets policy); a tenant may file a complaint with the Northern Marianas Housing Corporation's Corporate Director within one year or sue in the Superior Court within two years for actual and punitive damages, an injunction and attorney's fees; and coercing, threatening or interfering with someone exercising fair housing rights is separately unlawful. The fair housing law's criminal penalty is limited to using force or threat of force to injure, intimidate or interfere with someone because of disability or another protected trait. What to do: treat every assistance-animal request as a reasonable-accommodation request, answer it in writing, and never threaten or pressure a tenant over it (see "edu-assistance-animal-accommodation-mp").

title: Misrepresented Service Animals in the Northern Mariana Islands
bodyText: We found no Commonwealth statute or regulation that makes it an offense to misrepresent a pet as a service or assistance animal, in housing or anywhere else, and no Commonwealth service-animal statute at all (see "edu-assistance-animal-accommodation-mp"). So there is no misrepresentation penalty to rely on. What you can do is follow the fair-housing accommodation process: if the disability or the disability-related need for the animal isn't apparent, you may ask for reliable documentation of the need, and you may deny an accommodation that rests on information you can show is false. Knowingly false statements on a rental application can also be a lease breach under the "rental-application-accuracy-mp" clause (see "edu-rental-application-accuracy-mp"). What to do: don't accuse a tenant of faking a need without evidence; ask only for what the accommodation process allows, decide in writing, and get legal advice before denying a request on credibility grounds.

title: Assigned Parking Spaces in the Northern Mariana Islands
bodyText: We found no Commonwealth statute or regulation on assigning, reassigning or charging for a tenant's parking space, so the lease decides. The library's "assigned-parking-space" clause carries MP for the Northern Mariana Islands: it names the space and lets you reassign one of comparable convenience on reasonable notice, subject to any limits the law sets (the Commonwealth sets none on changing parking rules mid-term). Two rules can override an assignment. First, fair housing: a tenant with a disability may need a reserved space close to the unit as a reasonable accommodation, and you must consider such a request even if spaces are assigned. Second, the Vehicle Code requires every open off-street parking area with more than five spaces to set aside spaces for vehicles of persons with disabilities, close to a building entrance (see "edu-parking-mp"). What to do: list each tenant's space in the lease, reassign only on written notice to a comparable space, and grant reasonable accommodation requests for accessible parking.

title: EV Charging in the Northern Mariana Islands
bodyText: We found no Commonwealth statute or regulation that gives a tenant a right to install or use an electric vehicle charger, or that limits a landlord's ability to refuse one, require conditions, or charge for electricity used for charging. The only charging law requires the Commonwealth Utilities Corporation to provide public charging stations. So EV charging at a rental is a contract matter. If you are willing to allow a charger, the library's optional "ev-charger-installation-hi" clause, which carries MP for the Northern Mariana Islands, requires your written consent to the system and location, installation by a licensed contractor with any required permits, association approval where applicable, insurance, and reimbursement for the electricity used. If a tenant with a disability needs charging access as an accommodation, consider it under fair housing law like any other accommodation request. What to do: decide your EV policy, and if you allow chargers, use the optional clause and get every detail in writing.

title: EV Chargers at Move-Out in the Northern Mariana Islands
bodyText: We found no Commonwealth statute or regulation on who owns, removes or pays for a tenant-installed EV charger at the end of a tenancy. The lease decides. The Colorado-based end-of-tenancy clause is not used for the Northern Mariana Islands; if you allow a charger under the optional "ev-charger-installation-hi" clause, say in the same agreement whether the tenant must remove it and restore the property, may leave it in place, or must sell it to you, and who pays for any damage from removal. Without a term, fixtures and improvements questions fall to the general lease terms (see the tagged "improvements-ownership-la" clause) and the move-out deposit rules (deposit balance refunded within ten days after the property is returned). What to do: settle charger ownership and removal in writing before installation.

title: EV Charger Conditions in the Northern Mariana Islands
bodyText: We found no Commonwealth statute or regulation that sets requirements a tenant must meet to install an EV charger (insurance, licensed electrician, registration, metering) or that requires new or existing rental buildings to be EV-ready. So any requirements are yours to set by agreement. The library's optional "ev-charger-installation-hi" clause, which carries MP for the Northern Mariana Islands, lists the usual conditions: your prior written consent to the system and location, a licensed contractor, your specifications, applicable codes and permits, association rules and registration where the property is in an association, insurance naming you, and reimbursement for electricity by separate meter or your reasonable calculation. What to do: if you allow chargers, use that clause and confirm with the Building Safety office whether the installation needs a permit.

title: EV Chargers in Shared Parking in the Northern Mariana Islands
bodyText: We found no Commonwealth statute or regulation on EV chargers in shared parking areas: nothing lets a landlord charge a fee to reserve the space where a charger is installed, and nothing governs responsibility for damage in a common area. The Colorado-based shared-area clause is not used for the Northern Mariana Islands. If you allow a charger in a common parking area, cover it in the written agreement under the optional "ev-charger-installation-hi" clause: identify the space, any reservation charge, who maintains the equipment, and who pays for damage. In a condominium, the association's rules for common elements also apply. Keep any accessible parking spaces the Vehicle Code requires free of chargers and cords (see "edu-parking-mp"). What to do: agree all shared-area charger terms in writing before installation.

title: Parking Areas in the Northern Mariana Islands
bodyText: Northern Mariana Islands law doesn't regulate parking terms in a residential lease, but three public rules reach a rental's parking area. (1) Disability parking: every open off-street parking area must provide spaces for vehicles carrying persons with disabilities, starting at one space for more than 5 and up to 25 spaces, two for 26 to 50, three for 51 to 75 and four for 76 to 100 (then one per 25), at least half of them 13 by 18 feet, as close as possible to an accessible building entrance; a business or privately owned facility that provides goods or services to the public must meet the federal ADA accessible-parking standards, with a $100-a-day civil fine for failing to designate them. Whether an apartment lot is an "open off-street parking area" in the statute's sense is unsettled; the cautious course for any lot with more than five spaces is to mark the required accessible spaces with the blue paint and accessibility sign. (2) Fire lanes: if the Fire and EMS Commissioner designates a fire lane on your property (after written notice to owners and tenants, who may object), it must be marked and signed, parking in it or allowing it is an infraction (up to $150 a day), and a vehicle blocking it may be towed immediately. (3) Towing: there is no private towing statute; the Department of Public Safety may remove a vehicle found on private property when the owner or person in lawful possession asks (see "edu-towing-mp"). The library uses "parking-ks-oh-ca" for the Commonwealth (designated areas, no security provided, no clause excusing you from your own negligence). A tenant with a disability may need a reserved or accessible space as a reasonable accommodation (see "edu-assigned-parking-space-mp"). What to do: mark accessible spaces, keep any designated fire lane clear and signed, and put parking areas and rules in the lease.

title: Parking Rules Notice in the Northern Mariana Islands
bodyText: We found no Commonwealth statute or regulation on residential parking or towing rules: nothing requires you to deliver parking rules before the lease is signed, use a prescribed heading, limit mid-term changes, limit the vehicle information you may ask for, or make a parking permit run with the lease. So parking rules are lease terms. The tagged "rules-ia" clause sets the contract standard for rules the library uses for the Northern Mariana Islands, and "parking-vehicle-rules" covers vehicle limits, registration information, tags and decals (whose cost may be charged), and towing "in accordance with applicable law" (in the Commonwealth, removal by the Department of Public Safety; see "edu-towing-mp"). Public rules you can't change by lease: the Vehicle Code's accessible spaces and any designated fire lane (see "edu-parking-mp"). What to do: attach your parking rules to the lease before signing, change them only by written notice, and ask only for vehicle information you need (make, model, plate) to manage the lot.

title: Vehicle Rules and Removal in the Northern Mariana Islands
bodyText: The library's "parking-vehicle-rules" clause carries MP for the Northern Mariana Islands: only operable, registered passenger vehicles; registration information, tags or decals (their cost may be charged; no Commonwealth fee list limits it); towing "in accordance with applicable law"; no repairs except minor emergency ones. There is no private-towing statute here, so "applicable law" means the Vehicle Code's removal power: the Director of Public Safety may remove (or have a licensed garage remove) a vehicle found on private property when the owner or person in lawful possession of the property asks, and no one may abandon a vehicle on private property without the express or implied consent of the owner or person in lawful possession. The statute doesn't limit removal to vehicles parked without permission, but it puts the request in the hands of whoever lawfully possesses the property: for common parking areas that is you; for a leased single-family house or a space leased to the tenant, the tenant may be the person in lawful possession. Cautious course: don't ask for removal of a tenant's own vehicle from premises leased to that tenant; enforce vehicle rules there as a lease breach by written notice. For common areas, warn the tenant in writing before requesting removal for a rule violation, and remember that removal is the Department's decision ("may"). Removed vehicles are stored and the owner is notified by certified mail and has 10 days to reclaim them before appraisal and sale. What to do: post your vehicle rules, give written warnings, and use the Department of Public Safety rather than a private tow company to remove vehicles (see "edu-towing-mp").

title: Storage Space in the Northern Mariana Islands
bodyText: The Northern Mariana Islands has a self-service storage law (4 CMC § 51533 and following sections), and the question is whether it reaches storage you provide with a residential lease. Its "facility" is real property divided into individual spaces for storing personal property that are rented to individual occupants who have access, and it expressly excludes "a garage or storage area in a private residence". So a garage, shed or closet that comes with a house or apartment is outside it. A separate bank of storage lockers in an apartment building might fit the definition, but the act gives its lien and sale remedy only under a written storage rental agreement containing statutory statements (a 10-point warning that it is unlawful to use the facility as a residence, a statement that the occupant's property may be sold to satisfy a lien after 14 consecutive days of unpaid charges, and a space for an alternative notice address), and a clause excusing the operator from loss or theft is unenforceable unless it meets the act's insurance-statement and capital-letters rules. Cautious course: don't rely on the storage lien for property in storage that comes with a lease; treat items a tenant leaves in storage like other property left behind (see "abandoned-property-mp"). If you run a separate storage business, use a storage agreement that meets the act. The library uses "storage-space-ks-oh-ca" for the Commonwealth (assigned space; no hazardous, flammable or perishable items; no clause excusing you from your own negligence). What to do: identify any storage space in the lease, ban hazardous materials, and don't seize or sell stored items without legal advice.

title: Towing From Rental Property in the Northern Mariana Islands
bodyText: The Northern Mariana Islands has no private-property towing statute: no signage rule for ordinary lots, no written-authorization form, no rate caps, no ban on landlord kickbacks, and no rule against towing or booting only for expired registration. Removal works through the Department of Public Safety. (1) Any lot: the Director of Public Safety may remove a vehicle, or order a licensed garage to remove it, when it is found on private property and the owner or person in lawful possession of the property asks; abandoning a vehicle on private property without the consent of the owner or person in lawful possession is prohibited; the removed vehicle is stored, the registered owner is presumed liable for removal and storage costs, the owner gets certified-mail notice and 10 days to reclaim, and unclaimed vehicles are appraised and sold. In a single-family rental or a space leased to the tenant, the tenant may be the person in lawful possession, so don't ask for removal of the tenant's own vehicle there; enforce your vehicle rules as a lease breach instead (see "edu-parking-vehicle-rules-mp"). (2) Fire lanes: a vehicle blocking a designated fire lane may be towed immediately without notice, but each entrance must carry signs saying vehicles in fire lanes will be towed and giving the towing company's name, phone and address. (3) Accessible spaces: the Department removes vehicles without a disability placard from designated accessible spaces. A garage that tows or stores a vehicle at the owner's request or at the direction of an officer "or other authorized person" through an action permitted by law has a lien for its charges; whether a landlord is such a person is unsettled. What to do: post your parking rules, warn in writing, and call the Department of Public Safety rather than hiring a tow truck yourself.

title: Charging Separately for Parking in the Northern Mariana Islands
bodyText: We found no Commonwealth statute or regulation that requires parking to be rented or priced separately from a dwelling ("unbundled"), or that bars it. So you may include parking in the rent or charge for it separately, as the lease says; if you charge separately, state the amount and the space in the lease (see "assigned-parking-space"). Two cautions: a Governor's price freeze applies to "housing rentals", so don't start or raise a parking charge for an existing tenant during a freeze (cautious course); and on Saipan, zoning rules may set parking requirements for buildings, which we flag but haven't reviewed. What to do: decide whether parking is included, write that choice and any charge into the lease, and keep at least the spaces the Vehicle Code requires for persons with disabilities (see "edu-parking-mp").

title: Marijuana and Your Lease in the Northern Mariana Islands
bodyText: Adult-use and medical marijuana are legal under the Commonwealth's Taulamwaar Sensible CNMI Cannabis Act, but the Act expressly does not "amend or affect in any way" Commonwealth or federal landlord-tenant law, so your lease controls. You may ban marijuana smoking, vaping, other use, possession and growing anywhere on the property, including inside the unit (see "edu-smoking-policy-mp" and the optional "cannabis-restrictions-ak" clause, which carries MP for the Northern Mariana Islands). We found no Commonwealth rule protecting medical-marijuana patients or caregivers in housing: no bar on refusing to rent to a patient, no limit on banning a patient's use, and no rule limiting bans to smoking. Home growing: cultivation may occur only on property the grower lawfully possesses by appropriate lease or ownership, or with the consent of the person in lawful possession, and the Cannabis Commission's home-grow registration requires a renter to submit the landlord's agreement permitting growing plus the signed rental agreement; if you won't allow growing, say so in the lease and don't sign a consent. Liability: an owner, manager or lessor who knowingly suffers or permits a place to be used to sell marijuana unlawfully or as a place to resort for unlawful use commits a violation (see "edu-criminal-activity-mp" and "edu-nuisance-mp"), and smoking marijuana near anyone under 21 is unlawful except for medical patients. Federal law: the Act does not exempt anyone from federal law, and federal law still lists marihuana as a Schedule I controlled substance; in federally assisted housing (for example, Housing Choice Voucher tenancies) "drug-related criminal activity" includes the illegal use or possession for use of a controlled substance, and the Commonwealth's Cannabis Act doesn't make that use lawful under federal law. What to do: state your marijuana rules in the lease (use, smoking, growing), give or refuse growing consent in writing, and act promptly on any sales or unlawful use you learn of.

title: Common Areas and Balconies in the Northern Mariana Islands
bodyText: We found no Commonwealth statute or regulation that gives a residential tenant a right to keep a waterbed or other flotation bedding, use a clothesline or drying rack, install a solar device, or display a flag or religious or cultural item, and none that limits rules on balconies, porches, wall fastenings, candles or signs. So the library's "common-area-use" clause, which carries MP for the Northern Mariana Islands, sets these terms by contract, while keeping any display right that applicable law gives. Rules that do reach common areas: smoking is banned by statute in enclosed lobbies, hallways and other common areas of apartment buildings and condominiums (see "edu-smoking-policy-mp"); federal rules protect a tenant's right to install certain antennas and satellite dishes in areas under the tenant's exclusive use (see "edu-telecom-access-mp"); and fair housing law may require you to allow a reasonable accommodation or modification for a tenant with a disability (see "edu-disability-accommodation-mp"). On Saipan, the blight-maintenance law requires residential exterior areas to be kept clean and sanitary and free of trash and stored junk, and requires commercial premises' walks, driveways and parking areas to be kept free of hazards (whether a multi-family rental counts as commercial is unsettled). What to do: put your common-area and balcony rules in the lease or attached rules, and apply them evenly.

title: Housing Displaced Guests After a Disaster in the Northern Mariana Islands
bodyText: We found no Commonwealth statute, regulation or Governor's order in the materials reviewed that lets a tenant house people displaced by a typhoon or other disaster despite the lease's guest or occupancy limits, bars a landlord from enforcing those limits after a disaster, or lets the government place evacuees in private rentals. So the lease's guest and occupancy terms still apply (see the tagged "guest-policy" and "guest-policy-day-limit" clauses). The Commonwealth's disaster rules for landlords are covered in "edu-disaster-duties-mp": chiefly, while a Governor's price freeze is in effect you may not raise rent or charge more for added occupants as a rent increase (EO 2026-020 of September 23, 2026 kept a freeze in effect on Rota; whether it still is depends on the emergency declaration it rests on, so check the Governor's current orders). The interstate Emergency Management Assistance Compact the Commonwealth joined deals with housing evacuees between governments, not through private leases. Cautious course after a disaster: be flexible, agree in writing to any temporary extra occupants (who they are and for how long), don't treat temporary guests as grounds for a rent increase during a freeze, and remember that fair housing rules (including familial status) apply to occupancy decisions. What to do: if a tenant asks to shelter displaced family or friends, answer in writing with a time limit and any conditions.

title: Grills and Open Flames in the Northern Mariana Islands
bodyText: The Commonwealth's fire code regulations adopt the most up-to-date International Fire Code, and the fine schedule lists failing to comply with its open-burning and recreational-fire section (307) and open-flames section (308) at $500 each, so the model code's open-flame rules apply to rental property. The International Fire Code's open-flames section (308), which may contain rules on open-flame cooking devices, was not saved or read for this library (and whether the 2024 or the 2027 edition is the adopted one is unsettled), so we can't say whether or how the adopted code limits grilling at your building; ask the Department of Fire and EMS Fire Prevention unit what applies to your building type. Open burning of waste is separately regulated by environmental rules and needs a fire permit. The library's "fire-safety-grilling" clause, which carries MP for the Northern Mariana Islands, sets a contract rule (whether it is stricter than the adopted fire code was not checked, and the tenant must follow the fire code too): no barbecue, grill or other open-flame device on a porch or balcony or within 15 feet of a building, and no flammable materials beyond normal household quantities. What to do: keep the clause, provide a safe grilling area away from buildings if you can, and post the rule in multi-unit properties.

title: Firearms at Rental Property in the Northern Mariana Islands
bodyText: Northern Mariana Islands law does not stop you from limiting firearms in a lease, and no Commonwealth statute protects a tenant's right to keep a firearm in a rental or in a vehicle in your parking area. The firearms law (the Special Act for Firearms Enforcement) does set rules that reach your property. Anyone who acquires or possesses a firearm or ammunition must hold a current Firearm Owner's Identification Card from the Department of Public Safety. A firearm kept in a home or on private land must be in a locked container or disabled with a trigger lock unless it is carried by someone over 21 or is under a law enforcement officer's immediate control. Firing a gun is unlawful without a Department of Public Safety permit, except as the law allows (for example, legitimate self-defense), and firing in celebration is banned. You may not take a firearm or ammunition as security, deposit, pledge or pawn for anything a tenant owes. Gun-free posting: the owner, lessee or manager of private property may make it a gun-free zone by posting conspicuous signs at least 11 by 14 inches, with letters at least one inch high, saying the property is a Gun Free Zone and that possessing a firearm there is a felony; knowingly possessing a firearm in a posted place is a felony, and the property owner may sue for at least $10,000 in statutory damages plus fees. But the gun-free-zone rules let a person who lawfully lives inside a gun-free zone keep firearms at home and carry them to and from home in the lawful transport manner, so posting does not make a tenant's lawful firearm in the unit a crime. Whether a lease clause banning firearms inside the unit is enforceable is a contract question no Commonwealth statute answers (case law not searched). What to do: if you want firearm rules, use the optional "Firearms" clause ("firearms-mp"); if you post common areas, use signs that meet the size and wording rules and say in the lease that tenants keep their lawful right to keep firearms at home; never hold or sell a tenant's firearm left behind; call the Department of Public Safety instead.

title: Guest Rules in the Northern Mariana Islands
bodyText: We found no Commonwealth statute, regulation or court rule on guests in a rental: nothing caps or protects how long a guest may stay, requires notice or a grace period for guest rules, or protects a live-in care provider, and the Commonwealth has no mobile-home-lot law. So guest rules are lease terms; the library's "Guest Policy" clause ("guest-policy") carries MP. Three limits apply. First, the fair housing laws require reasonable accommodations in rules and policies for a person with a disability, so a guest limit must yield where a tenant with a disability needs a live-in aide or caregiver (see "edu-disability-accommodation-mp"). Second, apply guest rules the same way to every household; a rule enforced more harshly against families with children, or by race, national origin or another protected class, is discrimination. Third, in a Section 8 voucher tenancy the household is the one the housing agency approved, including any approved live-in aide, so check the program rules before treating an aide as an unauthorized occupant. What to do: set a clear guest limit in the lease, enforce it evenly, and handle a caregiver or aide request as an accommodation request.

title: Guest Stay Limits in the Northern Mariana Islands
bodyText: We found no Commonwealth statute, regulation or court rule that limits, or sets a minimum for, the number of days a guest may stay. A day limit is a lease term: the library's "Guest Policy (14-Day Limit)" clause ("guest-policy-day-limit") carries MP. Enforce it evenly, and let it yield to a reasonable accommodation for a tenant with a disability who needs a live-in aide or caregiver (see "edu-guest-policy-mp"). What to do: pick a limit that fits the property, put it in the lease, and apply it the same way to every household.

title: Guest and Visitor Rights in the Northern Mariana Islands
bodyText: We found no Commonwealth statute, regulation or court rule giving tenants a statutory right to receive guests, visitors or suppliers, barring a guest fee, or making such rights non-waivable, in any size of building. Guest access is a matter for the lease ("guest-policy" and "guest-policy-day-limit" carry MP; see "edu-guest-policy-mp"). The fair housing laws still require reasonable accommodations in rules for a tenant with a disability, which can include visits from or a live-in caregiver. Cautious course: we assume a tenant's right to quiet enjoyment of the home includes ordinary visitors, so don't bar ordinary visits or charge a fee just for having a guest. What to do: write reasonable, even-handed guest rules and treat caregiver access as an accommodation question.

title: Keys and Locks in the Northern Mariana Islands
bodyText: We found no Commonwealth statute, regulation or court rule on keys in a private rental: nothing sets how many keys you must give, caps a key, lock-change or key-deposit charge, requires rekeying between tenants, or lets a tenant change the locks. So key terms are contract terms; the library's "Keys" clause ("keys") carries MP. A key deposit is money you hold to secure the tenant's performance, so treat it like a security deposit and refund the balance within ten days after the property is returned (see "edu-security-deposit-return-mp"). Related rows: locks and security hardware ("edu-security-devices-mp"), master-key control ("edu-key-control-policy-mp") and lock changes for a domestic-violence victim with an order for protection ("edu-dv-lockchange-mp"). What to do: record the keys issued on a signed receipt, rekey before each new tenant, charge only the actual cost of replacing lost keys or rekeying when the lease allows it, and never use keys to lock a tenant out (as a cautious course, recover possession only through the Superior Court; no statute allows self-help).

title: Police Cooperation and Crime-Free Terms in the Northern Mariana Islands
bodyText: We found no Commonwealth statute, regulation or court rule that requires or regulates a crime-free lease addendum, requires you to give the Department of Public Safety access to a unit, or bars a lease from penalizing a tenant who calls the police or emergency help. But a general reporting duty binds you, your staff and your tenants, as it binds every person. Anyone who gains knowledge of a rape, an aggravated assault, or a death or injury from a knife or bullet wound, powder burn or other cause suffered in a suspicious or unusual way or suggesting poisoning or violence must report it immediately, and in any case within five days, to the police or the Director of Public Safety, giving the victim's name and location, the date, the cause and manner, and the name of whoever caused it if known. And anyone who gains knowledge of an offense under the Commonwealth criminal code must promptly notify the police, giving their own name and address, the nature, date, time and place of the offense, and a description of any known participants, even if that is a tenant. A violation can be punished by up to six months in jail, a $500 fine, or both (6 CMC § 3105). So if a tenant is found dead in suspicious circumstances, or you learn of a crime at the property, report it. The child-abuse reporting duty falls on health workers, teachers, day care providers, counselors, social workers and police, not on landlords as such, though anyone may report (6 CMC § 5313(a), (e)). Removal for criminal activity runs through ordinary notice and the Superior Court (see "edu-criminal-activity-mp"; the optional "criminal-activity-ky" clause carries MP), and federal law protects domestic-violence victims in federally assisted housing. The Constitution protects people's houses against unreasonable searches; whether you can consent to a police search of a tenant's unit is a question only case law could settle (not searched). Cautious course: let police into an occupied unit only with a warrant, the tenant's consent or a real emergency; give tenant records on a subpoena, warrant or other legal process, or with the tenant's consent; and never penalize a tenant, especially a crime victim, for calling for help. What to do: cooperate with lawful requests, keep a record of each request and what you gave, and talk to a lawyer before acting on an informal request.

title: Political Canvassing Access in the Northern Mariana Islands
bodyText: We found no Commonwealth statute, regulation or court rule that requires you to let political candidates, campaign workers, petition circulators or voter-registration workers into an apartment building or other multi-unit property to reach tenants' doors, or to set aside an area for voter information or campaign literature. The election law's ban on campaigning near polling places does not apply to activities on private property. So access by outsiders is your decision as owner, subject to your tenants' own right to invite guests (see "edu-guest-rights-mp"). Cautious course: apply any no-soliciting or access rule the same way to every campaign, cause and religion, since uneven enforcement against a religious group risks a fair-housing claim. What to do: decide your policy for common areas, post it, and apply it evenly; don't stop tenants from inviting a candidate or campaigner into their own unit.

title: Flags and Signs at Rentals in the Northern Mariana Islands
bodyText: We found no Commonwealth statute, regulation or court rule giving tenants (or condominium unit owners or occupants) a right to display a flag, a political or campaign sign, or other items at a rental, and none that limits what a landlord or condominium association may forbid. The only political-sign rules we found govern signboards on the public right-of-way (a Public Works permit, no earlier than six months before the election) and campaign material at polling places; neither reaches a sign on private property. The Constitution's free-speech and religion clauses are written as limits on lawmaking, and whether they reach a private landlord is a question only case law could settle (not searched). Federal law on flag display by condominium and homeowners' associations was not part of this library's sources. So display rules are lease terms: the library's "Use of Property & Common Areas" clause ("common-area-use") carries MP and keeps any display rights the law gives. Cautious course: if you limit signs or flags, write a content-neutral rule about size, placement, damage and safety, apply it to every tenant, and don't single out religious or national-origin displays. What to do: state any display rule in the lease or written rules, apply it evenly, and check condominium or association rules that bind the unit.

title: Religious and Cultural Displays in the Northern Mariana Islands
bodyText: We found no Commonwealth statute, regulation or court rule that gives a tenant a right to display religious or cultural items (for example a doorpost item, a family altar or a fiesta decoration) at a rental, or that limits a landlord's display rules. Two rules shape any limit you set. First, the Commonwealth Fair Housing Act bars discrimination in the terms, conditions or privileges of renting because of religion or national origin, and the federal Fair Housing Act does the same, so a rule that allows some displays but not those of a particular faith or culture, or is enforced that way, is risky. Second, the Constitution protects religious exercise against lawmaking and bars discrimination in civil rights on account of religion or ancestry; whether that reaches a private landlord is a question only case law could settle (not searched). What to do: keep any display rule content-neutral (size, placement, fire safety, damage to doors and walls), apply it to every tenant, and consider a small exception for doorpost or door-frame items that cause no damage (see "edu-tenant-display-rights-mp").

title: Window and Portable Air Conditioners in the Northern Mariana Islands
bodyText: We found no Commonwealth statute, regulation or court rule that gives a tenant a right to install a portable or window air conditioner or other cooling device, that limits a landlord's rules on window units, or that requires a lease to say whether they are allowed. We also found no rule requiring a landlord to provide air conditioning. So cooling devices are a lease matter. The library's "Use of Property & Common Areas" clause ("common-area-use") carries MP and bars fastening anything to the property's surfaces or fixtures without your consent, which covers a window or through-wall unit. Cautious course: a tenant with a disability may need a cooling device as a reasonable accommodation, so treat such a request under the fair housing rules (see "edu-disability-accommodation-mp"). What to do: say in the lease or written rules whether window, through-wall or portable units are allowed, who installs them, how they must be secured against typhoon winds and drainage, and who pays for the electricity and any damage.

title: Plug-In and Portable Solar at Rentals in the Northern Mariana Islands
bodyText: We found no Commonwealth statute, regulation or court rule that gives a tenant a right to install a plug-in or portable solar device or battery at a rental, that voids lease or deed restrictions on solar energy systems, or that limits what a landlord may require. The Commonwealth's net-metering law lets a metered residential customer of the Commonwealth Utilities Corporation who owns and operates a renewable energy system on the customer's premises connect it to the grid if it meets the utility's interconnection requirements and the electrical safety standards; it says nothing about landlords or tenants, so a tenant still needs your permission to put equipment on your building. What to do: if you allow solar or battery devices, say so in writing, require that any grid-connected system go through the utility's interconnection approval and meet the electrical codes, set rules on placement, typhoon securing and roof or wall penetrations, and say who owns and removes the equipment at the end of the tenancy (the library's "tenant-repair-agreement-pr" and "improvements-ownership-la" clauses carry MP for alterations and improvements).

title: Recycling and Garbage at Rentals in the Northern Mariana Islands
bodyText: We found no Commonwealth statute, regulation or court rule that requires a landlord to tell tenants where or how to recycle, or to provide recycling containers or service at a rental. The Commonwealth's solid-waste and recycling laws put the recycling duties on the operators of collection points, transfer stations and disposal sites and on licensed recyclers, and set the beverage-container program. Two related points: the Department of Public Works' lower "residential disposer" rates cover only an individual homeowner hauling refuse from his own residence, not self-hauled waste from apartment complexes or other multi-family dwellings; and on Saipan, the local blight law requires premises to be kept free of accumulated trash, rubbish and garbage. What to do: say in the lease who arranges and pays for garbage collection, where bins go and how often they are emptied, and, as a courtesy, tell tenants about the recycling drop-off points and the beverage-container redemption program.

title: House Rules and Rule Changes in the Northern Mariana Islands
bodyText: We found no Commonwealth statute, regulation or court rule on house rules in a residential rental: nothing sets when a rule is enforceable, whether a tenant is bound only by rules in force at signing, or how far a landlord may change rules during the tenancy, and the Commonwealth has no statutory retaliation presumption tied to changed terms (see "edu-retaliation-mp"). So rules are a matter of contract: they bind the tenant to the extent the lease makes them part of the deal. The library's "Rules and Changes to Rules" clause ("rules-ia") carries MP; it binds the tenant to the written rules in force at signing and lets you adopt new reasonable rules on notice, but not ones that substantially change the lease without the tenant's written consent. Condominium associations may adopt their own bylaws, rules and regulations, which reach your tenant through the lease (see "edu-hoa-compliance-mp"). Limits: rules must not discriminate or be enforced unevenly against a protected class, must allow reasonable accommodations for tenants with disabilities, and must not misstate tenants' rights (cautious reading of the consumer protection law). What to do: attach your written rules to the lease, give written notice of any new rule, and don't use a rule change to raise rent or take away a term the tenant bargained for.

title: Condominium Associations and Rentals in the Northern Mariana Islands
bodyText: The Commonwealth's only association law is the Uniform Condominium Act; we found no statute or regulation on homeowners' associations, planned communities or gated subdivisions. Under the Condominium Act, a unit owners' association may adopt bylaws and rules, collect assessments from unit owners, and, after notice and an opportunity to be heard, levy reasonable fines; it has a lien on the unit for assessments and for fines imposed against the owner, which can be foreclosed like a mortgage. The declaration may restrict use, occupancy and alienation of units, which can include limits on renting, so read the declaration and any amendments before you lease a unit. We found no Commonwealth rule that caps an association's lease-approval fee or deposit, lets an association collect rent directly from your tenant when you are behind on assessments, makes a rental restriction binding only on later buyers, limits the tenant information an association may demand, or protects a renter's home child care against the association. What to do: check the declaration, bylaws and rules for rental limits, approval steps and fees; use the "Association Approval of Lease" clause ("association-approval-la") if approval is required and the "Homeowner / Condominium Association Compliance" clause ("hoa-compliance"); and keep your own assessments current, since the association's remedies run against you and your unit.

title: Condominium Association Rules and Fines in the Northern Mariana Islands
bodyText: If your rental is a condominium unit, the unit owners' association may adopt rules and, after notice and an opportunity to be heard, levy reasonable fines for violations of the declaration, bylaws and rules; the fine is imposed against you as owner and becomes a lien on your unit. The Commonwealth sets no dollar cap on fines (the Act requires only that they be reasonable). We found no Commonwealth rule that requires you to deliver the association's rules to the tenant at signing, that makes the tenant's duty to comply depend on delivery, or that lets the association collect rent directly from your tenant when you are behind. The library's "Homeowner / Condominium Association Compliance" clause ("hoa-compliance") carries MP and makes the tenant follow the association's rules and pay fines the tenant causes; the "tenant-caused-fines-as" clause also carries MP. Satellite dishes and similar antennas: federal law limits lease and association rules that impair a tenant's antenna on property in the tenant's exclusive use (see "edu-telecom-access-mp"). What to do: give the tenant a copy of the declaration's use restrictions and the association's current rules at signing and get a receipt, pass on rule changes promptly, and ask the association to send you any violation notice so you can respond within the hearing process.

title: Association Documents and Leases in the Northern Mariana Islands
bodyText: We found no Commonwealth statute, regulation or court rule that requires a lease of a condominium unit (or a home in any association or access-controlled community) to disclose the association's obligations or documents to the tenant, to carry an owner's or tenant's statement about the condominium law or bylaws, or to be filed with the association's board. The Condominium Act's disclosure documents (the public offering statement and the resale certificate) apply to sales of units, not leases. What to do: because the association's rules bind your tenant only through the lease, give the tenant the declaration's use and occupancy restrictions and the current rules before signing, have the tenant sign for them, and use the "Homeowner / Condominium Association Compliance" clause ("hoa-compliance"; see "edu-hoa-compliance-mp").

title: Smoke Drift and Waivers in the Northern Mariana Islands
