bodyText: Northern Mariana Islands law bans smoking (including electronic cigarettes) in the enclosed lobbies, hallways and other common areas of apartment buildings, condominiums and other multiple-unit residential buildings, and within a reasonable distance of 25 feet outside an enclosed no-smoking area so that smoke does not get in through entrances, windows or ventilation. Where building staff work in those hallways, the workplace ban also applies, and an employer must tell people on the premises about it and report violations. We found no Commonwealth statute, regulation or court rule on smoke drift between units or on a tenant's waiver of claims about drifting smoke. Cautious course: we assume you owe a duty to keep the dwelling fit to live in and not to let a nuisance continue, so don't rely on a lease clause in which the tenant gives up claims about smoke drifting from other units or common areas; a non-smoking policy for units and balconies is the safer tool. What to do: post and enforce the common-area ban (see "edu-smoking-policy-mp"), keep smokers 25 feet from entrances, windows and vents of enclosed common areas, and use the "Smoking Policy" clause ("smoking-policy"), which carries MP, rather than a waiver.

title: Snow Removal in the Northern Mariana Islands
bodyText: Snow removal does not arise in the Northern Mariana Islands: the islands are tropical and do not get snow or ice, and we found no Commonwealth law on snow or ice removal. The library's "snow-removal" clauses do not carry MP. Exterior upkeep that does matter here, such as clearing walkways, steps and drains and securing loose items before a typhoon, is covered in the landscaping and disaster rows (see "edu-landscaping-irrigation-mp" and "edu-disaster-duties-mp"). What to do: leave snow terms out of an MP lease and assign walkway, drainage and storm-preparation duties instead.

title: Security Cameras and Video Doorbells in the Northern Mariana Islands
bodyText: We found no Commonwealth statute, regulation or court rule on tenant-installed security cameras or video doorbells, and none that requires every party's consent before audio is recorded (the Commonwealth has no general wiretap or eavesdropping statute of its own; federal interception law was not part of this library's sources). One criminal law sets a hard limit for everyone, landlord and tenant alike: it is a crime to view, photograph or record a person who reasonably expects not to be seen, while undressed, using the toilet or engaged in sexual activity, or in a way that captures intimate areas, for sexual purposes, and a further crime to share such images. Security recording is excepted only where notice of the cameras is clearly posted and the place is one where people have no reasonable expectation of privacy. The Constitution protects individual privacy; whether that reaches a private landlord or tenant is a question only case law could settle (not searched). So camera rules are lease terms. Cautious course: let tenants install a doorbell camera or camera aimed at their own entry if they don't drill without consent, don't aim it into other units, windows or shared bathrooms or laundry rooms, and remove it and repair holes at move-out; for your own cameras, cover only common areas, post clear notice, record no audio, and never put a camera inside a unit or a restroom. What to do: put a camera rule in the lease or written rules, and follow the alteration rules in the lease ("no-alterations" carries MP) for wiring and mounting.

title: Trespass Warnings at Rental Property in the Northern Mariana Islands
bodyText: Commonwealth criminal trespass has two parts: a person must make an unlawful and unauthorized entry onto, or interfere with the peaceful use and enjoyment of, another's property, and then refuse to leave promptly after being lawfully told to leave or stop; the penalty is up to six months in jail. There is no written trespass-warning form, posting rule or statutory list of defenses (such as for invited guests). So you, or your manager, may tell an unauthorized non-tenant to leave common areas you control, and a refusal can be reported to the police. But a tenant's home is in the tenant's possession, and a guest the tenant invites is not obviously "unauthorized"; whether you can bar a tenant's invited guest from the unit or the common areas the tenant uses is a question only case law could settle (not searched). Cautious course: give any trespass warning in writing (name, date, the areas covered and why), give a copy to the tenant whose guest it concerns, deal with a problem guest mainly through the tenant's lease obligations (see "edu-guest-policy-mp" and "edu-criminal-activity-mp"), and don't use trespass warnings against people because of a protected characteristic, or against a tenant's caregiver, social-service worker or police.

title: Waterbeds in the Northern Mariana Islands
bodyText: We found no Commonwealth statute, regulation or court rule on waterbeds or other water-filled furniture in rentals: nothing protects a tenant's right to have one, caps what you may require (such as insurance or an added deposit), or sets installation standards. The only waterbed rule we found bans waterbeds as sleeping surfaces for children in licensed child care. So waterbeds are a lease matter: the library's "Use of Property & Common Areas" clause ("common-area-use") carries MP and bars a waterbed or other water-filled furniture without your prior written consent. If you consent, put the conditions in writing (floor-load limits, a liner, professional installation, liability coverage) and treat any extra deposit as part of the security deposit (refund within ten days after the property is returned; see "edu-security-deposit-return-mp").

title: Bed Bug Disclosure in the Northern Mariana Islands
bodyText: We found no Commonwealth statute, regulation or court rule that requires a landlord to disclose bed bugs, give a bed-bug information sheet, or treat an infestation within a set time; the word does not appear anywhere in Commonwealth law. Commonwealth consumer law makes it an unlawful practice to fail to reveal a known defect in or damage to an item in commerce, and we treat that law as reaching residential leasing, so tell a prospective tenant in writing, before signing, about any current or recent infestation you know of; don't rely on an "as is" statement, because we also assume you owe a duty to keep the dwelling fit to live in. Treatment and cooperation are lease terms: the "Pest Reporting and Treatment" clause ("pest-cooperation-pr") carries MP (see "edu-bed-bug-cooperation-mp"). What to do: disclose any infestation you know of and when it was last treated, treat promptly with a licensed operator, and keep the treatment records.

title: Certificates of Occupancy and Rentals in the Northern Mariana Islands
bodyText: We found no Commonwealth rule that requires a lease to disclose whether the building has a certificate of occupancy or to give the tenant a copy. But the building rules themselves reach you. A newly built building may not be occupied until the Building Safety Official issues a certificate of occupancy, which must stay posted in a conspicuous place, and an enlarged or altered building that changes its occupancy needs a new one. Every apartment and residential rental also needs an annual Certificate of Compliance after a Building Safety inspection, posted conspicuously (see "edu-rental-inspection-mp" and the optional clause "rental-inspection-mp"). Renting space that has no certificate, such as a converted garage or an unpermitted addition, risks the building's occupancy permit and a non-habitability finding. What to do: confirm both certificates are current before you rent, keep them posted, and don't rent space that was never approved for living in.

title: Defective Drywall in the Northern Mariana Islands
bodyText: We found no Commonwealth statute, regulation or court rule on defective (corrosive) drywall or any duty to disclose it. Commonwealth consumer law makes it an unlawful practice to fail to reveal a known defect in or damage to an item in commerce, and we treat that law as reaching residential leasing, so tell a prospective tenant in writing, before signing, about any defective drywall you know of; don't rely on an "as is" statement, because we also assume you owe a duty to keep the dwelling fit to live in. What to do: if you know or suspect corrosive drywall (sulfur odor, blackened copper wiring or pipes), disclose it, get it assessed, and fix it before renting.

title: Electricity Submetering in the Northern Mariana Islands
bodyText: The Commonwealth Utilities Corporation's rules forbid a customer to resell electric power it buys from CUC to third parties, but let a commercial customer allocate the cost of electric power among tenants; where tenants are separately metered, the meters must be ANSI C12.1 rated with cyclometer dials. Water may not be resold without CUC's approval. So a landlord on a commercial CUC account may pass on its actual electricity cost to tenants (whether a residential-class landlord may is unsettled; see "edu-utility-interruption-submeter-mp"), but no one may run a resale business at a markup, and doing so doesn't make you a regulated utility under any Commonwealth rule we found. We found no Commonwealth rule that requires a special lease disclosure for submetered electricity or gas. For how to disclose and bill submetered charges, see "edu-utility-submetering-disclosure-mp" and "edu-utility-interruption-submeter-mp". What to do: bill only your actual CUC cost by a stated method, use compliant meters, and put the method in the lease.

title: Flood Risk Disclosure in the Northern Mariana Islands
bodyText: We found no Commonwealth statute, regulation or court rule that requires a landlord to tell a tenant that a rental is in a flood hazard zone, has flooded before, or lacks flood insurance, or that prescribes a flood rider. The Commonwealth's floodplain rules govern construction in designated flood hazard zones, and one of their stated purposes is to make sure potential buyers, not tenants, learn that property is in a special flood hazard area. Commonwealth consumer law makes it an unlawful practice to fail to reveal a known defect in or damage to an item in commerce, and we treat that law as reaching residential leasing, so tell a prospective tenant in writing, before signing, about any flood risk, past flooding or water intrusion you know of; don't rely on an "as is" statement, because we also assume you owe a duty to keep the dwelling fit to live in. What to do: check the official flood maps for the address, tell tenants in writing if the unit is in a flood hazard zone or has flooded, and remind them that your insurance won't cover their belongings, so renters' flood coverage is their call.

title: Foreclosure Disclosure in the Northern Mariana Islands
bodyText: We found no Commonwealth statute, regulation or court rule that requires you to tell a new or current tenant that the property is in foreclosure or that a foreclosure complaint has been filed. A mortgage can be foreclosed only through the court, and after the court-ordered sale the buyer is entitled to the rent during the redemption period; but a deed of trust (the usual security for federal-agency loans) may instead allow a trustee's sale without a court case and with no redemption (see "edu-foreclosure-mp"). Cautious course: under the consumer protection law, which we treat as reaching leasing, signing a new tenant to a lease you know may not survive a pending foreclosure without saying so risks being an unfair or deceptive practice. What to do: if a foreclosure case is filed against the property, or you receive a deed-of-trust notice of default or of sale, tell prospective tenants in writing before they sign, and tell current tenants who to pay if a sale happens.

title: Good Cause Eviction Notice in the Northern Mariana Islands
bodyText: The Northern Mariana Islands has no good-cause or just-cause eviction law and no rent-increase law that a lease must say it is or isn't covered by, so there is no good-cause notice to give. A periodic tenancy ends on written notice before the end of a period (15 days for month-to-month, unless the lease says otherwise) and a fixed term ends on its expiration date, without any stated reason (see "edu-termination-notice-mp" and "edu-for-cause-eviction-mp"). One exception: in a Housing Choice Voucher tenancy, federal rules let the owner end the tenancy during the lease term only for a serious or repeated lease violation, a violation of law tied to the tenant's occupancy, or other good cause. What to do: don't add a good-cause notice to a private lease; for a voucher tenant, follow the HUD tenancy addendum.

title: Disclosing Building Orders in the Northern Mariana Islands
bodyText: We found no Commonwealth statute, regulation or court rule that requires a landlord to disclose outstanding inspection, violation or condemnation orders to a prospective tenant. The orders themselves have teeth: unsafe buildings are public nuisances that must be repaired, vacated or demolished, the Building Safety Official can order a building vacated and post it against entry, and failing to keep the annual Certificate of Compliance raises non-habitability issues (see "edu-condemned-premises-rent-bar-mp" and "edu-rental-inspection-mp"). Commonwealth consumer law makes it an unlawful practice to fail to reveal a known defect in or damage to an item in commerce, and we treat that law as reaching residential leasing, so tell a prospective tenant in writing, before signing, about any outstanding violation, unsafe-building or vacate order you know of; don't rely on an "as is" statement, because we also assume you owe a duty to keep the dwelling fit to live in. What to do: clear any outstanding order before renting; if one is pending, disclose it in writing, and never rent a unit under a vacate order.

title: Contaminated Property and Leases in the Northern Mariana Islands
bodyText: We found no Commonwealth statute or regulation that requires a residential lease to state that property is a contaminated or cleaned-up site, or to repeat environmental use restrictions. Where the Division of Environmental Quality approves a cleanup that leaves contamination above the standard cleanup levels, it requires institutional controls: fences and signs, and legal limits on how the site may be used (for example, no use of the groundwater or no disturbing a cap); for an owner who is or could be a potentially liable person, those controls go into a restrictive covenant the owner signs and records, which runs with the land and binds the owner's successors and assigns. A tenant who doesn't know about such a restriction could break it. Commonwealth consumer law makes it an unlawful practice to fail to reveal a known defect in or damage to an item in commerce, and we treat that law as reaching residential leasing, so tell a prospective tenant in writing, before signing, about any contamination or recorded environmental restriction you know of; don't rely on an "as is" statement, because we also assume you owe a duty to keep the dwelling fit to live in. What to do: check the land records for any environmental covenant, attach its use restrictions to the lease, and tell the tenant what not to do (dig, use well water, disturb a cap).

title: Landlord Liability Insurance in the Northern Mariana Islands
bodyText: We found no Commonwealth statute, regulation or court rule that requires a residential landlord to carry liability insurance, to register insurance with any government office, or to tell tenants whether you are insured. Insurance duties in Commonwealth law fall on other activities (motor vehicles, boats, jet-ski and car rentals, firearm vendors, shooting ranges, some public-land occupants) and on lenders' conditions for NMHC and development loans. A condominium association must, to the extent reasonably available, carry property insurance and general liability insurance for the condominium, but that is no substitute for your own landlord policy. What to do: carry landlord liability coverage anyway (the Commonwealth's typhoon exposure makes property coverage important too), check any loan or association insurance condition, and tell tenants in the lease that your policy doesn't cover their belongings.

title: Lead-Based Paint Disclosure in the Northern Mariana Islands
bodyText: Federal lead-paint disclosure law applies in the Northern Mariana Islands. If the rental was built before 1978 (target housing), before the tenant is bound by the lease you must give the EPA lead-hazard pamphlet, disclose any lead-based paint or lead hazards you know of and give any lead reports you have, and include in the lease or an attachment the federal Lead Warning Statement word for word, your disclosure, a list of records given, the tenant's acknowledgment, any agent's statement, and dated signatures. Exempt: leases of 100 days or less with no renewal or extension, housing certified lead-free by a certified inspector, housing for the elderly or persons with disabilities and 0-bedroom units (unless a child under 6 lives or will live there), and renewals where you already disclosed and have no new information. A knowing violation can cost three times the tenant's damages plus fees. We found no Commonwealth lead law that adds to this for private rentals (no Commonwealth abatement, certificate or tenant-notice duty), though child-care facilities may not use lead paint on surfaces children reach, and Housing Corporation programs follow HUD's lead rules. What to do: use the "Lead-Based Paint Disclosure" clause ("lead-based-paint"), which carries MP, for every pre-1978 unit, and use lead-safe work practices when you repaint or renovate.

title: Lead-Safe Certificates in the Northern Mariana Islands
bodyText: We found no Commonwealth statute or regulation that requires a lead-safe or lead-free certificate for a rental, an inspection certificate attached to the lease, or a lead-safe registration. The only lead rules for private rentals are the federal disclosure rules (see "edu-lead-based-paint-mp"); a lead-free finding by a certified inspector matters there only because it exempts the lease from the federal disclosure. What to do: give the federal disclosure for pre-1978 housing; attach a certified inspector's lead-free report only if you have one and rely on that exemption.

title: Commonwealth Lead Notices in the Northern Mariana Islands
bodyText: Beyond the federal lead disclosure (see "edu-lead-based-paint-mp"), we found no Commonwealth lead notice, certificate, inspection report or information packet that must be delivered with a lease or repeated during the tenancy or at renewal. Under the federal rule a renewal needs no new disclosure if you already gave the full disclosure and have no new information; if you learn something new (for example a lead inspection result), disclose it at the next renewal. Housing Corporation voucher families get HUD's lead brochure in the Corporation's briefing packet; that doesn't replace your own disclosure. What to do: give the federal disclosure for pre-1978 units and update it whenever you get new lead information.

title: Recording Leases in the Northern Mariana Islands
bodyText: A lease for one year or less needs no recording. For a lease longer than one year: it must be a signed written instrument; documents that must be recorded, including leases exceeding one year, must be acknowledged before a notary public before the Recorder's Office takes them (lack of acknowledgment doesn't affect validity between you and the tenant); and an unrecorded interest other than a lease of one year or less is not valid against a later good-faith buyer or mortgagee who records first. Whether the Commonwealth's statute requiring recording of transfers that must be in writing makes recording a residential lease of more than one year mandatory is unsettled, and a knowing and wilful failure to record carries a fine of up to $10,000. Cautious course: have any lease longer than one year signed before a notary and recorded with the Recorder's Office (the tenant is the party receiving the interest; cooperate in recording). See "edu-lease-term-limitation-mp" and "edu-statute-of-frauds-lease-term-mp". Recording changes priority against later buyers and lenders (see "edu-foreclosure-mp"), not the tenant's rights against you.

title: Meter Conservation Charges in the Northern Mariana Islands
bodyText: We found no Commonwealth statute, regulation or court rule on meter conservation charges or utility on-bill financing for energy-efficiency improvements, and no notice a landlord must give tenants about one; the Commonwealth Utilities Corporation's rules contain no such program. What to do: if you ever finance improvements through a charge that appears on a tenant's utility bill, disclose the charge, its amount and its end date in the lease before signing (the consumer protection law, which we treat as reaching leasing, bars unfair or deceptive practices).

title: Former Drug Labs in the Northern Mariana Islands
bodyText: We found no Commonwealth statute, regulation or court rule on methamphetamine-lab contamination: no duty to disclose a former drug lab to tenants, report a suspected lab, test or decontaminate, and no ban on renting a contaminated unit. Commonwealth consumer law makes it an unlawful practice to fail to reveal a known defect in or damage to an item in commerce, and we treat that law as reaching residential leasing, so tell a prospective tenant in writing, before signing, about any past drug manufacturing or contamination you know of; don't rely on an "as is" statement, because we also assume you owe a duty to keep the dwelling fit to live in. Related rules: a person who knowingly maintains or allows a place in a condition harmful to others' health or safety commits criminal nuisance once aware or notified, and on Saipan the blight law lets the Zoning Administrator act against a property not occupied by its owner that provides a site for drug activity (see "edu-nuisance-mp"). What to do: if you know or suspect a unit was used to make drugs, report it to the Department of Public Safety, have it professionally tested and cleaned before re-renting, and disclose the history in writing.

title: Military Activity Disclosure in the Northern Mariana Islands
bodyText: We found no Commonwealth statute, regulation or court rule that requires a lease or sale disclosure for property near a military installation, in a military noise or accident-potential zone, or within a set distance of a base, and no tenant termination right tied to one. Under the Covenant, land on Tinian, at Tanapag Harbor on Saipan and on Farallon de Medinilla is made available to the United States by lease for defense purposes, and military training and activity may affect nearby areas. Commonwealth consumer law makes it an unlawful practice to fail to reveal a known defect in or damage to an item in commerce, and we treat that law as reaching residential leasing, so tell a prospective tenant in writing, before signing, about any regular aircraft noise, live-fire training or similar military activity that materially affects the home you know of; don't rely on an "as is" statement, because we also assume you owe a duty to keep the dwelling fit to live in. What to do: if the rental is close to an active military area, airfield or training range, say so in writing before signing.

title: Mold Disclosure in the Northern Mariana Islands
bodyText: We found no Commonwealth statute, regulation or court rule that requires a landlord to disclose mold, give a mold pamphlet, or remediate mold to a set standard. In the Commonwealth's humid, typhoon-prone climate mold is a common problem, and the only mold references we found are government repair appropriations and disaster-recovery rehabilitation rules. Commonwealth consumer law makes it an unlawful practice to fail to reveal a known defect in or damage to an item in commerce, and we treat that law as reaching residential leasing, so tell a prospective tenant in writing, before signing, about any mold or water intrusion you know of; don't rely on an "as is" statement, because we also assume you owe a duty to keep the dwelling fit to live in. What to do: inspect for mold and leaks before each tenancy, disclose any known mold and what was done about it, fix leaks and remediate promptly when a tenant reports mold, and set out in the lease how tenants should report moisture and ventilate.

title: Ordnance, Demolition and Shared Meter Disclosures in the Northern Mariana Islands
bodyText: We found no Commonwealth statute, regulation or court rule that requires a landlord to disclose that a rental is near a former military ordnance location, to disclose a pending demolition permit, or to disclose shared or common utility meters. World War II unexploded ordnance is still found in the islands; the rules we found deal with removing ordnance from beaches and disposing of munitions, not with leases. Shared meters are governed by the Commonwealth Utilities Corporation's rules on allocating and metering tenants' power (see "edu-electric-submetering-disclosure-mp" and "edu-utility-submetering-disclosure-mp"). Commonwealth consumer law makes it an unlawful practice to fail to reveal a known defect in or damage to an item in commerce, and we treat that law as reaching residential leasing, so tell a prospective tenant in writing, before signing, about any ordnance found on the property, planned demolition affecting the tenant, or shared meter arrangement you know of; don't rely on an "as is" statement, because we also assume you owe a duty to keep the dwelling fit to live in. What to do: if ordnance has been found on or near the property, tell tenants and not to dig or touch suspicious objects (call the Department of Public Safety); disclose any planned demolition before signing; and say in the lease how shared meters are split.

title: Owner and Manager Identity in the Northern Mariana Islands
bodyText: We found no Commonwealth statute, regulation or court rule that requires you to tell a tenant at or before signing who owns the property or who manages it, or to give an address for notices, and no rule that makes such a disclosure a condition of an eviction case. Your identity matters later: the three-day notice demanding rent must be in substantially the statutory form, which ends with the landlord's name, address and telephone number, and a possession case is filed in the Superior Court (see "edu-nonpayment-notice-mp" and "edu-nonresident-owner-agent-mp"). In a Housing Choice Voucher tenancy the lease must name the owner. Cautious course: name the owner (and any manager) and an address and phone for notices and repair requests in the lease, and update tenants in writing if ownership or management changes (see "edu-sale-or-management-change-mp").

title: Pest Control and Fumigation Notices in the Northern Mariana Islands
bodyText: The Commonwealth's pesticide rules require notice before a termite fumigation that needs a Division of Environmental Quality permit: the licensed applicator must give written notice to each household and business within seventy-five feet of the application, and if the site is a single-owner complex with several units, must inform every tenant, at least 14 days before the fumigation. The duty is the applicator's, not the landlord's, and we found no Commonwealth rule requiring a landlord to give tenants notice of routine pest-control treatments or a pesticide disclosure in the lease. What to do: book termite fumigation early enough for the 14-day notice, make sure the applicator's notice reaches every tenant, tell tenants yourself when and where any spraying will happen and how to prepare, and plan for tenants to stay elsewhere during a fumigation (the "pest-cooperation-pr" clause carries MP for tenant cooperation).

title: Well and Catchment Water at Rentals in the Northern Mariana Islands
bodyText: We found no Commonwealth statute, regulation or court rule that requires a landlord to test a private well or give tenants well-water test results. Wells need permits from the Division of Environmental Quality to be drilled and operated, and the drinking-water rules apply to a "public water system": one that supplies water for human consumption through pipes to at least fifteen service connections, or regularly serves an average of at least twenty-five people daily at least 60 days a year. If you supply water to your tenants from your own well or catchment system and reach either threshold, those rules (testing, reporting and treatment) may apply to you, so check with the Division. Commonwealth consumer law makes it an unlawful practice to fail to reveal a known defect in or damage to an item in commerce, and we treat that law as reaching residential leasing, so tell a prospective tenant in writing, before signing, about any well-water problem, contamination or failed test you know of; don't rely on an "as is" statement, because we also assume you owe a duty to keep the dwelling fit to live in. What to do: if tenants drink water from your well or catchment, test it regularly, share the results, and tell tenants whether the water is safe to drink.

title: Chemical Exposure Warnings in the Northern Mariana Islands
bodyText: California's Proposition 65 does not apply in the Northern Mariana Islands, and we found no Commonwealth law that requires a landlord to post or give a warning about chemicals that cause cancer or reproductive harm. The only Commonwealth carcinogen-warning rule we found is the labeling requirement for betel nut. What to do: no chemical-exposure warning is required for an MP rental; disclose known hazards such as lead, asbestos or mold under the rules in those rows.

title: Property Tax and Rent in the Northern Mariana Islands
bodyText: We found no Commonwealth statute, regulation or court rule that requires a landlord to tell tenants what part of the rent goes to property tax. The Commonwealth levies no general real property tax: the Constitution bars a tax on owner-occupied single-family residential, agricultural or unimproved land unless three-fourths of the voters in the senatorial district approve, and a senatorial district's local revenue law may impose a real property tax of up to two percent of appraised value. Your own taxes on rental income are covered in "edu-rent-tax-mp", and passing tax changes through to rent in "edu-tax-escalation-mp". What to do: no property-tax statement is required; if a local real property tax ever applies to your rental, check the local law before passing it through, and never during a Governor's price freeze.

title: Radon Disclosure in the Northern Mariana Islands
bodyText: We found no Commonwealth statute, regulation or court rule that requires radon testing, a radon disclosure to tenants, or radon-resistant construction, at any floor level. The only radon references are an airport definition of hazardous materials and the Housing Corporation's disaster-recovery rehabilitation standards, which call for radon testing and mitigation where the building's location makes it applicable. Commonwealth consumer law makes it an unlawful practice to fail to reveal a known defect in or damage to an item in commerce, and we treat that law as reaching residential leasing, so tell a prospective tenant in writing, before signing, about any radon test result above the federal action level you know of; don't rely on an "as is" statement, because we also assume you owe a duty to keep the dwelling fit to live in. What to do: no radon disclosure is required; if you have test results showing elevated radon, disclose them and mitigate.

title: Required Lease Disclosures in the Northern Mariana Islands
bodyText: The Northern Mariana Islands has no general list of lease disclosures, no state form that must be the first page of a lease, and no notice telling tenants whether a just-cause or rent-increase law covers the unit (it has neither). The disclosures that do apply are few: the federal lead-paint disclosure for pre-1978 housing (see "edu-lead-based-paint-mp"); the HUD tenancy addendum in a Housing Choice Voucher lease; a condominium declarant's 60-day conversion notice to tenants (see "edu-conversion-notice-mp"); and the pesticide applicator's 14-day notice before a termite fumigation in a multi-unit complex (see "edu-pest-control-notice-mp"). See "edu-lease-content-requirements-mp" for what a lease must contain. We found no Commonwealth seller-disclosure statute for real property, so adding a purchase option doesn't trigger one; but a purchase option or right of first refusal on land given to a tenant who is not of Northern Marianas descent can be void under the Constitution's land-alienation rule (see "edu-lease-term-limitation-mp"). Cautious course: because we treat the consumer protection law as reaching leasing, disclose in writing any known defect or condition that a reasonable tenant would want to know. What to do: include the disclosures above where they apply and keep signed copies.

title: Tenant Rights Guides in the Northern Mariana Islands
bodyText: We found no Commonwealth statute, regulation or court rule that requires a landlord to give tenants a government-published guide or summary of landlord and tenant rights, before signing, at renewal or at any other time, or to get a signed acknowledgment of one. The Housing Corporation makes brochures on landlord and tenant responsibilities under the federal Housing Quality Standards available for its voucher program, and the federal lead pamphlet is required for pre-1978 housing (see "edu-lead-based-paint-mp"). What to do: no rights guide is required; if you want tenants to know the key rules, a plain summary of the lease's notice, deposit and repair terms is good practice.

title: Health Code Variances and Rentals in the Northern Mariana Islands
bodyText: We found no Commonwealth rule that requires a landlord to give tenants, or attach to the lease, a health-code or sanitation variance that applies to a rental. Variances appear in the Commonwealth's environmental cleanup rules, Tinian's local regulations and the floodplain rules (where the Building Safety Official must tell the applicant in writing that building below base flood level raises flood insurance costs and risk), but none requires notice to tenants. What to do: if a variance from any health, sanitation, building or floodplain rule affects a rental unit, tell the tenant in writing before signing what it allows and why, since a hidden condition could be treated as an unfair or deceptive practice.

title: Sex Offender Registry Information in the Northern Mariana Islands
bodyText: We found no Commonwealth statute, regulation or court rule that requires a landlord to tell tenants about registered sex offenders living nearby, or to put a notice about the sex offender registry in the lease. The Department of Public Safety keeps a public sex offender registry website, searchable by name, place and radius, and offers email alerts when a registered offender starts living, working or studying in a chosen zip code or radius. It is a crime to willfully misuse or alter registry information about an offender or about anyone living or working at an offender's reported address, or to sell or exchange it for profit, and the website warns against using the information to injure, harass or commit a crime. In the Housing Choice Voucher program the Housing Corporation must deny assistance to a household with a member subject to lifetime sex offender registration. What to do: no registry notice is required; if you add one, point tenants to the official registry website, don't characterize particular neighbors, and if you consider registry status in screening, apply a written policy evenly and use only the official information.

title: Single-Family Rental Disclosures in the Northern Mariana Islands
bodyText: We found no Commonwealth statute, regulation or court rule that requires a special disclosure (with a set type size or first-page placement) when a single-family house is rented, or a statement about the house's permitted occupancy. Single-family rentals do appear in Commonwealth law: a single-family house rented by a private owner of no more than three such houses without a broker is exempt from most of the Commonwealth Fair Housing Act (but never from its advertising ban), and every single-family rental needs the annual Building Safety Certificate of Compliance, with the whole premises inspected (see "edu-rental-inspection-mp"). Saipan's zoning rules (local law) govern where single-family dwellings and home businesses may be. What to do: no special disclosure is required; get the annual certificate and check local zoning before renting a house or part of one.

title: Shoreline Access and Rentals in the Northern Mariana Islands
bodyText: We found no Commonwealth statute, regulation or court rule that requires a lease or sale of shoreline property to disclose public rights of way to the shore. Shoreline access rules in Commonwealth law run to public land: before public land abutting the sea is sold, leased or otherwise allocated, the Division of Lands and Surveys must lay out public roads and paths to the sea; submerged lands are managed for public recreation, fishing, shoreline access and navigation; and zoning and coastal policy favor beach access. Coastal permits may also limit what can be built near the shore. What to do: if a public path or easement crosses or borders the rental, or a coastal permit limits use of the shoreline area, tell the tenant in writing and don't block public access.

title: Special District Disclosure in the Northern Mariana Islands
bodyText: We found no Commonwealth statute, regulation or court rule that requires a landlord to tell a tenant, in the lease or otherwise, that the property lies in a special taxing, assessment, utility or improvement district. The Commonwealth has no general real property tax, and we found no special-assessment districts of the kind some states use (utility districts, Mello-Roos and similar). One thing to watch: since 2020 each senatorial district (Rota, Tinian and Aguiguan, Saipan and the Northern Islands) may create and regulate Community Improvement Districts by local law for infrastructure, beautification, community safety and business development; we found none created in the Commonwealth Code, but local laws are flagged rather than reviewed here. Separately, Saipan's blight law can put a special assessment lien on property for nuisance abatement costs (see "edu-nuisance-mp"). What to do: no district disclosure is needed in the lease; if your property is in a local improvement district or carries a local assessment, check the local law and tell the tenant only about any charge you plan to pass on, and put that charge in the lease (see "edu-property-tax-rent-disclosure-mp").

title: Fire Sprinkler Disclosure in the Northern Mariana Islands
bodyText: We found no Commonwealth statute, regulation or court rule that requires a landlord to tell a tenant, in the lease or a separate notice, whether the building has an automatic fire sprinkler system or when it was last inspected. Whether a building must have sprinklers is a building and fire code question, not a disclosure rule: the Commonwealth adopts the International Building Code (2018 edition onward) and the most current International Fire Code, and the fire code fine schedule sets a fine of up to $10,000 for violating the International Fire Code's automatic sprinkler section (see "edu-fire-sprinkler-duty-mp"). Because the Consumer Protection Act is treated here as reaching residential leasing, don't describe the unit as sprinklered, or a system as working, unless that is true. What to do: no sprinkler disclosure is required in the lease; if the building has sprinklers, it is sensible to tell tenants not to hang things from or paint sprinkler heads and to report damage, and keep the system maintained.

title: Stigmatized Property in the Northern Mariana Islands
bodyText: We found no Commonwealth statute, regulation or court rule on "stigmatized" property: nothing requires you to tell a tenant that a death, crime or suicide happened in the unit, and nothing protects you if you stay silent. Two general rules still matter, because the Consumer Protection Act is treated here as reaching residential leasing: you may not engage in any unfair or deceptive act, and a merchant may not fail to reveal a known defect in what it offers unless it is offered "as is". A past event is not a physical defect, but don't answer a direct question falsely. Sex offenders: the Commonwealth keeps a public sex offender registry website with names, photographs and residential addresses, and lets anyone sign up for email notice when an offender moves into an area. No Commonwealth law makes you disclose registry information to applicants, but misusing or altering registry information, or selling it for profit, is a crime; point a tenant who asks to the Department of Public Safety's registry site instead. HIV: we found no Commonwealth law naming HIV status in housing, but the Commonwealth Fair Housing Act bars discrimination because of disability, defined to match the federal disability standard, and federal fair housing law has the same handicap rule; treat HIV or AIDS as a disability (case law not searched). Don't ask about, refuse, or set terms because of an applicant's or occupant's HIV status, or tell others about it. What to do: don't volunteer or invent stigma information, answer honestly if asked about something you know, refer registry questions to the public website, and keep any health information you learn confidential.

title: Student Housing in the Northern Mariana Islands
bodyText: We found no Commonwealth statute, regulation or court rule written for student housing: nothing on student leases, parental guarantees, roommate matching, academic-year terms or disclosures to student tenants. An ordinary lease to a student follows the same rules as any other lease. Two general rules can matter. A dormitory or rooming house with four or more guest rooms is a "room accommodation" under the Commonwealth sanitation law and needs a sanitary permit (see "edu-health-district-rental-rules-mp"). And if a student tenant is under 18, check that someone of age signs or guarantees the lease (see "edu-minor-tenant-filing-mp"); a guarantor who signs the lease meets the writing rule for a promise to pay another's debt (the library's "guaranty-as" clause carries MP). Housing Corporation voucher programs check full-time student status as part of eligibility under their own rules. What to do: use the standard lease, name every occupant, add a guaranty where the student has no income, and get a sanitary permit if you run a dormitory or room-rental house.

title: Tenant Rights Statement in the Northern Mariana Islands
bodyText: We found no Commonwealth statute, regulation or court rule that makes a landlord give tenants a government-prepared statement of tenant rights, attach a summary to the lease, collect a signed acknowledgment, or that bars a landlord from suing until such a statement is given. No Commonwealth agency publishes a required tenant-rights form. The one rights notice in the Code is narrow: a developer converting a building to condominiums must give each tenant at least 60 days' written notice that sets out generally the tenants' rights under the conversion law (see "edu-conversion-notice-mp"). Federal lead-paint rules also require the EPA pamphlet and warning for pre-1978 housing (see "edu-lead-based-paint-mp"). What to do: no general rights statement is required; give the conversion notice and lead disclosures where they apply, and give every tenant a signed copy of the lease.

title: Tenant Opportunity to Purchase in the Northern Mariana Islands
bodyText: We found no Commonwealth statute, regulation or court rule giving residential tenants a general right to buy, or a right of first refusal, when the owner sells the building, and no notice of sale an owner must give tenants. The one exception is a condominium conversion: the developer (declarant) must give each tenant at least 60 days' notice before requiring them to leave, and for 30 days after that notice must offer to sell the tenant the unit the tenant rents; if the tenant doesn't buy, the developer can't offer the unit to anyone else on better price or terms for the next 60 days (see "edu-conversion-notice-mp"). Remember the land-alienation rule: only persons of Northern Marianas descent may acquire freehold interests, except an interest above the first floor of a condominium building on private land, so a tenant without that descent may be unable to accept an offer of a ground-floor unit. A lease clause giving the tenant a purchase option or right of first refusal is a private choice, limited by the same rule, and it should say so. What to do: on an ordinary sale no tenant notice or offer is required, but the lease continues and the buyer generally takes subject to it (for a lease over one year, record it, since an unrecorded one isn't valid against a good-faith buyer without notice who records first; see "edu-lease-registration-mp"); on a condominium conversion follow the notice and offer steps exactly.

title: Purchase-Right Exemption Notices in the Northern Mariana Islands
bodyText: Because the Commonwealth has no general tenant opportunity-to-purchase law, there is no exemption notice, exemption filing or statement of exempt sale for an owner to give tenants or file with any agency. We found no Commonwealth statute, regulation or court rule on the point. The only tenant purchase right is in a condominium conversion, and its own limits are built in: the offer to the tenant doesn't apply to a unit that will be used only for nonresidential purposes or whose boundaries don't substantially match the residential unit before conversion (see "edu-tpa-notice-mp"). What to do: nothing to file or send on an ordinary sale; on a condominium conversion, confirm in writing which units, if any, fall outside the tenant offer and why.

title: Truth in Renting in the Northern Mariana Islands
bodyText: We found no Commonwealth "truth in renting" law: no agency-published statement of landlord and tenant rights that you must hand out, and no rule voiding lease terms because they misstate the law. But the Consumer Protection Act covers much of the same ground. It is an offense for anyone advertising real property, in any medium, to make a statement about the property or the deal that is untrue or misleading and that they know, or with reasonable care should know, is untrue or misleading; the penalty is up to six months in jail or a $1,000 fine (the offense covers statements made to dispose of property or to get the public to enter an obligation relating to it; we assume rental advertising is covered, case law not searched). And because the Act is treated here as reaching residential leasing, a lease or ad must not represent that the deal gives or involves rights, remedies or obligations it doesn't, or that the law prohibits (for example, a clause saying the tenant waives the ten-day deposit refund or may be locked out without a court order), and must not contain an unconscionable term. A tenant harmed by a violation can sue for actual damages, an equal amount again for a wilful violation, and attorney's fees. What to do: describe the unit, rent and fees accurately in every ad and listing, and don't put terms in the lease that misstate what Commonwealth or federal law lets you do; the library's clauses for the Commonwealth are screened for this.

title: Leases by Life Holders and Customary Trustees in the Northern Mariana Islands
bodyText: The Commonwealth has no civil-law "usufruct", and we found no Commonwealth statute or court rule on what happens to a lease granted by someone who holds land only for life. But limited ownership is common here because of customary inheritance, and it matters when you sign a lease. Under Chamorro custom, when an owner dies without a will a surviving spouse takes ancestors' land only for life, with the children holding the remainder. Under Carolinian custom, family land is held by a customary trustee for the whole family, every family member has the same right to use it, and unless the family consents or agrees otherwise the customary trustee may not sell, lease, mortgage or otherwise dispose of it. So if you lease from (or as) a life-estate holder or customary trustee: for Carolinian family land, get the family's written consent to the lease, or the lease may be challenged; for a life estate, whether the lease survives the life holder's death is a common-law question (the Restatement has not been read and case law was not searched), so the cautious course is to have the remainder holders sign the lease too, or keep the term short. What to do: before signing, confirm who holds title and in what capacity (check the recorded documents and any probate decree), and have everyone with an interest sign the lease; a lease for more than one year must be in writing and signed (see "edu-statute-of-frauds-lease-term-mp").

title: Utility Disclosure Attachments in the Northern Mariana Islands
bodyText: We found no Commonwealth statute, regulation or court rule that requires a private residential lease to carry a utility disclosure attachment (for example, a statement of average utility costs, a billing history, or a separate signed page on how shared utilities are split). The only lease-attachment rule on utilities we found applies to government agencies' own leases (energy-efficiency terms), not to private landlords. Who pays which utility is a lease term (the library's "utilities-responsibility" clause carries MP; see "edu-utilities-responsibility-mp"). If you bill tenants for a shared or submetered utility, the cautious course in "edu-utility-submetering-disclosure-mp" and "edu-utility-apportionment-mp" applies: disclose the method before signing, pass on only your actual Commonwealth Utilities Corporation cost, and show the bill on request, because an undisclosed or marked-up charge risks being an unfair or deceptive practice. What to do: state in the lease which utilities the tenant pays and, for any landlord-billed utility, how the charge is figured; a separate attachment is optional.

title: Accessory Dwelling Units in the Northern Mariana Islands
bodyText: We found no Commonwealth statute or regulation about accessory dwelling units as such: nothing gives an owner a right to add and rent an ADU, and nothing bars local owner-occupancy rules. Zoning is local: Saipan has its own zoning law (adopted by reference and not reviewed here), and Tinian and Rota have their own local laws, so check the island's zoning before you build or rent a second unit. Commonwealth building rules do reach an ADU. You need a building permit before you build or convert space into a dwelling, and you may not change the use or occupancy of a building (for example, turning a garage, storeroom or small accessory structure into living space) without the Building Safety Official's approval; an accessory structure of 120 square feet or less needs no permit, but that exemption is not an approval to live in it. A house built under the free owner-builder permit is, by definition, one in which no part is to be leased or rented, so renting part of an owner-built house can put you outside that permit. Adding units can also trigger the 2% developer infrastructure tax: new residential construction of two or fewer dwelling units, and alterations that create no new unit, are exempt, but whether adding a unit to an existing house is exempt is unclear, so ask the Department of Finance and Building Safety before you start. Once rented, the ADU needs the annual Certificate of Compliance (see "edu-rental-inspection-mp") and a certificate of occupancy (see "edu-certificate-of-occupancy-disclosure-mp"). What to do: get the building permit and change-of-use approval, confirm zoning and any developer tax, and don't rent the unit until it has passed inspection.

title: Alarm Tampering Fees in the Northern Mariana Islands
bodyText: We found no Commonwealth statute, regulation or court rule that sets or limits a fee a landlord may charge a tenant for removing, disabling or tampering with a smoke or carbon monoxide alarm, and none that makes tampering with a dwelling's alarm a separate offense. The only tampering rule we found is for fire-extinguishing equipment at the airport. The adopted International Fire Code requires smoke alarms in existing residential occupancies and carbon monoxide detection where there is a fuel-burning source, and says carbon monoxide alarms that stop working must be replaced (see "edu-alarm-duties-mp"). Because no Commonwealth law lists or caps rental fees, a reasonable charge for the cost of replacing or reinstalling an alarm the tenant disabled is a contract term, but a flat penalty unrelated to cost risks being treated as an unconscionable provision under the Consumer Protection Act. What to do: use the library's detector-care clause ("detector-care-la"), which asks the tenant not to disable alarms and to report faults, and recover the actual cost of repair or replacement through "tenant-caused-fines-as" or the damage terms rather than a fixed fine; never leave a disabled alarm unrepaired.

title: Asbestos in the Northern Mariana Islands
bodyText: We found no Commonwealth statute, regulation or court rule that requires a landlord to inspect for asbestos, disclose known asbestos to a tenant, or abate it in a rental. Asbestos appears in Commonwealth law only in waste and program rules: friable asbestos is not ordinary construction and demolition waste, and a landfill may take friable asbestos-containing material only if it complies with the federal asbestos air-emission standards. Federal asbestos rules for renovation and demolition were not reviewed here. Because the Consumer Protection Act is treated here as reaching residential leasing, don't conceal asbestos you know about if a tenant asks, and under the cautious habitability course a known asbestos hazard that endangers occupants should be handled before you rent. What to do: if an older building may contain asbestos (old floor tiles, pipe insulation, cement sheeting), have it assessed before any renovation or demolition, hire qualified contractors, dispose of debris only through the Division of Environmental Quality's approved routes, and tell tenants about work that could disturb it.

title: Balcony Inspections in the Northern Mariana Islands
bodyText: We found no Commonwealth statute or regulation requiring periodic inspection of balconies, decks or other exterior elevated elements of rental buildings, or a report to tenants or an agency. The Building Safety Code says no inspection or certificate that the International Building Code would require applies in the Commonwealth unless the Building Safety Official adopts it by regulation, and we found none for balconies. General rules still reach a balcony. Every apartment building and residential rental needs the annual Building Safety inspection and Certificate of Compliance, which covers the premises (see "edu-rental-inspection-mp"); the owner must keep required safety devices and safeguards (such as guards and railings) maintained; a balcony or other building appendage in deteriorated condition or unable to carry its design loads is an "unsafe building appendage" and a public nuisance; and the fire code fine schedule fines violations of the International Fire Code's egress balcony and guard sections. Anyone injured by a Building Safety Code violation can sue for damages and attorney's fees. What to do: have balconies, railings and stairs checked as part of each annual inspection or sooner after a typhoon or earthquake, repair rot, rust and loose railings promptly, and close off any balcony you think is unsafe until it is repaired.

title: Waiving Casualty and Mitigation Rules in the Northern Mariana Islands
bodyText: Some states have statutory casualty and mitigation rules and say whether a lease may change them. The Commonwealth has neither: we found no Commonwealth statute, regulation or court rule on a residential lease after a fire or typhoon (see "edu-casualty-termination-mp") or on a landlord's duty to re-let after a tenant leaves (see "edu-abandonment-and-mitigation-mp"), and so nothing that says either rule can or can't be waived. The Holdover Tenancy Act leaves the parties free to add rights and duties by agreement. Where no statute speaks, the courts apply the common law as stated in the Restatements, which this library has not read (case law not searched). Cautious course: treat the lease's casualty clause as the rule between you, but don't rely on a clause that makes the tenant keep paying rent for a home that can't be lived in, or that says you have no duty at all to try to re-let; such one-sided terms risk being called unconscionable under the Consumer Protection Act. What to do: use the library's "casualty-termination-mp" clause and the tagged "default-by-tenant" clause, which promises reasonable mitigation efforts to the extent the law requires, and keep records of your re-letting efforts.

title: Children in Rental Housing in the Northern Mariana Islands
bodyText: We found no Commonwealth statute, regulation or court rule that requires a lease to say anything about children who will live in the unit. What the law does say is that you may not discriminate because of familial status: the Commonwealth Fair Housing Act and the federal Fair Housing Act both bar refusing to rent, setting different terms, or advertising a preference against households with children under 18 (or a pregnant person, or someone getting custody of a child). The advertising ban applies even to owners otherwise exempt (an owner of three or fewer single-family houses renting without a broker, or an owner living in a building of four or fewer units). The Act keeps any reasonable occupancy limit set by Commonwealth, local or federal law, but we found no general Commonwealth occupancy limit for private rentals, so your own limit must be reasonable and applied to everyone (see "edu-permitted-occupants-mp"). Qualifying housing for older persons is exempt from the familial-status rules, but see the age caution in "edu-fair-housing-mp". Housing Corporation voucher families must report the birth or custody of a child to the Corporation under its own rules. What to do: list all occupants, adults and children, in the "Permitted Occupants" clause ("permitted-occupants"), which carries MP; don't charge more, assign different units or set different rules (for example, pool or yard rules) because children live there; and don't use words like "adults only" or "no kids" in ads.

title: Family, Homestead and Public Land Leases in the Northern Mariana Islands
bodyText: The Commonwealth has no communal or tribal land system that requires a government officer to approve a private residential lease before it is valid. A private owner leasing private land needs no government approval. But three kinds of land carry their own consent rules, so confirm what kind of land you are leasing first. (1) Carolinian family land: land held by a customary trustee for the family may not be leased, sold or mortgaged by the trustee unless the family consents or agrees otherwise, so get the family's written consent to the lease (see "edu-usufructuary-lessor-mp"). (2) Homestead land still under a homestead permit: rights under a homestead permit may not be sold, assigned, leased, transferred or encumbered before the deed issues, so don't rent a house on a permitted homestead lot until the permittee holds the deed. (3) Public land: leases of public land are made by the Department of Public Lands, may not exceed 40 years including renewals under the statute (the Constitution's text says 25 years, and how the two fit was not resolved; a 15-year extension needs three-fourths of the Legislature), and large commercial transfers need legislative approval; if you hold a public-land lease, check its terms before subletting housing on it. Also, a lease (with renewals) of more than 55 years is restricted by Article XII of the Constitution. What to do: check the recorded title, and get the family's, Department's or other required consent in writing before the tenant moves in.

title: Confession of Judgment in the Northern Mariana Islands
bodyText: We found no Commonwealth statute, regulation or court rule that allows a landlord to take a judgment against a tenant on a confession of judgment or warrant of attorney in a lease, or to enter judgment without a lawsuit on a sworn writing; and none that abolishes such clauses expressly either. The court rules provide only an offer of judgment inside a pending case, and the possession process is the Superior Court summary procedure. The only confessed-judgment mention for private contracts is in the commercial paper law, which says such a term in a note doesn't affect negotiability (see "edu-possession-bond-mp"). On appeal from a possession judgment, a stay is obtained by a supersedeas bond under the civil rules; no rule sets its amount for residential cases. Cautious course: don't put a confession of judgment, warrant of attorney or similar clause in a residential lease. It would misstate the tenant's right to be heard in court and risks being an unconscionable provision under the Consumer Protection Act. What to do: recover possession and money through the summary possession case, and secure the lease with a deposit and, if needed, a guarantor.

title: Consumer Protection Act in the Northern Mariana Islands
bodyText: The Commonwealth's Consumer Protection Act (4 CMC §§ 5101-5123) lists unfair and deceptive practices "in the conduct of any trade or commerce", and "commerce" includes dealing in property "real, personal, or tangible". Whether a residential landlord is covered has not been settled in the materials we reviewed (case law not searched), so this library treats the Act as reaching residential leasing. The listed practices that matter most for a lease are: any act or practice that is unfair or deceptive to the consumer; failing to reveal a known defect unless the item is offered "as is"; representing that a deal confers or involves rights, remedies or obligations it doesn't, or that the law prohibits; and inserting an unconscionable provision in a contract. Separately, untrue or misleading advertising of real property is an offense for anyone. The Act does not list leaving blank spaces in a contract at signing, or failing to give a copy at signing, as unlawful practices, and we found no Commonwealth rule on either for residential leases (see "edu-confirmed-absences-misc-mp"). Government landlords are exempt. Remedies: a tenant can sue in the Superior Court within four years for actual damages, an equal amount again for a wilful violation, and costs and attorney's fees if the tenant wins; the Attorney General can seek an injunction and civil penalties of up to $2,500 per violation ($10,000 for violating an injunction); and a merchant who knowingly or recklessly violates the Act can be fined up to $2,000 or jailed up to six months. Courts read any ambiguity in the Act in the consumer's favor. What to do: fill in every blank before anyone signs, give the tenant a signed copy, describe the unit and charges truthfully, and don't use lease terms that misstate the tenant's rights or are one-sided penalties.

title: Confidentiality of Abuse Information in the Northern Mariana Islands
bodyText: We found no Commonwealth statute, regulation or court rule that makes a private landlord keep confidential what a tenant tells it about domestic violence, dating violence, sexual assault or stalking. Commonwealth confidentiality rules on this subject bind others: employers must keep confidential an employee's request for domestic-violence leave; victims and victim counselors can't be forced to disclose confidential counseling communications; and a person seeking a protection order may leave their address and telephone number off court papers. If your unit is in a federal covered housing program (for example, Section 8 vouchers, public housing, HOME or tax-credit housing), the federal Violence Against Women Act housing protections apply (see "edu-dv-eviction-protection-mp"); that law requires you to keep confidential any information a tenant or applicant gives you to claim its protection, including the fact that they are a victim; you may not put it in a shared database or disclose it to anyone unless the person asks or consents in writing, it is needed in an eviction case under that law, or other law requires it. Cautious course for every landlord: keep any information or documents a tenant gives you about abuse, including a new address or a protection order, in a separate confidential file; share it only with the tenant's written consent, as the law requires, or when needed in a court case; and never tell the abuser or other tenants where the victim lives or why they moved. What to do: limit access to these records to the people who must act on them, and don't put the information in shared tenant files or online portals.

title: Calling for Emergency Help in the Northern Mariana Islands
bodyText: We found no Commonwealth statute, regulation or court rule that gives tenants an express right to call the police or emergency services, or that bars a lease from penalizing tenants (for example under a nuisance or "too many police calls" clause) for doing so. Cautious course: don't put any term in the lease that limits or penalizes calling the police, fire, ambulance or other emergency help, and don't end a tenancy or raise the rent because a tenant or a victim called for help. Such a term could keep a crime victim from getting help, which in federally covered housing conflicts with the Violence Against Women Act's protections (see "edu-dv-eviction-protection-mp"); and the cautious anti-retaliation course this library follows (see "edu-retaliation-mp") and the Consumer Protection Act's bar on unconscionable terms point the same way. What to do: if you use a crime-free or nuisance clause (the tagged "criminal-activity-ky" clause excludes victims), apply it to the conduct, never to the call for help.

title: Eviction Penalty Clauses in the Northern Mariana Islands
bodyText: We found no Commonwealth statute, regulation or court rule that expressly bans lease clauses imposing a penalty, fee or forfeiture on a tenant because the landlord files an eviction (summary possession) case. What the law does provide are two court remedies: a tenant who holds over after the tenancy ends without your permission can be made to pay double the rent for the period of refusal (see "edu-holdover-mp" and the clause "holdover-mp"), and in any Holdover Tenancy Act case the winning party, landlord or tenant, may recover reasonable court costs and attorney's fees (see "edu-attorney-fees-mp"). Cautious course: don't add an "eviction fee", a forfeiture of the whole deposit, or a fixed penalty for being sued on top of those remedies. A one-sided penalty risks being an unconscionable provision under the Consumer Protection Act, and a clause suggesting the tenant must pay your fees even if the tenant wins would misstate the two-way fee rule (see "edu-liquidated-damages-mp" and "edu-notice-service-fee-mp"). What to do: rely on actual unpaid rent and damages, the double-rent holdover remedy and court-awarded costs and fees, and keep any lease fee clause to real costs.

title: Liability Waivers in Leases in the Northern Mariana Islands
bodyText: We found no Commonwealth statute, regulation or court rule that voids, or expressly allows, a lease clause that releases the landlord from liability or makes the tenant indemnify the landlord for the landlord's own negligence. The only similar statutory rule is for car rentals (a rental company's damage waiver may not exclude damage from the renter's ordinary negligence), which doesn't reach leases. Where no statute speaks, the Commonwealth's courts apply the common law as stated in the Restatements, which this library has not read (case law not searched). Cautious course: don't rely on a clause that excuses you from liability for your own negligence or for failing to keep the dwelling fit to live in; it may not hold up, and an overbroad disclaimer risks being an unconscionable provision or a misstatement of the tenant's rights under the Consumer Protection Act. That is why the library uses, for the Commonwealth, the versions of the tenant's-insurance, parking and storage clauses without a blanket disclaimer ("tenants-property-insurance-ks-oh-ca", "parking-ks-oh-ca", "storage-space-ks-oh-ca", "services-utilities-provided-ks-oh"). What to do: carry your own liability insurance, ask tenants to carry renter's insurance for their belongings, and limit any indemnity clause to harm the tenant or the tenant's guests cause.

title: Fair Housing in the Northern Mariana Islands
bodyText: Two fair housing laws apply in the Northern Mariana Islands, and a third rule is followed here cautiously. (1) The Commonwealth Fair Housing Act bars refusing to rent, setting different terms, misrepresenting availability, steering, or advertising a preference because of race, color, religion, sex, familial status, marital status, disability or national origin. Marital status is a class the federal law doesn't list. It also requires reasonable accommodations and modifications for people with disabilities (see "edu-disability-accommodation-mp"), and bars coercing, intimidating or interfering with anyone exercising these rights. (2) The federal Fair Housing Act applies here too, with the same classes except marital status. (3) The Consumer Protection Act makes it an offense for a merchant to discriminate in commerce because of race, color, creed, religion, sex, age, ethnic background, national origin, citizenship, or place of birth or residence; this library treats every landlord as covered, so don't screen or set terms by age, citizenship, place of birth or where someone lives now. Exemptions: an individual owner of no more than three single-family houses renting without a broker, and an owner who lives in a building of four or fewer units, are exempt from the Commonwealth and federal bans except the advertising ban, which still applies to them; the 4 CMC § 5120 rule has no such exemption. Religious organizations and private clubs have limited exemptions, reasonable occupancy limits set by law are kept, and qualifying 55+ or 62+ housing is exempt from the familial-status rules (but see the age rule above). We found no Commonwealth protection for source of income (such as housing vouchers), no separate crime of landlord sexual harassment (though we assume harassment because of sex counts as sex discrimination under these laws (federal harassment rule not saved; case law not searched), and using force or threats to interfere with housing rights is a crime), and no real-estate-licensing discrimination rule beyond the Act's own ban on discrimination in brokerage services. The Commonwealth Constitution also bars discrimination in civil rights on account of race, color, religion, ancestry or sex; whether it reaches private landlords is unsettled. Enforcement: a complaint to the Northern Marianas Housing Corporation within one year, or a lawsuit in the Superior Court within two years, with actual and punitive damages and fees; either side, including the landlord, may elect to have a charge decided in court instead of an administrative hearing. What to do: use the same written criteria for every applicant, keep ads neutral (no "adults only", "no kids", "locals only" or "citizens only"), and train anyone who shows units.

title: Hunting on Rented Land in the Northern Mariana Islands
bodyText: We found no Commonwealth statute, regulation or court rule on whether a tenant of farmland or other rented land has hunting or fishing rights on it. The hunting regulations say only that hunting may be done on public lands the Director designates or on private lands with permission from the landowner, with a hunting license and in season; they don't say whether a tenant in possession counts as the "landowner" for this purpose. Cautious course: if you lease agricultural or rural land, say in the lease whether the tenant (and the tenant's guests) may hunt, trap or fish on it, and whether you keep the right to hunt or to let others hunt there. A tenant should get the owner's written permission before hunting, and any hunting must follow the licensing, season and firearm rules. Game animals, including coconut crabs, may be taken only during the designated hunting season. What to do: add a short written term on hunting and fishing to any farm or rural lease, and keep firearm limits in mind (see "edu-firearms-mp").

title: Fire Code Standard in the Northern Mariana Islands
bodyText: The fire safety standard for buildings in the Commonwealth, including rentals, comes from the Commonwealth Fire Safety Code Act (2 CMC §§ 7301-7340) and the fire code regulations (NMIAC ch. 72-10), which adopt the most up-to-date version of the International Fire Code. The Act applies to all persons and to existing conditions; older conditions that don't strictly comply may continue only if the fire commissioner finds they are not a serious hazard. The Act still refers in places to the older Uniform Fire Code, but the regulations' adoption of the International Fire Code is what the Department of Fire and Emergency Medical Services enforces. The building code is separate: the International Building Code, from the 2018 edition. We found no recent law moving or renumbering the fire code; the last structural change was the 2015 law that created the Department of Fire and Emergency Medical Services. Violations carry a civil fine of $5,000 to $10,000 (each ten days counts again), with a regulatory fine schedule for specific International Fire Code sections, and anyone harmed by a violation may sue for damages and attorney's fees. The fire division may also close a building that is unsafe. What to do: treat the current International Fire Code as the standard for smoke alarms, exits, extinguishers and similar features in your rental (see "edu-alarm-duties-mp"), and ask the Fire Prevention and Arson Investigation Division which edition it is applying when you renovate.

title: Fire Sprinklers in the Northern Mariana Islands
bodyText: We found no Commonwealth statute or regulation of its own that requires fire sprinklers in rental housing or makes owners retrofit existing buildings with them. Whether a building needs sprinklers is set by the model codes the Commonwealth adopts: the International Building Code (2018 edition onward) for new construction and the most current International Fire Code, whose automatic sprinkler section carries a $10,000 fine in the Commonwealth's fire code fine schedule. The text of those sprinkler sections is not in the materials this library was built from, so we can't say which residential buildings need them (new multi-family buildings may well be covered); check with the Department of Fire and Emergency Medical Services and the Building Safety Division. If your building has a sprinkler system, you must keep it maintained: the Building Safety Code makes the owner maintain every required safety device, and the fire division regulates sprinkler installation in commercial buildings. What to do: if you build, convert or substantially renovate a multi-unit building, ask Building Safety and Fire Prevention in writing whether sprinklers are required; keep any existing system inspected and in service, and tell tenants not to hang things from or cover sprinkler heads.

title: Land Ownership Limits and Leases in the Northern Mariana Islands
bodyText: The Commonwealth has no "foreign adversary" or alien land law aimed at particular countries, and we found no rule requiring a lease to a foreign national or nonresident to name or describe them, or requiring government approval of a lease to a corporation (such as employer staff housing). What it has is broader and applies to everyone who is not a person of Northern Marianas descent (including U.S. citizens without that descent): Article XII of the Constitution restricts the acquisition of permanent and long-term interests in land to persons of Northern Marianas descent, and acquisition includes acquisition by lease. For a residential lease this matters only at the long end: a long-term interest means a freehold or a lease of more than 55 years counting renewal rights (an interest above the first floor of a condominium building on private land is excepted). An ordinary lease of 55 years or less, including any renewal options, may be made to anyone, of any nationality, and to any company. A transaction that violates Article XII is void from the start. A corporation counts as a person of Northern Marianas descent only if it is incorporated and based in the Commonwealth and 100% of its directors and voting shares are held by such persons; this matters for a corporate tenant only if the lease or an option would give a long-term interest. What to do: keep the total term with all options at 55 years or less, and don't give a tenant who isn't of Northern Marianas descent a purchase option or right of first refusal on land (see "edu-lease-term-limitation-mp" and "edu-tpa-notice-mp"). Citizenship and place of birth also can't be used to screen tenants (see "edu-fair-housing-mp").

title: Which Code Edition Applies in the Northern Mariana Islands
bodyText: Whether a model code is adopted as a fixed edition or as it changes over time decides which version applies to your building. The Commonwealth does both. Fire code: the fire regulations adopt "the most up to date version" of the International Fire Code, so on its face the fire standard moves with each new edition without a new regulation (subject to Commonwealth amendments); whether it does so without rulemaking is unsettled (case law not searched), which matters now that the 2027 edition has been published. Building code: the statute adopts the International Building Code "commencing with the 2018 Edition" and lets the Building Safety Official adopt updates and new editions by regulation after public notice; the current building regulations adopt the IBC of 2018, including its family of codes such as the International Residential Code. We found no regulation adopting a later IBC edition, so 2018 is the building edition in force (one definitions section of the regulations still says 2009, which the Law Revision Commission notes is probably an error). The Tropical Energy Code (2014) is adopted as part of the building code. Existing buildings generally keep their lawful existing use, and safety devices must be maintained at least to the code in effect when they were installed; new work must meet the code in force when it is permitted. What to do: build and renovate to IBC 2018 unless Building Safety tells you a newer edition has been adopted, and check the current International Fire Code edition with Fire Prevention for alarms, exits and other fire features.

title: Waiving Habitability in the Northern Mariana Islands
