bodyText: We found no Commonwealth statute, regulation or court rule that lets a written agreement remove a habitability requirement, lets a tenant accept stated defects in return for a rent reduction, or requires such an agreement to be a separate document. The Commonwealth has no statutory habitability duty for private landlords to waive in the first place (see "edu-confirmed-absences-habitability-mp" and "edu-habitability-modifiable-mp"). But public safety rules that reach rentals can't be waived by a lease at all: every rented dwelling needs the annual Building Safety Certificate of Compliance, and failing to get one "raised issues of non-habitability"; unsafe or unsanitary buildings, or ones unfit for human habitation, may be ordered repaired or vacated; and fire and building code violations carry fines and a private damages action. Cautious course: where no statute speaks, courts apply the Restatement, which this library has not read; assume the core duty to keep the dwelling fit to live in can't be waived. A lease may describe a known, minor condition the tenant accepts (with any agreed rent reduction stated in writing), but don't use it for anything affecting health or safety. What to do: fix health and safety problems before renting rather than writing them into the lease, and record minor accepted conditions in the move-in report ("move-in-condition-report-as").

title: Immigration Status and Renting in the Northern Mariana Islands
bodyText: We found no Commonwealth statute, regulation or court rule that bars a landlord from asking about an applicant's immigration status, that protects immigrant tenants as such, or that makes it unlawful to rent to someone who is unlawfully present. Most of the Commonwealth's own immigration chapters, including a former immigration-status offense, have been repealed or deleted; federal immigration law, including its harboring rule, was not reviewed here. Two rules point toward caution. The Consumer Protection Act makes it an offense for a merchant to discriminate in commerce because of national origin, citizenship, or place of birth or residence, and this library treats every landlord as covered; the fair housing laws also bar national-origin discrimination. So don't refuse applicants, charge more, or set different terms because they aren't U.S. citizens, were born elsewhere, or hold a particular visa or status. If you verify identity or income, ask every applicant for the same kinds of documents and accept any reasonable form. Programs are different: the Northern Marianas Housing Corporation verifies citizenship or eligible immigration status for federal housing assistance under its own rules, and that check is the Corporation's, not the private landlord's. What to do: screen on rental history, income and references applied the same way to everyone, and don't ask about immigration status unless a program you participate in requires it.

title: Jury Waivers in Leases in the Northern Mariana Islands
bodyText: In the Commonwealth the right to a civil jury comes from statute, not the Constitution (which only lets the Legislature provide for jury trials). In an eviction (summary possession) case a jury trial is authorized and any party may demand one within five days after the case comes to issue; the party demanding a jury when a special panel must be summoned deposits the jury fees. In other civil cases over $1,000, parties are entitled to a jury on legal issues, and a party who doesn't make a proper, timely demand waives it under the court rules. We found no Commonwealth statute, regulation or court rule on a jury-trial or class-action waiver written into a lease or other consumer contract before any dispute, and no writing rule for waivers of constitutional rights. Whether such a waiver is enforceable turns on case law, which was not searched. Cautious course: don't rely on a lease clause that waives the tenant's right to a jury in a possession case or bars class actions; it could be treated as an unconscionable provision under the Consumer Protection Act, which expressly lets consumers bring class actions. If you include a mutual jury waiver anyway, make it conspicuous, mutual and separately initialed, and expect a court to look at it closely. What to do: leave jury rights to the court rules, and use the fast summary possession procedure as written.

title: Penalties for Unlawful Lease Terms in the Northern Mariana Islands
bodyText: The Commonwealth has no list of prohibited lease terms and no specific money penalty for knowingly using a lease that contains one. We found no Commonwealth statute, regulation or court rule of that kind. The Consumer Protection Act, which this library treats as reaching residential leasing, fills part of the gap. Inserting an unconscionable provision in a contract, or representing that a deal gives or involves rights or obligations it doesn't or that the law prohibits, is an unlawful practice. A tenant harmed by it can recover actual damages, an equal amount again if the violation was wilful (the Act's civil-penalty section defines wilful as knowing or having reason to know the conduct violated the Act; assume the same test applies here), and attorney's fees; the Attorney General can seek up to $2,500 per violation; and a merchant who knowingly or recklessly violates the Act can be fined up to $2,000 or jailed up to six months, each violation a separate offense. What to do: don't use lease terms that misstate Commonwealth or federal law (for example, waiving the ten-day deposit refund, allowing a lockout, or making the tenant pay your fees even if the tenant wins); the library's Commonwealth clauses are screened for this, so avoid adding your own one-sided terms.

title: Rules a Lease Cannot Change in the Northern Mariana Islands
bodyText: The Commonwealth has no general rule declaring tenant rights non-waivable, and no list of rights a lease may not waive; we found no Commonwealth statute, regulation or court rule of that kind. The Holdover Tenancy Act expressly leaves the parties free to add rights and duties in the rental agreement. But some rules apply whatever the lease says, because they are written as commands, protect the public, or are enforced by the courts or agencies. Treat these as rules your lease cannot change: (1) the three-day nonpayment notice must be in writing, in substantially the statutory form, and served by hand or, if the tenant is absent, left at the premises; (2) recover possession through the Superior Court (the summary procedure), never by lockout or self-help (our cautious course; self-help is a common-law question, Restatement not read); (3) the winning party in a Holdover Tenancy Act case, landlord or tenant, may recover reasonable costs and attorney's fees; (4) the security deposit balance must be refunded within ten days after the property is returned; (5) no rent increase while a Governor's price freeze is in effect; (6) fair housing protections, including reasonable accommodations; (7) federal lead-paint disclosure for pre-1978 housing and servicemember protections; (8) the annual Building Safety certificate and building and fire code duties; (9) the Article XII limit on leases over 55 years; and (10) the Consumer Protection Act's bar on terms that misstate rights or are unconscionable. By contrast, a few statutory defaults are expressly variable (rent timing, periodic-tenancy notice periods, and the non-rent cure notice and service method): see "edu-optional-lease-terms-mp". Where no statute speaks, the cautious course in this library is that the duty to keep the dwelling fit to live in and the bar on retaliation can't be waived (Restatement not read; case law not searched). What to do: don't write any of these rules out of the lease; use the library's Commonwealth clauses, which are built around them.

title: Plain Language Leases in the Northern Mariana Islands
bodyText: We found no Commonwealth plain-language or consumer-contract statute that reaches residential leases: no readability test, no rule that a lease be divided and captioned by sections, no front-page statement of landlord-protective terms, and no dollar threshold. The only plain-language rules in the Code are for car-rental damage waivers, where "plain language" means clear and coherent wording using words with common and everyday meanings, in at least ten-point bold type. Type-size and form rules also exist for self-storage agreements, not leases (see "edu-confirmed-absences-misc-mp"). Because the Consumer Protection Act is treated here as reaching residential leasing, and courts read any ambiguity in that Act in the consumer's favor, a confusing or hidden term carries risk even without a plain-language law. What to do: write the lease in plain English with headings for each section, put key money terms (rent, deposit, fees) near the start, and give the tenant time to read it before signing. Translating key terms for a tenant who reads Chamorro, Carolinian or another language better than English is good practice (see "edu-translation-duty-mp").

title: Consumer Restriction Statements in the Northern Mariana Islands
bodyText: We found no Commonwealth statute, regulation or court rule that requires a residential lease to pass a readability test, to carry a statement listing every waiver or restriction on the consumer, or that offers Attorney General preapproval of a lease form; and so there is no dollar exclusion either. The Consumer Protection Act's consumer counsel in the Attorney General's office enforces that Act generally but has no lease-preapproval program in the Code. See "edu-plain-language-mp" for the related absence and the cautious course: write the lease clearly, avoid hidden waivers, and make any term that limits the tenant's rights easy to find.

title: Pool Safety in the Northern Mariana Islands
bodyText: We found no Commonwealth statute or regulation requiring a residential landlord to fence a pool, install a barrier or alarm, or give tenants a pool-safety notice at signing. Pool rules here come from public health and lifeguard laws, and their reach depends on who uses the pool. Health permit: operating a "swimming pool" needs a sanitary permit from the environmental health office. A swimming pool means one used by the public or by the customers, clients, guests or employees of any person, including a community pool or a pool at a hotel, club or school; it does not include a private residential pool on private residential property under the direct control of the owner or lessee and used only by them, their family and guests. So a pool at a single-family rental used only by your tenant is outside the permit rule, but a shared pool at an apartment complex used by many tenants may be a "community pool" that needs one; that is unsettled, so ask the environmental health office in writing. Lifeguard: hotels and property owners using pools for commercial recreational purposes (charging guests for services) must have a qualified lifeguard on duty during open hours, or post signs saying no lifeguard is on duty when closed; a fine of up to $100 per violation applies. On Saipan, a pool so cloudy that the main drain can't be seen from the deck, or with missing or broken circulation or disinfection equipment, can be declared a nuisance under the blight law. The adopted building code's pool and barrier provisions (IBC 2018 and the International Residential Code it includes) were not reviewed here. What to do: fence and gate any pool you provide, keep water clear and equipment working, post pool rules and "no lifeguard on duty" signs at shared pools, and confirm in writing whether your pool needs a sanitary permit.

title: Prohibited Lease Terms in the Northern Mariana Islands
bodyText: The Commonwealth has no list of prohibited lease provisions. We found no Commonwealth statute, regulation or court rule that bans particular residential lease clauses as such (no confession-of-judgment ban, no exculpation or indemnity ban, no ban on passing home-warranty deductibles or repair fees to tenants, no list of "annullable" adhesion-contract clauses, and no rule voiding a lease because of when it was delivered). The Holdover Tenancy Act leaves the parties free to add terms. Limits come from other law, and together they work like a list: (1) the Consumer Protection Act, treated here as reaching residential leasing, makes it unlawful to insert an unconscionable provision or to represent that the deal confers rights or obligations it doesn't or that the law prohibits; (2) statutory rules a lease can't change (see "edu-part5-nonwaivable-mp"), so a clause contradicting them misstates the law; (3) Article XII voids a lease or option giving a long-term interest to someone not of Northern Marianas descent; (4) fair housing law bars discriminatory terms; and (5) where no statute speaks, the courts apply the Restatement (not read here), so the cautious course is not to rely on clauses excusing your own negligence, waiving habitability, or confessing judgment (see "edu-exculpatory-clauses-mp", "edu-confession-of-judgment-mp", "edu-habitability-waiver-mp"). Penalties are the Consumer Protection Act's (see "edu-knowing-use-penalty-mp"). Charging the tenant for repairs the tenant didn't cause isn't banned by statute, but under the cautious habitability course keep repair costs for ordinary wear and building systems with you. What to do: use the library's Commonwealth clauses, don't add one-sided penalties or waivers, and don't change a lease mid-term without the tenant's signature.

title: Questions About Protected Traits in the Northern Mariana Islands
bodyText: We found no Commonwealth statute, regulation or court rule that separately bans asking applicants about, or keeping records of, their race, religion, national origin, marital status, disability or other protected traits. The fair housing laws ban discrimination and any notice or statement that indicates a preference, limitation or discrimination based on those traits; an application form or interview question about a protected trait can be evidence of exactly that, and the Housing Corporation keeps such data only for its federal programs. Cautious course: don't ask applicants about race, color, religion, sex, national origin, ancestry, marital status, familial status (beyond who will live in the unit), disability or the nature or severity of a disability, age, citizenship, or place of birth; and don't keep notes about them. You may ask every applicant the same neutral questions (names and number of occupants, income, rental history), and where a tenant asks for a disability accommodation you may ask only for what is needed to verify the need when it isn't obvious (see "edu-disability-accommodation-mp"). What to do: review your application form and screening script against the protected classes in "edu-fair-housing-mp" and remove any question that isn't needed to decide whether the applicant can meet the lease.

title: Registered Sex Offenders as Tenants in the Northern Mariana Islands
bodyText: We found no Commonwealth statute, regulation or court rule that limits where a registered sex offender may live (for example, near schools or parks), that makes it a crime or a fine to rent to two offenders living together, or that gives a landlord a safe harbor for a lease statement. The CNMI Sex Offender Registry Act puts the duties on the offender: to register and to update in person any change of residence or temporary lodging. It is a crime, though, to knowingly harbor, or help harbor, an offender who is in violation of the Act, to help one evade police, or to give police false information about one. Housing Corporation voucher programs must deny assistance to any household member who is a registered sex offender, under the Corporation's own rules for federal assistance. For private rentals, the cautious course on screening is in "edu-tenant-screening-mp": apply any criminal-history policy the same way to everyone, and use the public registry rather than rumor (see "edu-stigmatized-property-mp"). What to do: you are not required to check the registry or to refuse a registered offender, but if you learn that a tenant or occupant is hiding from registration, don't help conceal them, and answer police questions truthfully.

title: Renting in Single-Family Zones in the Northern Mariana Islands
bodyText: We found no Commonwealth statute or regulation that limits renting a house in a single-family zone, or that requires the owner to live on the lot before renting. Zoning is local: on Saipan, the Saipan Zoning Law (adopted by reference and not reviewed here) sets the uses allowed in each district, and the Zoning Board's regulations we reviewed deal with other matters (such as limiting ATV and motorcycle rental businesses to rural districts) rather than residential rentals. Tinian and Rota have their own local laws. Commonwealth rules still reach a rented house: it needs the annual Building Safety Certificate of Compliance as a "residential rental" (the regulation expressly includes single-family houses and Airbnb-type rentals; see "edu-rental-inspection-mp"), a change of use needs Building Safety approval, and a house built under a free owner-builder permit is defined as one no part of which is rented (see "edu-accessory-dwelling-unit-mp"). What to do: before renting a house, check its zoning district and any conditional-use rules with the Zoning Office (on Saipan) or the municipality, and get the annual certificate.

title: Source of Income and Vouchers in the Northern Mariana Islands
bodyText: We found no Commonwealth statute, regulation or court rule that protects tenants because of their source of income, requires landlords to accept housing vouchers (Section 8) or other rental assistance, or requires a lease statement about it. So a private landlord in the Commonwealth may decide whether to take part in the Northern Marianas Housing Corporation's voucher program. Cautions: don't use "no Section 8" or similar as a stand-in for refusing a protected group, for example families with children or people with disabilities, because a neutral-sounding policy used to exclude a protected group can still be discrimination under the fair housing laws (case law not searched; see "edu-fair-housing-mp"); and if a voucher is needed as a reasonable accommodation for a person with a disability, consider it on its merits (see "edu-disability-accommodation-mp"). If you do accept a voucher, federal rules apply: the lease must be in writing and signed, must name the parties, unit, term, rent and who supplies which utilities and appliances, and the HUD tenancy addendum must be added word for word and controls over any other lease term; rent changes need 60 days' notice to the Housing Corporation. What to do: decide your voucher policy in advance, apply it the same way to everyone, and if you participate, attach the HUD tenancy addendum to the library's lease.

title: Radiator Covers in the Northern Mariana Islands
bodyText: Steam radiator covers don't arise in the Northern Mariana Islands: the islands are tropical, buildings aren't heated by steam or radiators, and we found no Commonwealth statute, regulation or court rule on radiator covers, steam heat or a lease rider about them (see "edu-heating-mp"). If a unit has any hot surface a child could touch (for example, an exposed water heater or generator), the general cautious course on keeping the dwelling safe applies, and the library's maintenance clauses cover it. Nothing to add to the lease.

title: Inspections in Voucher Units in the Northern Mariana Islands
bodyText: If your unit is rented under the Northern Marianas Housing Corporation's voucher program, its rules govern inspections. The assisted family must allow the Corporation to inspect the unit at reasonable times after reasonable notice, as a condition of staying in the program, and the family is responsible for housing quality breaches it causes. The unit must meet federal Housing Quality Standards throughout the tenancy and is inspected at least annually (and quarterly under the Corporation's rules). Federal rules require you to correct a life-threatening deficiency within 24 hours of notice and others within 30 calendar days (or an approved extension); damage the family or a guest causes beyond ordinary wear and tear is the family's responsibility. If you don't correct a violation, the Corporation must stop (abate) its payments to you: after 24 hours for a life-threatening violation and after 30 days for a routine one, unless it extends the time, with 30 days' written notice of the abatement for non-emergency items; six months of abatement terminates the payment contract. We found no Commonwealth rule on what happens when a tenant in a private (unsubsidized) rental refuses a government inspection such as the annual Building Safety inspection; the fire regulations let the fire officials seek a warrant if an owner or occupant refuses entry. A tenant's refusal to let you or an inspector in is a lease matter: use the library's access clause and, if the refusal is a material breach, the non-rent cure notice (see "edu-cure-and-eviction-grounds-mp"). What to do: in voucher units, tell the Corporation promptly if a tenant blocks an inspection so the refusal isn't treated as your failure, and fix any deficiency within the time the notice gives.

title: Keeping Tenant Information Private in the Northern Mariana Islands
bodyText: We found no Commonwealth statute, regulation or court rule that bars a private landlord from disclosing a tenant's or applicant's information, or that sets a consent rule for sharing it, and no data-security or breach-notification law for businesses (see "edu-tenant-records-mp"). The Constitution's privacy clause and the confidentiality rules we found bind the government and its agencies (for example, the Housing Corporation keeps its own applicants' information confidential), not private landlords; whether the privacy clause reaches private persons was not researched. Commonwealth law does recognize that invasion of privacy can be a tort (the single-publication rule refers to it), but the elements come from common law, which this library has not read. Federal credit-reporting rules do reach you in one respect: if you keep credit or tenant-screening report information for a business purpose, you must dispose of it by reasonable measures that protect against unauthorized access, such as shredding papers and wiping electronic files (see also "edu-tenant-screening-mp"), and information about domestic violence deserves special care (see "edu-dv-confidentiality-mp"). Cautious course: share a tenant's personal, financial or payment information only with the tenant's written consent, with your own agents and service providers who need it, or when the law or a court requires it; give references limited to facts (dates of tenancy, rent amount, payment record); and store applications and ID copies securely and shred them when no longer needed. What to do: put a short consent line in your application for the checks you will run and the references you will give, and stick to it.

title: Employee Housing in the Northern Mariana Islands
bodyText: Housing you give an employee is governed mainly by Commonwealth labor law, not by a landlord-tenant statute. Employers of foreign national workers may, but need not, provide housing, and may not require a worker to use it. If you do provide employee housing, the Department of Labor applies the U.S. Department of Labor's employer-supplied housing standards as the minimum unless you get a variance; Labor inspectors may inspect it (the federal standards' detailed requirements were not reviewed here); you may not require a worker to stay in the housing outside working hours or punish a refusal; and wage deductions for housing are limited (a non-business employer, such as a household employer, may deduct up to $100 a month for housing). Benefits the law mandates for non-resident workers (the regulation names housing among its examples) must also be given, in kind or in cash, to resident workers in jobs paying less than the federal minimum wage (or $5.15 an hour, if higher); because employer housing is optional, whether this reaches housing you choose to provide is unclear, so ask the Department of Labor. Staff houses and barracks may also need a sanitary permit (see "edu-health-district-rental-rules-mp"). We found no Commonwealth rule requiring a signed disclosure of the conditions for occupying and vacating employee housing, an offer of a regular rental agreement when the job ends, or a rent agreement filed with the government; and no rule making a sponsor answer for a worker's rent. Whether the Holdover Tenancy Act's summary procedure reaches an employee or caretaker who occupies only as part of the job is unsettled (it covers tenancies and those holding under a tenant); case law not searched. Housing on public land leases is limited (see "edu-communal-land-lease-approval-mp"). What to do: put employee housing terms in writing (who may live there, any charge, what happens when employment ends, and a reasonable time to leave), keep the housing to the labor standards, and if an ex-employee won't leave, get legal advice and use the court rather than self-help.

title: Tenant Organizing in the Northern Mariana Islands
bodyText: We found no Commonwealth statute, regulation or court rule giving private-housing tenants a right to form or join a tenant association, or barring a landlord from interfering with one. The Constitution's speech and assembly clause limits the government ("No law shall be made ..."), not private landlords. The Housing Corporation's own public-housing rules give resident organizations a role (for example, commenting on hearing officers), but those apply only to its programs. Two rules point toward caution: the fair housing laws make it unlawful to coerce, intimidate or interfere with anyone who helps or encourages others to exercise fair housing rights, which can include a tenants' group raising discrimination complaints; and this library's cautious course is not to retaliate against tenants for lawful complaints or organizing (see "edu-retaliation-mp"). What to do: don't end tenancies, raise rent or cut services because tenants meet, organize or complain together; you may set neutral, reasonable rules for using common rooms that apply to everyone (see "edu-common-area-use-mp" and "edu-political-access-mp").

title: Tenant Screening in the Northern Mariana Islands
bodyText: The Commonwealth has no tenant-screening statute: we found no rule limiting criminal-history checks to after a conditional offer, no look-back periods, no cap on minimum-income tests, no screening-fee limit, no negligence shield for renting to someone with a record, and no special rule for tax-credit properties. What does apply: (1) Fair housing: screen by the same written criteria for everyone and don't screen on race, color, religion, sex, familial status, marital status, disability or national origin, or, cautiously, on age, citizenship or place of birth or residence (see "edu-fair-housing-mp"). (2) Cleared records: an applicant whose first-offense drug case was discharged and expunged, whose juvenile record was expunged, or whose conviction was set aside after probation may answer as if it never happened, so don't treat their "no" as a lie or deny them for that record (see "edu-rental-application-accuracy-mp"). (3) Federal credit-reporting law: if you deny an application or take other adverse action against an applicant based even partly on a credit or tenant-screening report, you must give the adverse-action notice (the agency's name, address and phone number, that the agency didn't make the decision, and the right to a free report within 60 days and to dispute it) (see "edu-tenant-records-mp"). (4) Housing Corporation voucher programs run their own criminal-background screening; a private landlord's own screening is separate. What to do: write down your criteria (income, rental history, any criminal-history policy limited to recent, relevant offenses), apply them consistently, keep the reasons for each decision, and send the federal notice whenever a report affects the outcome.

title: Unconscionable Lease Terms in the Northern Mariana Islands
bodyText: There is no unconscionability rule written for residential leases in the Commonwealth, but three statutes use the idea. (1) The Consumer Protection Act lists "inserting an unconscionable provision in a contract" as an unlawful practice; this library treats the Act as reaching residential leasing, so an unconscionable lease term exposes you to damages (doubled if wilful), attorney's fees and penalties. (2) The Uniform Condominium Act lets a court refuse to enforce, cut out, or limit an unconscionable contract or clause, after hearing evidence about the setting, whether one side knowingly took advantage of the other's infirmity, illiteracy or inability to understand the language of the agreement, and the clause's purpose and effect; whether that reaches a lease of a condominium unit is unsettled. (3) The commercial code has a similar rule for sales of goods, which doesn't reach leases of real property. We found no Commonwealth rule letting a court revise or end a running lease because circumstances made it excessively onerous, and no statute declaring any particular lease clause fully enforceable. Where no statute speaks, the courts apply the Restatements (not read here; case law not searched). What to do: avoid one-sided penalties, forfeitures and waivers; make sure a tenant who reads English poorly understands key terms; and keep fees tied to real costs.

title: Veterans Rental Incentives in the Northern Mariana Islands
bodyText: We found no Commonwealth statute, regulation or court rule giving landlords a tax credit, fee waiver or other incentive for renting to veterans, and none that requires or regulates a veterans' rent discount or preference in private housing. Commonwealth veterans' benefits are in other areas: a voluntary veterans' preference in private employment, a veterans' preference in government hiring, vehicle-registration discounts and plates, and tuition waivers for disabled veterans. The Housing Corporation's HOME and disaster-recovery programs bar discrimination on military status in those programs only. Federal servicemember protections (lease termination on orders, default judgments) apply to active-duty tenants (see "edu-servicemember-rights-mp"). What to do: you may offer a voluntary veterans' discount if you like, since no Commonwealth law bars it, but offer it the same way to all eligible veterans and don't let it become a way to prefer or exclude a protected group.

title: Water Heater Temperature in the Northern Mariana Islands
bodyText: We found no Commonwealth statute or regulation that requires a landlord to set a unit's water heater to a maximum temperature, or to reset it at each new occupancy. The only hot-water temperature limit we found is for schools and child-care facilities, where hot water at hand-washing sinks may be no hotter than 120 °F. Plumbing and energy code rules on water heaters come through the adopted International Building Code family of codes, whose text this library has not reviewed. Cautious course: under the general duty to keep the dwelling safe, set tank water heaters to about 120 °F at each turnover (hot enough for use, low enough to reduce scald risk), keep the temperature-and-pressure relief valve and its discharge line working, and tell tenants how to adjust the setting safely; the library's maintenance clauses cover the equipment. What to do: add a water-heater check (temperature, relief valve, leaks) to your move-in inspection.

title: Window Guards and Grilles in the Northern Mariana Islands
bodyText: We found no Commonwealth statute or regulation that requires landlords to install window guards to prevent children's falls, or to give a window-guard notice in the lease (bold or otherwise). The Commonwealth rule runs the other way: the Building Safety Official may prohibit installing certain grilled windows (window grilles or security bars) found to be a fire safety hazard, because bars can trap people inside in a fire. The Housing Corporation's rehabilitation inspection checklist also treats security bars that prevent escape as a deficiency. The adopted International Building Code's emergency escape opening and window-sill rules were not reviewed here. Cautious course: if you install grilles or security bars on bedroom or other windows, use ones that open from inside without a key or special tool, and keep them unlocked from inside; where young children live in upper-floor units, consider fall-prevention devices that still allow emergency release. What to do: check grilled windows during the annual Building Safety inspection, and fix any that can't be opened from inside.

title: Checks Marked 'Paid in Full'
bodyText: The Northern Mariana Islands never adopted the revised Uniform Commercial Code rule on checks marked 'paid in full': its commercial-paper law is the older version, with no section on settling a claim by cashing such a check. Its reservation-of-rights rule (5 CMC § 1207) also lacks the later sentence saying it does not apply to an accord and satisfaction, and courts elsewhere have split on whether cashing a full-payment check 'under protest' under that older rule keeps the balance. Where no written law applies, the Commonwealth follows the common law as the American Law Institute's Restatements express it (7 CMC § 3401), under which cashing a check offered in full satisfaction of a genuinely disputed claim can settle it; no Commonwealth case on this has been reviewed. The cautious course: don't cash a check for less than you claim that is marked as payment in full of a disputed amount; return it uncashed.

title: Duty of Good Faith
bodyText: The Northern Mariana Islands' landlord-tenant statutes impose no general duty of good faith of the kind in the Uniform Residential Landlord and Tenant Act (the Holdover Tenancy Act (the Commonwealth has no residential landlord-tenant act) searched); good faith appears only in specific rules. Courts in many states read a covenant of good faith and fair dealing into every contract, a lease included; whether and how the Northern Mariana Islands' courts do is case law this library has not reviewed, so act as if the duty applies. In practice: give notices, enter, handle the deposit, enforce lease terms and end a tenancy honestly and for the purpose the law or the lease gives you the right, not as a pretext.
